stem: Fifteen minutes after starting a packed red blood cell transfusion, a client reports chills and new flank pain. Temperature has risen from 36.8°C to 38.2°C. After the nurse stops the transfusion, which concurrent action is most appropriate?
options:
A) Flush the blood tubing with the remaining packed cells to clear the line.
B) Keep the intravenous line open with normal saline using new tubing, and notify the blood bank.
C) Restart the same unit at a slower rate after giving acetaminophen.
D) Discard the blood bag immediately so it cannot be returned for investigation.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. The transfusion must remain stopped; continuing to infuse residual cells from the implicated unit risks further hemolysis.
B: Correct. For suspected transfusion reaction (fever, chills, flank pain), stop the transfusion, keep venous access open with normal saline, and send the remaining product and samples to the blood bank for investigation.
C: Incorrect. The same unit must not be restarted. Febrile symptoms can herald acute hemolytic reaction and require investigation first.
D: Incorrect. The remainder of the blood product is needed for blood-bank investigation; it should not be discarded.
topic: Transfusion reaction — stop infusion and keep IV open with saline
source_2_section: Transfusion Reactions; Managing a Blood or Blood Product Transfusion Reaction

stem: A postoperative client has brisk wound drainage into a surgical drain. The client is anxious. Capillary refill is delayed, skin is cool and clammy, heart rate is 118 beats/min, and blood pressure is 118/78 mm Hg. Which interpretation best fits these findings?
options:
A) Early compensatory response to hypovolemia; tachycardia can precede frank hypotension.
B) Cardiogenic shock is most likely because blood pressure is still near the client's baseline.
C) Findings are reassuring; hypovolemic shock is excluded until systolic blood pressure falls below 90 mm Hg.
D) Neurogenic shock is most likely because the client is anxious after surgery.
rationales:
A: Correct. In early hypovolemic compensation, sympathetic activation raises heart rate and vascular tone; blood pressure may remain normal or only slightly changed while tachycardia, cool clammy skin, and anxiety appear.
B: Incorrect. Cardiogenic shock involves pump failure; this picture of volume loss with compensatory tachycardia fits hypovolemia, not a primary cardiac pump problem.
C: Incorrect. Hypotension is common in shock but is not required early; clients may be normotensive while compensation is still effective.
D: Incorrect. Neurogenic shock typically features bradycardia and warm dry skin from loss of sympathetic tone, not compensatory tachycardia with cool clammy skin.
topic: Hypovolemic shock — early compensatory tachycardia
source_1_section: Pathophysiology of Shock; Etiology — Hypovolemic shock; Compensation
source_2_section: Pathophysiology of Hypovolemic Shock; Clinical Manifestations

stem: At a preconception visit in Canada, a client who could become pregnant asks what daily folic acid dose is recommended to help prevent neural tube defects, assuming no high-risk history. Which teaching is correct?
options:
A) Take a daily multivitamin that provides 0.4 mg (400 mcg) of folic acid.
B) Take 4 mg of folic acid daily without speaking with a health-care provider.
C) Folic acid is needed only after the pregnancy is confirmed on ultrasound.
D) Dietary folate alone is sufficient; a supplement is unnecessary for most people.
rationales:
A: Correct. PHAC and Merck advise a daily multivitamin with 0.4 mg (400 mcg) folic acid for people who could become pregnant, to reduce neural tube defect risk.
B: Incorrect. Higher doses (for example, about 4 mg) are reserved for selected higher-risk situations and require provider guidance; routine self-escalation is not advised.
C: Incorrect. Neural tube closure occurs in the first weeks of pregnancy, often before pregnancy is recognized; supplementation should start before conception when possible.
D: Incorrect. Diet alone is not enough to reach the folic acid level needed for neural tube defect prevention; a supplement is recommended.
topic: Folic acid — 0.4 mg daily for neural tube defect prevention
jurisdiction_note: Keyed to PHAC healthy-pregnancy guidance (0.4 mg daily multivitamin). Merck recommends 400–800 mcg, which includes the Canadian 0.4 mg teaching point.
source_1_title: Your Guide to a Healthy Pregnancy — Folic acid
source_1_publisher: Public Health Agency of Canada / Canada.ca

stem: An Ontario nurse reviews what must be included for consent to treatment to be informed under the Health Care Consent Act and CNO Consent guideline. Which pieces of information must be provided? Select all that apply.
options:
A) The nature of the proposed treatment
B) The expected benefits of the treatment
C) The material risks and material side effects of the treatment
D) Alternative courses of action
E) The likely consequences of not having the treatment
F) A guarantee that the treatment will succeed
rationales:
A: Correct. Informed consent requires information about the nature of the treatment.
B: Correct. Expected benefits must be explained.
C: Correct. Material risks and material side effects must be disclosed.
D: Correct. Alternative courses of action must be included.
E: Correct. Likely consequences of declining the treatment must be included.
F: Incorrect. Neither the HCCA nor CNO requires a guarantee of success; promising certainty is not an element of informed consent.
topic: Informed consent — required information elements (HCCA/CNO)
jurisdiction_note: Elements keyed to Ontario HCCA s. 11 and CNO Consent practice guideline (updated July 2025).
source_2_section: s. 11 — Elements of consent; Informed consent

stem: An RN is organizing care with an unregulated care provider (UCP/assistive personnel). Which activity must the RN retain and NOT delegate?
options:
A) Assisting a stable client to the bathroom after the RN has assessed mobility
B) Delivering a meal tray to a client who is able to feed themselves
C) Performing the initial assessment of a newly admitted client who has new chest pain
D) Reminding a stable client to use an incentive spirometer as previously taught
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Assisting with toileting for a stable client after nursing assessment can be an appropriate delegated/assigned supportive task when policy and competence allow.
B: Incorrect. Routine delivery of a meal tray does not require nursing judgment and may be assigned to assistive personnel.
C: Correct. Clinical reasoning, nursing judgment, and critical decision-making — including assessing a new symptomatic client — cannot be delegated.
D: Incorrect. Reminding a stable client to use previously taught incentive spirometry is a supportive task that does not transfer nursing judgment.
topic: Delegation — nursing judgment cannot be delegated
jurisdiction_note: Uses NCSBN/ANA national delegation guidelines and OpenStax; Ontario nurses must also follow CNO/employer scope rules (not separately keyed).

stem: A client is newly identified as colonized with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) on a wound swab. The client has no cough. In addition to routine/standard practices and hand hygiene, which precautions should the nurse initiate for direct care?
options:
A) Airborne precautions with an N95 respirator as the only required PPE
B) Contact precautions, including gown and gloves for direct care
C) Droplet precautions alone, with a surgical mask and no gown
D) No additional precautions; colonization never requires PPE beyond hand hygiene
rationales:
A: Incorrect. MRSA is not managed with airborne precautions; N95-only airborne precautions are for pathogens such as tuberculosis.
B: Correct. CDC and Ontario PHO guidance place MRSA on Contact Precautions; gown and gloves are used for direct care in addition to hand hygiene.
C: Incorrect. Droplet precautions alone are not the baseline for MRSA colonization without a specified respiratory indication.
D: Incorrect. Colonized as well as infected clients with MRSA warrant Contact Precautions in acute care settings per CDC; PHO likewise lists MRSA under Contact Precautions.
topic: MRSA — Contact Precautions with gown and gloves
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
jurisdiction_note: PHO clinical syndromes list Contact (+ Droplet if sputum/coughing). Stem specifies no cough so Contact is keyed; CDC recommends Contact Precautions for MRSA colonization/infection.
source_1_title: Infection Control Guidance: Preventing MRSA in Healthcare Facilities
source_1_publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
source_1_section: For acute care settings: Contact Precautions
source_1_source_date: Updated Nov 24, 2026 (page also notes Published May 15, 2024)
source_2_title: Infection Prevention and Control for Home and Community Care
source_2_section: Contact Precautions — Antibiotic Resistant Organisms / MRSA

stem: A client who received IV morphine becomes difficult to arouse. Respirations are 6 breaths/min and shallow. After supporting the airway and calling for help, which medication should the nurse prepare to reverse the opioid effect?
options:
A) Flumazenil
B) Naloxone
C) Acetylcysteine
D) Protamine sulfate
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Flumazenil antagonizes benzodiazepines, not opioids.
B: Correct. Naloxone is an opioid antagonist indicated to reverse opioid-induced respiratory depression and overdose.
C: Incorrect. Acetylcysteine is the antidote used for acetaminophen toxicity, not opioid overdose.
D: Incorrect. Protamine is used to reverse heparin anticoagulation, not opioid effects.
topic: Naloxone — reverse opioid-induced respiratory depression
source_2_title: Naloxone Hydrochloride Injection USP — Product Monograph

stem: A client rates postoperative pain as 8 on a 0–10 numeric scale while talking calmly with visitors. Vital signs are near baseline. Which nursing action best reflects evidence-based pain assessment?
options:
A) Document the pain as mild because the client is conversing calmly.
B) Accept the client's self-report of pain intensity and proceed with the pain-management plan.
C) Withhold analgesia until vital signs show tachycardia and hypertension.
D) Ask visitors to leave and reassess only after the client appears distressed.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Calm behaviour does not override a client's reported intensity; pain is subjective and may not show outward distress.
B: Correct. Pain is a subjective experience; the client's report should be respected and used to guide management.
C: Incorrect. Vital-sign changes are inconsistent markers and are not required before treating reported pain.
D: Incorrect. Delaying care until visible distress appears dismisses the client's report and is not therapeutic.
topic: Pain assessment — respect client self-report

stem: A client with known left-sided heart failure reports increasing shortness of breath when lying flat and needs three pillows to sleep. On auscultation, the nurse hears early inspiratory basilar crackles that do not clear with coughing. Which problem do these findings best indicate?
options:
A) Pulmonary congestion from elevated left-sided filling pressures
B) Isolated right-sided failure with systemic venous congestion only
C) Community-acquired pneumonia as the only plausible explanation
D) Acute hypovolemia from inadequate oral fluid intake
rationales:
A: Correct. Left-sided failure causes dyspnea, orthopnea, and pulmonary findings such as basilar crackles from elevated pulmonary venous pressures and pulmonary edema.
B: Incorrect. Isolated right-sided failure more classically produces systemic congestion (for example, jugular venous distention, peripheral edema) rather than orthopnea with pulmonary crackles as the primary picture.
C: Incorrect. Pneumonia can cause crackles, but orthopnea with known left-sided HF and non-clearing basilar crackles fits pulmonary congestion from HF; pneumonia is not the only or best explanation here.
D: Incorrect. Hypovolemia would not explain orthopnea with pulmonary crackles; HF congestion reflects fluid backing into the lungs.
topic: Left-sided heart failure — orthopnea and pulmonary crackles

stem: A client receiving a unit of packed red blood cells develops sudden dyspnea, fever, and back pain. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order from first to last.
options:
A) Notify the health-care provider and the blood bank, and send the remaining product and required blood samples for investigation.
B) Stop the transfusion immediately.
C) Maintain intravenous access with normal saline (new tubing as per protocol).
D) Document the event and continue close monitoring of vital signs and urine output.
rationales:
B: Correct (first). Stopping the transfusion immediately is the priority when a reaction is suspected.
C: Correct (second). Keep the IV line open with normal saline so access is preserved for treatment and sampling.
A: Correct (third). After the infusion is stopped and access secured, notify the provider/blood bank and send the product and samples for investigation.
D: Correct (fourth). Documentation and ongoing monitoring continue after immediate safety and reporting steps.
topic: Transfusion reaction — priority action sequence
source_2_section: What If Your Patient Experiences a Transfusion Reaction?; Managing a Blood or Blood Product Transfusion Reaction

stem: A client is on the first postoperative day after open abdominal surgery. Oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. Breath sounds are diminished at both bases. Which nursing action best helps reduce the risk of atelectasis?
options:
A) Encourage the client to remain flat in bed to conserve oxygen.
B) Coach the client to use an incentive spirometer and take deep breaths with coughing as tolerated.
C) Withhold prescribed analgesia so the client will not become sedated.
D) Limit oral fluids until the lungs are fully clear on auscultation.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Prolonged supine rest and limited lung expansion increase atelectasis risk after abdominal surgery.
B: Correct. Postoperative clients are at risk for atelectasis; lung-expansion measures such as incentive spirometry, deep breathing, and coughing (with adequate analgesia) help reopen collapsed alveoli and clear secretions.
C: Incorrect. Uncontrolled incision pain impairs deep breathing and coughing; adequate analgesia supports pulmonary expansion rather than being withheld.
D: Incorrect. Restricting fluids is not a standard measure to prevent atelectasis and does not expand alveoli.
topic: Postoperative atelectasis prevention — incentive spirometry and deep breathing
source_1_section: Treatment of Atelectasis; Prevention of Atelectasis

stem: An older adult client is admitted after a fall at home. The client is oriented but unsteady when standing. Which intervention is most appropriate to reduce in-hospital fall risk?
options:
A) Raise all four bed rails and apply a waist restraint so the client cannot leave the bed.
B) Keep the bed at its lowest position when care is not being given, clear pathways, and place the call light within reach.
C) Encourage the client to walk alone to the bathroom at night to rebuild confidence.
D) Administer a routine bedtime hypnotic to keep the client asleep until morning.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Physical restraints and routinely raised bed rails can increase agitation and fall injury risk; restraints should generally not be used as a fall-prevention strategy.
B: Correct. Evidence-based fall-risk reduction includes keeping the bed low when not providing care, removing clutter and hazards from pathways, and ensuring the client can call for help.
C: Incorrect. Unsupervised nighttime ambulation to the bathroom is a common setting for hospital falls in older adults.
D: Incorrect. Hypnotics and sedatives increase fall and delirium risk in older adults and should be minimized.
topic: Hospital fall prevention — low bed, clear pathways, avoid restraints
source_2_section: Prevention of Falls and Injury Mitigation — Environmental and situational management

stem: Immediately after a term vaginal birth, the vigorous newborn is placed on the birthing person's chest. Which nursing action best prevents evaporative heat loss in the first minutes of life?
options:
A) Delay drying until the first bath so vernix can protect the skin.
B) Dry the newborn thoroughly and then keep the infant covered or in skin-to-skin contact.
C) Place the wet newborn under a fan to promote convective cooling.
D) Leave the newborn uncovered on a cool scale for an immediate accurate weight.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Amniotic fluid on the skin causes evaporative heat loss; drying should not be delayed for that reason in the delivery setting.
B: Correct. Evaporative heat loss occurs as wet amniotic fluid vaporizes; immediate drying followed by covering or skin-to-skin contact is a primary prevention step for neonatal hypothermia.
C: Incorrect. Forced cool airflow increases convective heat loss and is opposite of thermal protection.
D: Incorrect. Contact with a cool surface and prolonged exposure promote conductive and radiant heat loss.
topic: Newborn thermoregulation — prevent evaporative heat loss by drying
source_1_section: Prevention of Hypothermia in Neonates; Key Points

stem: A postpartum client has Rh-negative blood and is not already sensitized. The newborn's blood type is Rh-positive. Which action is indicated?
options:
A) Administer Rho(D) immune globulin within 72 hours of birth.
B) Withhold Rho(D) immune globulin because sensitization only occurs in subsequent pregnancies and never after the first birth.
C) Give Rho(D) immune globulin only if the client's direct Coombs test is already positive.
D) Delay Rho(D) immune globulin until the 6-week postpartum visit so antibodies can form first.
rationales:
A: Correct. An unsensitized Rh-negative parent who delivers an Rh-positive newborn should receive Rho(D) immune globulin, typically within 72 hours, to prevent alloimmunization that could harm future pregnancies.
B: Incorrect. Fetomaternal hemorrhage at birth can sensitize the parent after the current pregnancy; postpartum prophylaxis exists to prevent that sensitization.
C: Incorrect. Prophylaxis is for clients who are not already sensitized; a positive antibody screen indicating sensitization changes management and is not the indication for routine Rho(D) immune globulin.
D: Incorrect. Waiting weeks allows time for sensitization; the standard window is within 72 hours after birth.
topic: Postpartum Rh immune globulin within 72 hours
source_1_section: Postpartum Preventive Care — Prevention of Rh sensitization
source_2_title: 20.3 Nursing Care During the Postpartum Period

stem: A client with alcohol use disorder is beginning medically supervised withdrawal. Which interventions are appropriate components of withdrawal care? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Administer prescribed benzodiazepines based on withdrawal severity.
B) Give thiamine to help prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
C) Start routine daily phenytoin for every client even without a seizure disorder.
D) Use haloperidol alone as the first medication for autonomic hyperactivity.
E) Continue high-dose benzodiazepines indefinitely after detoxification for craving control.
rationales:
A: Correct. Benzodiazepines are the mainstay for alcohol-withdrawal agitation and seizure prevention.
B: Correct. Thiamine is given during withdrawal care to help prevent Wernicke encephalopathy associated with thiamine deficiency.
C: Incorrect. Routine phenytoin is not indicated for uncomplicated alcohol-withdrawal seizures.
D: Incorrect. Antipsychotics are not recommended as initial monotherapy and may lower the seizure threshold.
E: Incorrect. Benzodiazepines used for detoxification should not continue after the detoxification period.
topic: Alcohol withdrawal care — benzodiazepines and thiamine
source_1_section: Treatment of Alcohol Toxicity and Withdrawal — Withdrawal
source_2_section: Treatment for Withdrawal from Alcohol Use

stem: An 78-year-old hospitalized client develops sudden confusion that worsens at night, has difficulty focusing attention, and returns nearly to baseline later the same day. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options:
A) Findings are typical of Alzheimer dementia because cognition declined overnight.
B) Findings suggest delirium: an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition that warrants evaluation for a medical cause.
C) Fluctuating attention excludes delirium and confirms a primary psychotic disorder.
D) No further assessment is needed once orientation returns briefly to baseline.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Dementia typically has a more gradual course and primarily affects memory; an abrupt, fluctuating inattention pattern is characteristic of delirium, which can occur in people with or without underlying dementia.
B: Correct. Delirium is an acute, usually reversible, fluctuating disturbance in attention, cognition, and consciousness that often signals an underlying medical problem and requires prompt evaluation.
C: Incorrect. Fluctuating attention is a hallmark of delirium, not a finding that excludes it.
D: Incorrect. Temporary clearing does not remove the need to identify and treat the precipitating cause.
topic: Delirium — acute fluctuating disturbance of attention

stem: A client is admitted with suspected seasonal influenza and is placed on Droplet Precautions in a private room. Which personal protective equipment action is required when the nurse enters the room for routine care?
options:
A) Don a fit-tested N95 respirator and keep the door closed at all times as for airborne isolation.
B) Don a facemask upon room entry and remove it after leaving the room, with hand hygiene.
C) Enter without a mask if standing more than one metre from the client.
D) Wear sterile gloves and a sterile gown for every entry, even without anticipated contact with body fluids.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Seasonal influenza is managed with Droplet Precautions; an N95 and airborne (negative-pressure) setup are not the routine requirement for standard droplet care.
B: Correct. For Droplet Precautions, including suspected or confirmed influenza, health-care personnel don a facemask on room entry and remove/dispose of it on exit with hand hygiene.
C: Incorrect. Guidance directs masking upon entry into the droplet precaution space, not only during close contact at an arbitrary distance.
D: Incorrect. Sterile gown and sterile gloves are not the droplet PPE standard for routine entry; gown/gloves follow Standard Precautions when contact with body fluids is anticipated.
topic: Droplet Precautions — mask on room entry for influenza
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_1_title: Infection Prevention and Control Strategies for Seasonal Influenza in Healthcare Settings
source_1_publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

stem: A nurse in Ontario finishes documenting for an assigned client. A colleague asks the nurse to look up laboratory results in the electronic record of a neighbour who is not on the nurse's assignment and for whom the nurse has no care role. Which response best meets confidentiality and privacy accountabilities?
options:
A) Access the neighbour's chart briefly because curiosity among staff is an accepted professional purpose.
B) Decline to access the record, explaining that personal health information may be accessed only when needed for an authorized care purpose.
C) Print the full chart and leave it at the nursing station so anyone on the unit can answer questions.
D) Share the neighbour's results aloud in the cafeteria so the colleague does not need system access.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Accessing a record without a professional care purpose violates CNO confidentiality standards and PHIPA limits on collection and use.
B: Correct. Nurses must access only the personal health information needed for an authorized purpose; PHIPA requires that no more personal health information be collected, used, or disclosed than is reasonably necessary.
C: Incorrect. Leaving identifiable charts available for unnecessary viewing increases unauthorized access risk.
D: Incorrect. Discussing client information in public places such as cafeterias breaches confidentiality.
topic: Confidentiality — access PHI only for authorized care purpose
jurisdiction_note: Keyed to CNO Confidentiality and Privacy practice standard and Ontario PHIPA s. 30 limiting collection/use/disclosure to what is reasonably necessary. US HIPAA has analogous minimization concepts but this item is framed for Ontario practice.
source_1_title: Confidentiality and Privacy — Personal Health Information
source_2_title: Personal Health Information Protection Act, 2004, S.O. 2004, c. 3, Sched. A
source_2_section: s. 30 Other information — limiting collection, use and disclosure

stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has severe neutropenia. The client reports feeling unwell. Oral temperature is 38.5°C. There is no obvious focus of infection on brief examination. Which action is the priority?
options:
A) Document the temperature and reassess in 4 hours before notifying the provider.
B) Recognize fever as a presumed serious infection and promptly notify the provider so empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics can be started.
C) Encourage fresh fruit and a floral arrangement to improve nutrition and mood while awaiting culture results.
D) Hold all antimicrobial therapy until a definitive organism is identified on culture.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. In severe neutropenia, fever is treated as a medical emergency; waiting hours delays needed empiric therapy.
B: Correct. When severe neutropenia is present, fever usually indicates infection even if a focus is not obvious, and immediate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics are required.
C: Incorrect. Neutropenic precautions include avoiding fresh fruit and fresh flowers because of infection risk; these are not supportive measures during febrile neutropenia.
D: Incorrect. Empiric antibiotics are started promptly; waiting for culture identification is unsafe in febrile neutropenia.
topic: Febrile neutropenia — fever warrants prompt empiric antibiotics
units_note: Temperature reported in °C (38.5°C).
source_1_section: Overview; Treatment of Neutropenia — Acute neutropenia
source_2_section: Clinical Manifestations; Prioritizing Hypotheses, Generating Solutions, and Taking Action

stem: An ambulatory adult client reports hard stools every 4 to 5 days and abdominal bloating. The nurse is teaching nonpharmacologic measures to promote bowel regularity. Which instruction is most appropriate?
options:
A) Restrict oral fluids so the stool becomes firmer and easier to pass.
B) Increase dietary fibre and fluid intake and maintain regular physical activity.
C) Remain on bed rest until bowel movements return to once daily.
D) Stop eating fruits and vegetables to reduce intestinal gas and bloating.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Adequate hydration softens stool; restricting fluids worsens constipation.
B: Correct. Constipation is commonly linked to low fibre, dehydration, and decreased activity; teaching fibre-rich foods, adequate fluids, and regular activity supports bowel regularity.
C: Incorrect. Decreased activity slows peristalsis and contributes to constipation rather than relieving it.
D: Incorrect. Fruits and vegetables are recommended fibre sources for constipation; eliminating them is counterproductive.
topic: Constipation — fibre, fluids, and activity teaching
source_1_section: Treatment of Constipation; Diet and behavior

stem: A client reports difficulty falling asleep most nights. The nurse is teaching sleep hygiene. Which client statement shows correct understanding?
options:
A) I will drink coffee after supper to stay awake until a later bedtime.
B) I will keep a consistent sleep–wake schedule even on days off.
C) I will use my phone in bed until I feel drowsy.
D) I will do vigorous exercise right before lights out so I am exhausted.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Caffeine near bedtime (and for sensitive people even in the afternoon) impairs sleep hygiene.
B: Correct. Maintaining a consistent sleep–wake schedule supports sleep promotion; irregular schedules make it harder to establish restful sleep.
C: Incorrect. Electronic device light and stimulation make falling asleep more difficult; devices should be avoided before sleep.
D: Incorrect. Exercise or excitement late in the evening can impair sleep; vigorous activity immediately before bedtime is poor sleep hygiene.
topic: Sleep hygiene — consistent schedule; avoid late caffeine, electronics, and late vigorous exercise
source_2_title: 28.4 Nursing Care to Promote Sleep and Rest
source_2_section: Education to Encourage Good Sleep Hygiene Practices; Maintain a Consistent Schedule for Sleep; Avoid Electronics Prior to Sleep

stem: The nurse is teaching new parents about reducing the risk of sudden infant death and sleep-related infant death. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Place the baby on the back for every sleep, including naps.
B) Use a firm, flat crib, cradle, or bassinet mattress with a fitted sheet.
C) Add bumper pads and a soft quilt to keep the baby warm and protected.
D) Keep soft toys, pillows, and loose bedding out of the sleep space.
E) Have the baby sleep alone in the crib while room-sharing with parents.
F) Place the baby prone for sleep if the baby spit up during the last feed.
rationales:
A: Correct. Back (supine) sleep for every sleep reduces SIDS risk and is recommended in Canadian and OpenStax/CDC–AAP aligned teaching.
B: Correct. A firm, flat sleep surface in a crib, cradle, or bassinet is the safest infant sleep surface.
C: Incorrect. Soft bedding, bumper pads, quilts, and similar items increase suffocation risk and should not be in the sleep space.
D: Correct. Soft objects and loose bedding should be kept out of the infant sleep area.
E: Correct. Room-sharing without bed-sharing (baby alone in crib in parents’ room) is recommended; Canada specifies the first 6 months for room-sharing.
F: Incorrect. Even infants who regurgitate should be placed on their backs; prone sleep increases SIDS risk.
topic: Newborn safe sleep — back, alone, crib; no soft bedding
jurisdiction_note: Canadian Joint Statement / Health Canada safe-sleep guidance keyed (back, alone, crib/cradle/bassinet, no soft bedding, room-share). OpenStax cites CDC/AAP with concordant ABC messaging; Canada’s room-sharing duration (first 6 months) is noted but not over-precise in options.
source_1_title: Joint Statement on Safe Sleep: Reducing Sudden Infant Deaths in Canada
source_1_publisher: Public Health Agency of Canada / Canada.ca
source_2_section: Safe sleep for every sleep; ABCs of Safe Sleep
source_3_title: 24.3 Newborn Discharge Planning and Parent Education

stem: A client with schizophrenia stares at an empty corner and says, “Angry voices are telling me I am in danger.” The client is distressed but not expressing a command to harm self or others. Which nursing response is most therapeutic?
options:
A) Those voices are not real — ignore them and you will be fine.
B) I do not hear those voices, but that must be very frightening for you.
C) Prove to me that someone is speaking so we can call security.
D) You should argue with the voices until they stop talking.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Trying to convince the client the hallucinations are not real and offering false reassurance is nontherapeutic and can increase distress.
B: Correct. Offer your perception of reality without arguing, and acknowledge the client’s feelings with empathy.
C: Incorrect. Challenging or demanding proof of the hallucination/delusional content increases defensiveness and erodes trust.
D: Incorrect. Arguing with or challenging psychotic content is not a therapeutic strategy and can escalate distress.
topic: Auditory hallucinations — acknowledge feelings; do not argue or convince
source_1_title: Chapter 11 Psychosis and Schizophrenia — Nursing: Mental Health and Community Concepts
source_1_section: Helping Clients Who Are Experiencing Hallucinations
source_2_section: Barriers to Therapeutic Communication — Disagreeing with the Client; Providing False Reassurance

stem: A client suddenly develops a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which nursing action best protects the airway during the seizure?
options:
A) Insert a padded tongue blade between the teeth.
B) Hold the client supine and restrain the arms and legs.
C) Turn the client onto the side and do not place objects in the mouth.
D) Sit the client upright and offer sips of water between convulsions.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Attempting to protect the tongue with objects in the mouth is futile and risks dental injury and rescuer injury.
B: Incorrect. Restraining limbs can cause injury; the priority airway measure is side-lying positioning, not forced restraint.
C: Correct. Rolling the client onto the side helps prevent aspiration, and nothing should be placed in the mouth during the seizure.
D: Incorrect. Oral fluids during a seizure risk aspiration; upright sitting is not the recommended airway-protective position during convulsions.
topic: Seizure — side-lying position; nothing in the mouth
source_1_section: Treatment of Seizure Disorders — General measures
source_2_section: Prioritizing Hypotheses, Generating Solutions, and Taking Action

stem: A client started ramipril 3 weeks ago for hypertension. At follow-up the client reports a persistent dry, irritating cough with no fever, sputum, or dyspnea. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
options:
A) Reassure the client that cough always means pneumonia and schedule a chest radiograph first.
B) Recognize that a dry cough is a common ACE inhibitor adverse effect and notify the provider.
C) Advise the client to double the next ramipril dose so the cough adapts more quickly.
D) Tell the client to stop all antihypertensive therapy immediately without contacting the provider.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. A dry, nonproductive ACE inhibitor cough is a common adverse effect; assuming pneumonia without clinical features of infection is not the first nursing interpretation.
B: Correct. A persistent dry, irritating cough is the most common ACE inhibitor adverse effect; the nurse should recognize it and communicate with the provider about possible medication change.
C: Incorrect. Increasing the dose does not treat ACE inhibitor cough and may worsen adverse effects; dose changes require a provider order.
D: Incorrect. Abrupt unsupervised cessation of antihypertensives is unsafe; the provider should guide any change (often to an ARB if cough is intolerable).
topic: ACE inhibitors — dry cough as common adverse effect

stem: A nurse is teaching a client who uses mealtime insulin about hypoglycemia risk. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
options:
A) Hypoglycemia risk is highest when insulin is peaking.
B) Insulin never causes low blood glucose if meals are skipped.
C) Long-acting basal insulin has the sharpest peak and highest hypoglycemia risk of all types.
D) Hypoglycemia is a rare complication that nurses can ignore during peak times.
rationales:
A: Correct. Peak time is when insulin’s glucose-lowering effect is strongest, and clients are at higher risk of hypoglycemia symptoms then.
B: Incorrect. Skipping meals while insulin is active increases hypoglycemia risk.
C: Incorrect. Common long-acting basal insulins are described as having little or no peak relative to mealtime insulins; they are not the sharpest-peaking type.
D: Incorrect. Hypoglycemia is the most common complication of insulin treatment and warrants monitoring, especially around peak action.
topic: Insulin — hypoglycemia risk highest around peak action
source_1_title: 28.2 Insulin and Non-Insulin Injectable Diabetes Drugs

stem: A client receiving a loop diuretic reports new muscle weakness and cramps. Serum potassium is 2.7 mmol/L (2.7 mEq/L). Which nursing action is the priority?
options:
A) Encourage unrestricted oral water intake to dilute serum electrolytes.
B) Place the client on continuous cardiac monitoring and notify the provider.
C) Administer the next scheduled dose of the loop diuretic as ordered.
D) Withhold all oral potassium-containing foods until the potassium normalizes.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Free-water loading does not correct potassium deficit and is not the priority for symptomatic hypokalemia with arrhythmia risk.
B: Correct. Moderate to severe hypokalemia causes muscle weakness and can produce life-threatening cardiac dysrhythmias; continuous cardiac/telemetry monitoring and prompt provider notification are priority nursing actions.
C: Incorrect. Loop diuretics increase urinary potassium loss and would worsen hypokalemia; the diuretic should not be given until the provider reassesses.
D: Incorrect. Dietary potassium is usually increased, not withheld, when treating hypokalemia unless the provider directs otherwise.
topic: Hypokalemia — muscle weakness and cardiac monitoring priority
units_note: Potassium in mmol/L equals mEq/L numerically.
source_2_section: Nursing Care of Patients with Hypokalemia; Prioritizing Hypotheses, Generating Solutions, and Taking Action

stem: After thyroidectomy, a client develops perioral tingling and muscle cramps. Which assessment finding best supports latent tetany from hypocalcemia?
options:
A) Tall, peaked T waves on the cardiac monitor
B) Facial muscle twitching when the facial nerve is tapped anterior to the ear (Chvostek sign)
C) Absent deep tendon reflexes in all extremities
D) Bilateral pitting edema of the ankles
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Tall, peaked T waves are associated with hyperkalemia, not hypocalcemia.
B: Correct. Chvostek sign (facial twitching after tapping the facial nerve) and Trousseau sign are bedside findings used to identify latent tetany from hypocalcemia, which can follow parathyroid injury during thyroid surgery.
C: Incorrect. Hypocalcemia tends toward hyperreflexia and tetany rather than absent reflexes.
D: Incorrect. Ankle edema is not a classic bedside sign of latent hypocalcemic tetany.
topic: Hypocalcemia — Chvostek sign / latent tetany after thyroidectomy

stem: A client with deep vein thrombosis is receiving continuous IV unfractionated heparin. Which laboratory result does the nurse monitor to guide dose titration?
options:
A) International normalized ratio (INR)
B) Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) or PTT per protocol
C) Hemoglobin A1C
D) Serum digoxin level
rationales:
A: Incorrect. INR is used primarily to monitor warfarin (vitamin K antagonist) therapy, not unfractionated heparin infusions.
B: Correct. Unfractionated heparin infusions are titrated using aPTT (or PTT/anti-Xa per institutional protocol) to a therapeutic range such as about 1.5–2.5 times the reference range.
C: Incorrect. Hemoglobin A1C reflects longer-term glycemic control and does not guide heparin dosing.
D: Incorrect. Digoxin levels monitor digoxin therapy, not anticoagulation with heparin.
topic: Unfractionated heparin — aPTT/PTT monitoring

stem: A client with type 2 diabetes who takes metformin is scheduled for a radiologic study with intravascular iodinated contrast. Which instruction is most appropriate?
options:
A) Double the metformin dose the morning of the contrast study to prevent hyperglycemia.
B) Continue metformin without change because contrast dye does not affect metformin safety.
C) Temporarily discontinue metformin around the contrast study as directed, because contrast-related renal impairment raises lactic acidosis risk.
D) Replace metformin with aspirin for 1 week after contrast exposure.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Increasing metformin near contrast exposure increases, rather than decreases, risk related to drug accumulation if renal function falls.
B: Incorrect. Product labeling and nursing references advise temporary interruption of metformin for intravascular iodinated contrast studies because contrast can impair renal function and increase lactic acidosis risk.
C: Correct. Metformin should be temporarily discontinued for intravascular iodinated contrast studies because contrast can alter renal function and metformin accumulation can cause lactic acidosis; timing follows facility/prescriber protocol.
D: Incorrect. Aspirin is not a substitute for metformin and does not address contrast-related lactic acidosis risk.
topic: Metformin — temporary discontinuation with iodinated contrast
jurisdiction_note: Keyed to Canadian product monograph principle of temporary discontinuation with intravascular iodinated contrast; exact hold/restart hours follow local protocol and were not keyed because OpenStax timing detail (24 h before/48 h after if eGFR <30) is more specific than the Canadian monograph wording.
source_1_publisher: Health Canada Drug Product Database — Laboratoire Riva Inc. product monograph
source_1_section: CONTRAINDICATIONS; WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS — lactic acidosis / radiocontrast

stem: A client started atorvastatin 2 weeks ago for hyperlipidemia. Which client statement shows correct understanding of safety teaching?
options:
A) I will ignore new muscle aches because they are never related to this medicine.
B) I will report unexplained muscle pain or weakness to my health care provider.
C) I will stop checking my cholesterol because the drug works immediately.
D) I will take a double dose if I miss one day.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Muscle symptoms are a recognized statin adverse effect and should not be ignored.
B: Correct. Statins can cause myalgia, myositis, or rare rhabdomyolysis; clients are taught to report muscular signs and symptoms to the provider.
C: Incorrect. Lipid response is monitored over time; stopping monitoring is unsafe teaching.
D: Incorrect. Doubling a missed statin dose is not appropriate and may increase adverse-effect risk.
topic: Statins — report muscle pain / myopathy risk
source_2_title: 21.2 Statins (HMG-CoA Reductase Inhibitors) and PCSK9 Inhibitors
source_2_section: Nursing Implications; Adverse Effects and Contraindications

stem: Before administering a scheduled oral beta blocker, the nurse assesses the client. Which finding is the strongest reason to withhold the dose and contact the provider?
options:
A) Blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg and heart rate 54/min with sinus bradycardia
B) Blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg and heart rate 76/min
C) Client reports a mild headache after breakfast
D) Client requests a glass of water with the tablet
rationales:
A: Correct. Beta blockers decrease heart rate; nursing references advise not administering when the client is bradycardic/hypotensive, and product labeling lists sinus bradycardia as a contraindication—withhold and notify the provider.
B: Incorrect. This heart rate and blood pressure are within a typical range for administering a beta blocker when ordered.
C: Incorrect. Mild headache alone is not the primary reason to withhold a beta blocker.
D: Incorrect. Taking oral medication with water is appropriate and not a reason to withhold.
topic: Beta blockers — withhold for bradycardia
jurisdiction_note: OpenStax cites hold for heart rate less than 60; Canadian metoprolol monograph contraindicates sinus bradycardia (and heart rate <45 in the MI subsection). Item keys bradycardia as a withhold cue without asserting a single universal numeric cut-off.
source_1_section: Introduction and Use; Adverse Effects and Contraindications
source_2_publisher: Health Canada Drug Product Database — Apotex Inc. product monograph

stem: A provider orders IV potassium chloride for a client with serum potassium 2.6 mmol/L (2.6 mEq/L). Which action is correct?
options:
A) Give the potassium chloride as a rapid IV push over 1 minute.
B) Infuse the potassium chloride at a controlled rate using an IV pump, never as an IV push.
C) Mix the entire daily potassium replacement into one IV push syringe for convenience.
D) Add undiluted potassium chloride directly into a running IV without a pump.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Rapid IV push of potassium can cause life-threatening cardiac dysrhythmias and is not an acceptable administration method.
B: Correct. IV potassium is given as a controlled infusion (commonly via IV pump); it must not be given as an IV push because excessive or rapid administration can cause lethal arrhythmias.
C: Incorrect. Concentrating potassium into an IV push syringe is unsafe and does not follow controlled-infusion requirements.
D: Incorrect. Undiluted free-flow addition without rate control is unsafe; concentration and infusion rate must be controlled.
topic: IV potassium chloride — controlled infusion, not IV push
units_note: Potassium mmol/L = mEq/L numerically.
source_1_section: Prioritizing Hypotheses, Generating Solutions, and Taking Action — Hypokalemia

stem: A client develops urticaria, wheezing, and hypotension within minutes after receiving IV antibiotic. Which action is the priority?
options:
A) Reassure the client that symptoms will resolve without treatment.
B) Administer epinephrine immediately as ordered/protocol and support airway and circulation.
C) Wait 30 minutes to see whether antihistamine cream alone improves the rash.
D) Document the findings and continue the antibiotic infusion at a slower rate.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Anaphylaxis is life-threatening and requires immediate treatment, not reassurance alone.
B: Correct. Epinephrine is the cornerstone/first-line treatment for anaphylaxis and should be given immediately, along with airway and circulatory support.
C: Incorrect. Delaying epinephrine for topical antihistamine observation risks rapid progression of anaphylaxis.
D: Incorrect. The likely allergen infusion should be stopped; continuing the antibiotic worsens exposure.
topic: Anaphylaxis — immediate epinephrine
source_2_section: Prioritizing Hypotheses, Generating Solutions, and Taking Action

stem: A client with advanced COPD is dyspneic at rest. The nurse observes the client exhaling slowly through pursed lips. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options:
A) It is an unexpected abnormal behaviour that always indicates impending respiratory arrest.
B) It is a common compensatory breathing pattern used in COPD to help control dyspnea and prolong exhalation.
C) It means the client should immediately stop all prescribed inhaled bronchodilators.
D) It indicates the client no longer needs supplemental oxygen under any circumstances.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Pursed-lip breathing is a recognized COPD compensatory pattern, not by itself a universal sign of imminent arrest.
B: Correct. Pursed-lip breathing is a common sign/technique in COPD that helps prolong exhalation and is observed with dyspnea or taught as a breathing strategy.
C: Incorrect. Bronchodilators remain a core COPD therapy; pursed-lip breathing does not replace them.
D: Incorrect. Oxygen needs are based on saturation/ABG and clinical status, not on the presence of pursed-lip breathing alone.
topic: COPD — pursed-lip breathing as compensatory pattern
source_2_title: 11.5 Disorders of the Lower Respiratory System: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease

stem: A client with known heart failure reports a 2 kg weight gain in 3 days and shoes that feel tight. Which assessment finding best supports fluid volume overload related to heart failure?
options:
A) Clear lung fields and flat neck veins with dry mucous membranes
B) Dependent peripheral edema and jugular venous distention
C) Sunken eyes and poor skin turgor only
D) Urine output of 2 L in 8 hours with thirst
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Flat neck veins and dry mucous membranes suggest hypovolemia, not overload.
B: Correct. Peripheral (dependent) edema and jugular venous distention are classic physical findings of heart failure–related fluid overload, consistent with recent weight gain.
C: Incorrect. Sunken eyes and poor turgor suggest dehydration.
D: Incorrect. High urine output with thirst is not the typical overload picture of decompensated HF.
topic: Heart failure — peripheral edema and jugular venous distention
source_1_section: Symptoms and Signs of Chronic Heart Failure

stem: The nurse is maintaining a sterile field for a procedure. Which actions or events break sterile technique? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Turning the back so the sterile field is out of view
B) Keeping sterile-gloved hands above the waist and in view
C) Allowing a sterile drape to become wet
D) Reaching an unsterile sleeve across the sterile field
E) Holding a sterile package edge outside the 2.5 cm (1 in) border
rationales:
A: Correct. If the nurse turns away and can no longer see the field, sterility is considered broken.
B: Incorrect. Keeping sterile-gloved hands above the waist and within view helps maintain sterility; this does not break technique.
C: Correct. Wet sterile items/fields are considered contaminated because moisture can carry microorganisms.
D: Correct. Reaching over the sterile field with nonsterile arms/sleeves contaminates the field.
E: Incorrect. The outer 2.5 cm (1 in) border of a sterile package/field is considered unsterile; holding/handling that border is expected technique, not a break.
topic: Sterile field — contamination rules (wet, out of view, reaching over)
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_1_section: Preparing and Maintaining a Sterile Field; Opening a Sterile Package
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A client’s serum sodium has fallen to 118 mmol/L (118 mEq/L). Which assessment finding is most consistent with this electrolyte imbalance?
options:
A) Improved concentration and heightened alertness
B) Confusion or decreased level of consciousness
C) Flushed dry skin with intense thirst only, without neurologic change
D) Bilateral crackles as the only expected finding
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Severe hyponatremia causes neurologic depression, not improved alertness.
B: Correct. Hyponatremia produces primarily neurologic manifestations from brain cell swelling, including confusion and decreased level of consciousness; seizures may occur in severe cases.
C: Incorrect. Intense thirst with dry flushed skin is more typical of hypernatremia teaching patterns; hyponatremia centers on neurologic changes.
D: Incorrect. Crackles suggest pulmonary fluid overload but are not the hallmark neurologic finding of hyponatremia.
topic: Hyponatremia — neurologic manifestations
units_note: Sodium mmol/L = mEq/L numerically.
source_1_section: Hyponatremia (overview); Symptoms and Signs of Hyponatremia
source_2_section: Nursing Care of Patients with Hyponatremia

stem: A hospitalized adult with decreased level of consciousness is at risk for aspiration. Which nursing action best reduces aspiration risk during care?
options:
A) Keep the client flat in a fully supine position for all oral care and feeding attempts.
B) Elevate the head of the bed to greater than 30 degrees (semi-upright) unless contraindicated, and avoid oral intake while consciousness is decreased.
C) Offer large boluses of thin liquids quickly to clear residual oral secretions.
D) Increase sedating medications so the client sleeps through meals.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Fully supine positioning increases gastroesophageal reflux and aspiration risk compared with semi-upright positioning.
B: Correct. For clients with decreased consciousness, elevating the head of the bed above 30 degrees and avoiding oral feeding/medications are evidence-based aspiration-prevention strategies; OpenStax likewise advises an upright position of at least 30 degrees.
C: Incorrect. Rapid large thin-liquid boluses increase aspiration risk and are not a protective strategy.
D: Incorrect. Sedating medications should be minimized or stopped when possible because sedation worsens protective airway reflexes.
topic: Aspiration precautions — elevate head of bed >30°; avoid oral intake if LOC decreased
source_1_section: Prevention of Chemical Pneumonitis and Aspiration Pneumonia
source_2_title: 11.7 Disorders of the Lower Respiratory System: Pneumonia and Aspiration
source_2_section: Evidence-Based Practice: Strategies to Prevent Aspiration Pneumonia

stem: An immobile client after a stroke has flaccid extremities and cannot participate in active exercise. Which nursing intervention best helps prevent joint contractures?
options:
A) Keep all joints immobilized in a fully flexed position to promote rest.
B) Perform passive range-of-motion exercises through each joint’s normal range several times daily.
C) Restrict turning and repositioning to once every 8 hours to conserve energy.
D) Apply resistive exercises to the flaccid limbs immediately to build strength quickly.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Prolonged immobilization in flexion promotes contractures rather than preventing them.
B: Correct. Passive range-of-motion through each joint’s normal range (several times daily when the client cannot move actively) helps prevent contractures associated with immobility and flaccid extremities.
C: Incorrect. Immobile clients need frequent repositioning; limiting turns worsens immobility complications including pressure injury and stiffness.
D: Incorrect. Resistive exercise on hemiplegic/flaccid limbs early may be controversial or inappropriate; passive ROM is the initial contracture-prevention measure when the client cannot participate.
topic: Immobility — passive ROM to prevent contractures
source_2_section: Effects of Immobility on Major Body Systems — Musculoskeletal Effects

stem: The nurse prepares to provide oral care for a dependent adult who cannot manage secretions independently. Which action is most appropriate to reduce aspiration risk during the procedure?
options:
A) Place the client flat and irrigate the mouth with large volumes of water.
B) Raise the head of the bed to 30–45 degrees and ensure suction equipment is available.
C) Omit oral care until the client can sit independently at the edge of the bed.
D) Have the client drink a full glass of water immediately before brushing.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Flat positioning and large fluid volumes increase aspiration risk during oral care.
B: Correct. For clients needing assisted oral care, elevating the head of the bed to 30–45 degrees and having suction available helps prevent aspiration of fluids and secretions.
C: Incorrect. Dependent clients still require oral hygiene; delaying care allows bacterial colonization that contributes to aspiration pneumonia risk.
D: Incorrect. Forcing oral fluid intake before care is not an aspiration-prevention measure and may worsen risk if swallowing is impaired.
topic: Oral care — HOB 30–45° and suction available for dependent clients
source_2_section: Prevention of Chemical Pneumonitis and Aspiration Pneumonia

stem: Immediately after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of a healthy term newborn, which action best supports breastfeeding initiation and newborn transition?
options:
A) Separate the newborn for a routine nursery bath and full examination before any parental contact.
B) Place the newborn in uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact with the birthing parent for at least the first hour or until the first feeding is completed.
C) Keep the newborn wrapped tightly beside the parent but delay any chest-to-chest contact for 6 hours.
D) Offer formula supplementation before any attempt at breastfeeding to check glucose.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Routine separation for baths/exams interrupts skin-to-skin care that should begin immediately after birth unless resuscitation is required.
B: Correct. Canadian guidance recommends immediate, uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact for at least an hour or until the first feed is completed to support breastfeeding initiation and physiologic transition.
C: Incorrect. Delayed skin-to-skin contact undermines early breastfeeding behaviours that typically emerge within the first hour.
D: Incorrect. Routine early formula before breastfeeding is not indicated for a healthy term newborn and can interfere with breastfeeding establishment.
topic: Newborn skin-to-skin contact — uninterrupted ≥1 hour after birth
jurisdiction_note: Keyed to PHAC Family-Centred Maternity and Newborn Care Chapter 6 and Canadian Paediatric Society SSC position (immediate uninterrupted SSC ≥1 hour / until first feed).
source_1_title: Family-Centred Maternity and Newborn Care: National Guidelines — Chapter 6 Breastfeeding
source_1_publisher: Public Health Agency of Canada / Canada.ca
source_2_title: Skin-to-skin care (SSC) for term and preterm infants

stem: A postmenopausal client asks how to help protect bone health and reduce fracture risk. Which teaching point is most appropriate?
options:
A) Avoid all weight-bearing activity because it stresses fragile bones.
B) Include regular weight-bearing physical activity and ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D intake.
C) Increase daily alcohol intake to improve bone density.
D) Stop all dairy and plant calcium sources once a bisphosphonate is prescribed.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Weight-bearing exercise helps maintain or improve bone mineral density and is recommended, not avoided.
B: Correct. Risk-factor modification for osteoporosis includes weight-bearing exercise plus adequate calcium and vitamin D from diet or supplements as needed.
C: Incorrect. Alcohol should be moderated; excess intake is not a bone-protective strategy.
D: Incorrect. Adequate calcium and vitamin D remain important alongside pharmacotherapy; dietary sources should not be stopped without clinical reason.
topic: Osteoporosis prevention — weight-bearing exercise; calcium and vitamin D
source_1_section: Risk factor modification; Calcium and vitamin D
source_2_section: Medical Therapies and Related Care / Nursing Care

stem: A community health nurse is explaining levels of prevention to nursing students. Which example correctly illustrates primary prevention?
options:
A) Mammography to detect early breast cancer before symptoms appear.
B) Administering routine immunizations to prevent infectious disease before it occurs.
C) Cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction to limit disability.
D) Screening blood pressure to identify hypertension in its earliest stages.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Screening for early disease (e.g., mammography) is secondary prevention.
B: Correct. Primary prevention intervenes before health effects occur; immunizations/vaccinations are classic primary prevention.
C: Incorrect. Rehabilitation after established disease is tertiary prevention.
D: Incorrect. Blood pressure screening to detect disease early is secondary prevention.
topic: Levels of prevention — immunization as primary prevention
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: An adult client presents for a routine clinic visit accompanied by a partner. The nurse plans intimate partner violence screening. Which action is most appropriate?
options:
A) Ask screening questions while the partner remains in the room to show transparency.
B) Ensure the client is alone in a private setting before screening, asking the partner to step away.
C) Skip screening whenever a partner attends because disclosure is unlikely.
D) Leave a printed screening form for the couple to complete together at home.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Screening with a partner present can endanger the client and suppress disclosure.
B: Correct. IPV screening requires privacy and confidentiality; clients should be alone, and accompanying persons (including partners) should be asked to step away.
C: Incorrect. Partner presence is a reason to create private screening opportunity, not to omit screening.
D: Incorrect. Home or shared completion with a partner compromises confidentiality and safety.
topic: Intimate partner violence — screen privately when client is alone
source_2_title: A Better Approach for Screening Women for Intimate Partner Violence in Primary Care
source_2_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)

stem: The nurse is planning a home safety assessment for a client with progressive dementia who still lives at home. Which focus is the priority?
options:
A) Encourage leaving medications in unmarked bowls on the kitchen table for easy access.
B) Identify and reduce environmental hazards (for example, throw rugs, poor lighting, unsafe kitchen appliances) that increase fall and injury risk.
C) Remove all familiar furniture so the home feels like a new therapeutic environment.
D) Advise the family to keep the stove fully available without safeguards so cooking independence is preserved at all costs.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Unsecured medications increase poisoning and dosing errors in cognitively impaired clients.
B: Correct. Dementia care includes assessing the environment for safety hazards (falls, kitchen risks) and arranging protective measures as cognition declines.
C: Incorrect. Familiar environments are preferred; abrupt removal of familiar cues can increase confusion.
D: Incorrect. When deficits are present, protective measures such as disabling or securing the stove may be required to prevent accidents.
topic: Dementia — home environmental hazard assessment and safety
source_2_section: Planning Nursing Care for a Client with Major NCD

stem: A client whose spouse died 2 weeks ago says, “I still can’t believe this is real,” and begins to cry. Which nursing response is most therapeutic?
options:
A) “You need to stay strong now for everyone else in the family.”
B) “Try not to cry; focusing on happy memories will make this pass faster.”
C) Sit with the client, listen, and acknowledge that disbelief and sadness are understandable responses to loss.
D) “You should avoid talking about the death until at least 6 months have passed.”
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Telling a grieving person to “stay strong” dismisses emotion and is nontherapeutic.
B: Incorrect. Discouraging crying and imposing a timeline minimizes grief and blocks expression.
C: Correct. Therapeutic support includes presence, listening, and validating grief reactions such as disbelief and sadness; psychological support and allowing expression of concerns are first-line approaches.
D: Incorrect. Avoiding discussion of the loss can increase isolation; clients should be supported to express grief in their own time.
topic: Grief — supportive presence, listening, and validation
source_1_section: Kübler-Ross Model of Grief — Denial / Depression stages (nursing actions)
source_2_title: Symptom Relief for the Dying Patient
source_2_section: Stress and Grief Surrounding the Dying Patient

stem: A capable adult client in Ontario clearly refuses a recommended non-emergency medication after receiving information about risks and benefits. What is the nurse’s most appropriate action?
options:
A) Administer the medication anyway because the provider ordered it.
B) Honour the refusal, do not administer the medication, and notify the provider / document according to organizational policy.
C) Ask the spouse to override the client’s refusal and sign consent.
D) Wait until the client is asleep and then give the dose covertly.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Under the Health Care Consent Act, a health practitioner must not administer treatment to a capable person without that person’s consent.
B: Correct. Capable clients have a legal and ethical right to refuse treatment; consent may also be withdrawn. The nurse does not administer the refused treatment and follows communication/documentation requirements.
C: Incorrect. A spouse cannot override a capable client’s refusal; substitute decision-makers act only when the client is incapable with respect to the treatment.
D: Incorrect. Covert administration violates consent requirements and professional obligations.
topic: Consent — capable client’s right to refuse treatment (HCCA/CNO)
jurisdiction_note: Keyed to Ontario Health Care Consent Act, 1996 s. 10 (no treatment without consent) and CNO Consent practice guideline (right to refuse). Emergency exceptions not tested.
source_1_title: Health Care Consent Act, 1996, S.O. 1996, c. 2, Sched. A
source_1_section: Consent to Treatment — s. 10 No treatment without consent; s. 14 Withdrawal of consent

stem: A capable adult asks why the nurse is encouraging completion of an advance directive (living will / health-care proxy documents). Which explanation is most accurate?
options:
A) Advance directives allow the client to communicate care preferences in case of future incapacity.
B) Advance directives are only for clients older than 80 years.
C) Once signed, advance directives prevent any change in treatment preferences forever.
D) Advance directives authorize the nurse to make all medical decisions without consulting anyone.
rationales:
A: Correct. Advance directives (such as a living will and/or appointment of a health-care proxy/agent) communicate preferences and decision-maker choices before the person becomes unable to decide.
B: Incorrect. Adults of any age can complete advance directives; they are not limited to the oldest clients.
C: Incorrect. Preferences can be reviewed and updated while the person remains capable; documents should be revisited as circumstances change.
D: Incorrect. Directives guide care and may appoint a proxy; they do not transfer decision-making authority to the nurse unilaterally.
topic: Advance directives — document care preferences before incapacity
jurisdiction_note: Tests the concordant purpose of advance directives/living will/proxy. Ontario naming often emphasizes Power of Attorney for Personal Care / advance care planning; US sources use living will and durable power of attorney for health care.
source_1_section: Advance Directives; Living will; Durable power of attorney for health care

stem: The nurse is teaching a client with osteopenia about lifestyle measures to support bone health. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Perform regular weight-bearing physical activity as tolerated.
B) Ensure adequate calcium intake from diet and supplements if needed.
C) Ensure adequate vitamin D intake.
D) Remain on strict bed rest to protect the bones.
E) Stop smoking.
F) Drink large amounts of alcohol daily to stimulate bone formation.
rationales:
A: Correct. Weight-bearing exercise helps maintain bone mineral density.
B: Correct. Adequate calcium intake (diet ± supplements) supports bone health.
C: Correct. Adequate vitamin D is required along with calcium for bone health.
D: Incorrect. Immobility/bed rest worsens bone loss; activity is encouraged as tolerated.
E: Correct. Smoking cessation is a recommended risk-factor modification.
F: Incorrect. Alcohol should be moderated; excess intake is not bone-protective.
topic: Osteoporosis/osteopenia lifestyle teaching — exercise, calcium, vitamin D, smoking cessation
source_1_section: Risk factor modification; Calcium and vitamin D

stem: After completing a venipuncture with a nonsafety needle and syringe, which action best reduces the risk of needlestick injury?
options:
A) Recap the used needle carefully using both hands before carrying it to the utility room.
B) Place the used needle and attached device immediately into a marked sharps container without recapping.
C) Leave the uncapped needle on the bedside table until housekeeping empties the room.
D) Bend the needle tip against a hard surface so it cannot puncture skin, then discard in regular trash.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Recapping used nonsafety needles increases needlestick risk and is not recommended when a sharps container is available.
B: Correct. Used blood-collection devices should be deposited immediately into an appropriate sharps container; OpenStax likewise directs immediate disposal in a marked sharps container and never recapping a used needle.
C: Incorrect. Leaving uncapped needles exposed creates an occupational hazard for staff and others.
D: Incorrect. Bending needles and discarding sharps in regular trash are unsafe practices that increase injury and blood-borne pathogen risk.
topic: Sharps safety — never recap used needle; immediate sharps-container disposal

source_2_section: QSEN Competency: Safety: Disposing Sharps Safely

stem: The nurse prepares to irrigate a bleeding wound that is likely to splash blood and body fluids. Which personal protective equipment is most appropriate in addition to gloves?
options:
A) No additional PPE is needed because gloves alone provide complete mucous-membrane protection.
B) Protective eyewear such as goggles or a face shield to protect the eyes (and face as indicated) from splashes.
C) An N95 respirator only, without eye or face barrier protection.
D) Shoe covers alone, without any eye or face protection.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Gloves protect hands but do not protect eye, nose, or mouth mucous membranes from splashes.
B: Correct. Eyewear/face shields are indicated for tasks that may produce splashes of blood or body fluids; CDC Standard Precautions likewise require PPE for eyes, nose, and mouth during splash-generating procedures.
C: Incorrect. An N95 alone does not address splash protection of the eyes and is selected for airborne/aerosol risks, not as a substitute for eye protection during splash-generating wound care.
D: Incorrect. Shoe covers do not protect facial mucous membranes from splashes.
topic: Standard Precautions — eye/face protection for splash-generating procedures
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A nursing student asks when Standard Precautions should be used. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options:
A) Only for clients with a confirmed multidrug-resistant organism.
B) For all clients, regardless of diagnosis or presumed infection status.
C) Only during sterile surgical procedures in the operating room.
D) Only after laboratory confirmation of a blood-borne infection.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Multidrug-resistant organisms typically require Transmission-Based Precautions in addition to Standard Precautions, not Standard Precautions alone as the only time they apply.
B: Correct. Standard Precautions are the first tier of infection control and apply to all patients regardless of diagnosis or presumed infection status; CDC likewise recommends Standard Precautions for all patient interactions.
C: Incorrect. Surgical asepsis is procedure-specific; Standard Precautions apply broadly across care settings, not only in the OR.
D: Incorrect. Waiting for laboratory confirmation would leave unprotected exposures; Standard Precautions assume all blood and body fluids may be infectious.
topic: Standard Precautions — apply to all clients regardless of diagnosis
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: Which nursing action is the most effective strategy to prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) in a hospitalized adult?
options:
A) Leave the indwelling catheter in place indefinitely once inserted to avoid repeated catheterization.
B) Avoid unnecessary catheterization and remove the indwelling catheter as soon as it is no longer needed.
C) Open the closed drainage system daily to irrigate with antiseptic solution.
D) Insert an indwelling catheter for convenience when managing incontinence without other indications.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Prolonged catheterization is the major CAUTI risk factor; catheters should not remain indefinitely without indication.
B: Correct. The most effective preventive measures are avoiding unnecessary catheterization and removing catheters as soon as possible; CDC likewise recommends inserting only for appropriate indications and leaving in place only as long as needed.
C: Incorrect. Maintaining a closed drainage system reduces risk; routinely opening the system for antiseptic irrigation is not recommended prevention.
D: Incorrect. Using catheters solely to manage incontinence is an avoidable indication that increases CAUTI risk.
topic: CAUTI prevention — avoid unnecessary catheters; remove as soon as possible

source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: After providing care that required gloves, the nurse prepares to see the next client. Which practice is correct?
options:
A) Wash the same pair of gloves with soap and water and reuse them for the next client.
B) Remove the gloves after the client encounter, perform hand hygiene, and don a new pair for the next client.
C) Keep the same gloves on between clients if neither client has a known infection.
D) Remove gloves only at the end of the shift to conserve supplies.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Washing gloves for reuse has been associated with pathogen transmission and is not acceptable.
B: Correct. Gloves are single-use; remove them after contact with a client/environment and perform hand hygiene; do not wear the same pair for more than one patient.
C: Incorrect. The same gloves must not be worn for care of more than one patient, regardless of known infection status.
D: Incorrect. Delayed glove removal contaminates the environment and hands and violates Standard Precautions.
topic: Glove use — single-use; remove and hand hygiene between clients

stem: Which actions help reduce the risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Insert an indwelling catheter only when there is an appropriate clinical indication.
B) Remove the indwelling catheter as soon as it is no longer needed.
C) Maintain a closed urinary drainage system.
D) Use an indwelling catheter routinely for all incontinent nursing-home residents without other indications.
E) Open the drainage system daily to culture the bag routinely in asymptomatic clients.
F) Use aseptic technique for catheter insertion.
rationales:
A: Correct. Catheters should be inserted only for appropriate indications.
B: Correct. Prompt removal when no longer needed is a core CAUTI prevention strategy.
C: Correct. Maintaining a closed drainage system reduces infection risk.
D: Incorrect. Avoid using catheters solely to manage incontinence.
E: Incorrect. Routinely opening the system for asymptomatic culture of the bag breaks closed drainage and is not recommended prevention.
F: Correct. Aseptic insertion technique is part of CAUTI prevention bundles.
topic: CAUTI prevention SATA — indication, prompt removal, closed system, asepsis
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

source_2_title: Prevention of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections: Summary of Recommendations
