stem: A client with severe neutropenia is on protective infection-prevention measures. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Practice meticulous hand hygiene before contact with the client.
B) Avoid fresh flowers in the room to reduce exposure to environmental fungi such as Aspergillus.
C) Encourage unrestricted fresh fruit and uncooked meats without food-safety precautions.
D) Monitor for fever because serious infection may present with muted focal findings.
E) Stop all hand hygiene because gloves alone replace cleaning hands.
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax neutropenia care includes meticulous hand hygiene to reduce nosocomial infection.
B: Correct. OpenStax states fresh flowers are avoided to decrease exposure to chemicals or Aspergillus fungi.
C: Incorrect. OpenStax states fresh fruit and uncooked meats are avoided to reduce foodborne contaminants.
D: Correct. Merck notes fever is present during most serious infections in neutropenia and that the inflammatory response may be muted; OpenStax includes fever among infection manifestations and emphasizes temperature surveillance.
E: Incorrect. Hand hygiene remains essential; gloves do not replace hand hygiene between contacts.
topic: Neutropenia — protective precautions SATA
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
units_note: Neutrophil counts in Merck use ×10⁹/L (SI); infection risk rises as counts fall.
source_1_section: Nursing Care — protective measures; clinical manifestations
source_2_section: Symptoms and Signs; Key Points; Treatment of acute neutropenia

stem: A postoperative client suddenly develops shortness of breath and sharp chest pain that worsens with inhalation. Which complication should the nurse suspect first?
options:
A) Pulmonary embolism.
B) Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis without respiratory distress.
C) Resolved postoperative pain that requires no further assessment.
D) A dietary craving for ice cream.
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax describes PE manifestations including sudden shortness of breath and chest pain sharper with inhalation; Merck lists dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain among PE symptoms and tachypnea/tachycardia among signs.
B: Incorrect. Sudden dyspnea with pleuritic chest pain is not explained by uncomplicated allergic rhinitis.
C: Incorrect. New sudden respiratory symptoms require urgent evaluation, not dismissal as resolved pain.
D: Incorrect. Irrelevant to acute dyspnea and pleuritic pain.
topic: Pulmonary embolism — sudden dyspnea and pleuritic pain
source_1_section: Symptoms and Signs of Pulmonary Embolism
source_2_section: Clinical Manifestations of VTE — pulmonary embolism

stem: Which finding is an early symptom the nurse should associate with rising serum sodium (hypernatremia)?
options:
A) Thirst.
B) Complete absence of any fluid or neurologic symptoms in every client with severe hypernatremia.
C) Sudden productive cough with green sputum as the defining early feature of hypernatremia.
D) Bright yellow skin as the first and only sign of high sodium.
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax states that in early hypernatremia one of the only symptoms may be thirst, with confusion or seizures as sodium rises; Merck identifies thirst as the major symptom of hypernatremia and CNS signs (confusion, seizures, coma) from brain-cell shrinkage.
B: Incorrect. Hypernatremia produces thirst and can progress to neurologic dysfunction; it is not asymptomatic by definition when severe.
C: Incorrect. Productive green sputum suggests pulmonary infection, not the early hallmark of hypernatremia.
D: Incorrect. Jaundice-like yellow skin is not the early defining sign of hypernatremia.
topic: Hypernatremia — thirst as early cue
units_note: Serum sodium in mmol/L (= mEq/L); OpenStax table uses >145 mEq/L for hypernatremia; reference intervals vary by laboratory.
source_1_section: Nursing Care of Patients with Hypernatremia — Recognizing and Analyzing Cues

stem: A nurse finishes a dressing change and is about to leave the unit for break. According to College of Nurses of Ontario documentation expectations and standard nursing documentation practice, which action is required?
options:
A) Document the dressing change before providing the care so the record is ready.
B) Document the care at the time it is provided or as soon as possible afterward, including date and time.
C) Wait until the end of the week and write one summary note for all dressing changes.
D) Ask a colleague who did not provide the care to document the dressing change later.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. CNO states nurses do not document before the care is provided.
B: Correct. CNO requires documentation in a timely manner at the time care is provided or as soon as possible afterward, with date and time; OpenStax emphasizes charting in real time to keep records accurate and current.
C: Incorrect. Delayed weekly summary charting does not meet timely, contemporaneous documentation expectations.
D: Incorrect. CNO directs nurses to document care they provide and not document care provided by another individual (except designated recorder situations).
topic: Documentation — timely; do not document before care
jurisdiction_note: CNO Documentation practice standard sets Ontario nursing documentation accountabilities; OpenStax supports real-time charting as general best practice.
source_1_section: Accountabilities — timely documentation; do not document before care

stem: A former inpatient sends a personal social media friend request to the nurse who provided care. Which response best maintains professional boundaries?
options:
A) Accept the request and discuss the client’s hospital stay privately in direct messages.
B) Decline connecting on personal social media and maintain professional boundaries online.
C) Accept the request only if the client promises not to mention health information.
D) Accept the request because the therapeutic relationship ended at discharge, so boundaries no longer apply.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Discussing care on personal social media risks privacy breaches and blurs professional boundaries.
B: Correct. CNO directs nurses not to accept friend requests from clients on personal social media; NCSBN advises caution with online social contact because it blurs professional and personal relationships even if the patient initiates contact.
C: Incorrect. Conditional acceptance still creates an inappropriate personal online relationship.
D: Incorrect. NCSBN notes online contact with former patients also blurs professional and personal relationships; CNO requires maintaining boundaries.
topic: Professional boundaries — no personal social media connections with clients
jurisdiction_note: CNO Professional Boundaries is the Ontario regulator authority; NCSBN social media guidance independently supports avoiding personal online relationships with patients/former patients.
source_1_section: Technology use / social media — refrain from friend requests
source_2_title: A Nurse's Guide to the Use of Social Media

stem: Under Ontario’s Health Care Consent Act and CNO Consent guidance, which statement about decision-making capacity is accurate?
options:
A) A finding of incapacity for one treatment means the person is incapable for all treatments indefinitely.
B) A person may be incapable with respect to some treatments and capable with respect to others.
C) Only a court can ever determine that a person is capable of consenting to treatment.
D) Capacity is assessed once on admission and never reassessed during the hospital stay.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Capacity is treatment-specific; incapacity for one treatment does not automatically apply to all treatments.
B: Correct. HCCA s.15 and CNO Consent state a person may be capable for some treatments and incapable for others; capacity can also change over time.
C: Incorrect. Health practitioners assess capacity related to specific treatment decisions under the HCCA framework.
D: Incorrect. HCCA recognizes capacity may change with time; consent is an ongoing process.
topic: Capacity — treatment-specific under HCCA
jurisdiction_note: HCCA s.15 and CNO Consent are Ontario authorities for capacity assessment.
source_2_section: HCCA — capacity relates to a specific treatment

stem: A client becomes angry about a delayed procedure and raises their voice at the nurse. Which initial conflict-management action best aligns with College of Nurses of Ontario guidance?
options:
A) Argue that the delay is not the nurse’s fault and criticize the client’s tone.
B) Remain calm, encourage the client to express concerns, and avoid arguing or judging.
C) Ignore the behaviour because conflict is never an issue nurses should address.
D) Immediately permanently discontinue all nursing services without assessing safety or planning alternatives.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. CNO advises nurses to avoid arguing, criticizing, defending, or judging.
B: Correct. CNO conflict-management strategies include remaining calm, encouraging expression of concerns, and avoiding arguing/criticizing; OpenStax notes good communication promotes better handling of conflicts and emphasizes respectful, assertive professional communication.
C: Incorrect. CNO states unmanaged conflict can hinder care and escalate into violence/abuse; nurses must be prepared to prevent or manage conflict.
D: Incorrect. Withdrawal of services is a last-resort safety option with decision-tree guidance, not the first response to voiced frustration.
topic: Conflict prevention and management — calm, non-argumentative response
jurisdiction_note: CNO Conflict Prevention and Management is the Ontario practice guideline; OpenStax supports communication skills that help manage conflict.

stem: Which documentation practices meet College of Nurses of Ontario accountabilities? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Include the date and time with documentation entries.
B) Document care before it is provided to save time.
C) Clearly identify a late entry and refer to the date and time the care occurred.
D) Falsify a record if asked by a colleague to “fix” a missed note.
E) Document in a timely manner at or soon after the care or event.
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO requires all documentation entries include the date and time; OpenStax notes entries need an accurate date and time stamp.
B: Incorrect. CNO states nurses do not document before care is provided.
C: Correct. CNO requires late entries to be indicated with the date/time the care or action occurred.
D: Incorrect. CNO prohibits falsifying a record relating to practice.
E: Correct. CNO requires timely documentation at the time of care or as soon as possible afterward; OpenStax supports real-time charting.
topic: Documentation accountabilities SATA — date/time, timely, late entry, no falsify
jurisdiction_note: CNO Documentation is Ontario regulator authority; OpenStax supports date/time stamp and timely documentation principles.
source_1_section: Accountabilities — date/time, timely, late entry, no falsify
source_2_section: ANA documentation principles; Chart in Real Time

stem: According to Ontario’s Health Care Consent Act definition of capacity (also reflected in CNO Consent guidance), a person is capable with respect to a treatment if the person is able to:
options:
A) Recite the hospital mission statement from memory.
B) Understand relevant information and appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of a decision or lack of decision.
C) Name three nurses on the unit and state their years of experience.
D) Sign any form placed in front of them, regardless of understanding.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Capacity concerns decision-relevant treatment information, not institutional trivia.
B: Correct. HCCA s.4 and CNO Consent define capacity as ability to understand relevant information and appreciate reasonably foreseeable consequences of a decision or lack of decision.
C: Incorrect. Naming staff is unrelated to treatment decision-making capacity.
D: Incorrect. A signature without understanding does not constitute capable informed consent.
topic: Capacity definition — understand and appreciate consequences
jurisdiction_note: HCCA s.4 capacity definition is Ontario statute; CNO Consent restates the understand/appreciate test for nurses.

stem: Fifteen minutes after a packed red blood cell transfusion is started, the client develops chills, fever, and low back pain. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
options:
A) Slow the transfusion rate and reassess in 30 minutes.
B) Stop the transfusion immediately and keep the IV line open with normal saline.
C) Administer prescribed acetaminophen and continue the same unit at the previous rate.
D) Complete the remaining unit quickly so the reaction can be evaluated afterward.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Suspected transfusion reactions require immediate stop, not merely slowing the infusion.
B: Correct. Merck directs stopping the transfusion immediately and keeping the IV open with normal saline; OpenStax likewise prioritizes immediately stopping the transfusion when a reaction is occurring.
C: Incorrect. Continuing the same unit after systemic reaction symptoms is unsafe; the unit should not be restarted.
D: Incorrect. Completing the unit would increase exposure to the implicated product.
topic: Transfusion reaction — stop transfusion immediately
source_2_section: Prioritizing Hypotheses, Generating Solutions, and Taking Action

stem: A nurse is teaching a client newly started on warfarin. Which instruction is the priority safety teaching point?
options:
A) Stop all follow-up blood tests once you feel well.
B) Report signs and symptoms of bleeding and keep scheduled INR monitoring appointments.
C) Double the next dose if a dose is missed, without contacting the prescriber.
D) Take an extra aspirin daily to enhance warfarin’s effect.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. DailyMed requires regular INR monitoring in all treated patients.
B: Correct. DailyMed boxed warning instructs patients about prevention measures and to report bleeding signs/symptoms, with regular INR monitoring; Merck notes warfarin requires close INR monitoring and carries bleeding risk.
C: Incorrect. Missed-dose management should follow prescriber/label guidance; doubling without advice increases bleeding risk.
D: Incorrect. Combining with antiplatelet agents can increase bleeding risk and is not routine teaching.
topic: Warfarin — report bleeding; INR monitoring
jurisdiction_note: DailyMed is a US FDA label source; bleeding risk and INR monitoring teaching is concordant with Canadian warfarin practice.
source_1_publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed
source_2_section: Anticoagulation strategies — warfarin INR monitoring; bleeding

stem: A client is receiving IV gentamicin. Which adverse effects should the nurse monitor for most closely because of aminoglycoside toxicity?
options:
A) Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity (vestibular/auditory).
B) Only mild transient hair loss without other risks.
C) Hyperglycemia as the primary expected effect.
D) Permanent blue-green skin discoloration in all clients.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck states all aminoglycosides cause renal toxicity and vestibular/auditory toxicity; DailyMed gentamicin boxed warning highlights nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity (vestibular and auditory).
B: Incorrect. Hair loss is not the primary boxed aminoglycoside toxicity concern.
C: Incorrect. Hyperglycemia is not the hallmark aminoglycoside toxicity described in these sources.
D: Incorrect. Not a described primary toxicity of gentamicin/aminoglycosides in the cited sources.
topic: Aminoglycosides — nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity monitoring
source_2_publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed

stem: A client is admitted with suspected chickenpox (varicella) and active vesicular lesions. Which transmission-based precautions are indicated?
options:
A) Standard Precautions only; no room placement considerations.
B) Airborne Precautions plus Contact Precautions (with Standard Precautions).
C) Droplet Precautions alone without airborne controls.
D) Protective (neutropenic) precautions only, without isolation of the infectious client.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. CDC lists varicella as Airborne + Contact + Standard, not Standard alone.
B: Correct. CDC Appendix A specifies Airborne + Contact + Standard for varicella until lesions are dry and crusted; Merck describes spread by infected airborne droplets/aerosolized particles and by direct contact with virus from skin lesions.
C: Incorrect. Droplet alone is insufficient for varicella; airborne controls are required.
D: Incorrect. Protective precautions protect immunocompromised hosts; the infectious varicella client needs source isolation.
topic: Varicella (chickenpox) — Airborne and Contact Precautions
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

stem: A client is diagnosed with pertussis (whooping cough). Which precautions should the nurse implement?
options:
A) Airborne Precautions with an airborne infection isolation room as first-line for all cases.
B) Droplet Precautions (with Standard Precautions), continued per guidance until effective antibiotic therapy criteria are met.
C) Contact Precautions only, because pertussis is spread solely by fomites.
D) No precautions are needed after the first hour of hospitalization.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. CDC lists pertussis under Droplet Precautions, not Airborne.
B: Correct. CDC specifies Droplet + Standard for pertussis until 5 days after initiation of effective antibiotic therapy; Merck notes droplet transmission and recommends respiratory droplet isolation until antibiotics have been given for 5 days.
C: Incorrect. Merck states transmission by contaminated articles is rare; primary spread is respiratory droplets.
D: Incorrect. Isolation continues for the CDC/Merck antibiotic-duration window, not one hour.
topic: Pertussis — Droplet Precautions
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_1_title: Isolation Precautions Appendix A — Type and Duration
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A postoperative client after thyroid surgery has perioral tingling and a positive Chvostek sign. Which electrolyte imbalance should the nurse suspect?
options:
A) Hypernatremia
B) Hypocalcemia
C) Hypermagnesemia as the only explanation
D) Isolated hyperchloremia without calcium change
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Hypernatremia presents with thirst/neurologic changes, not Chvostek sign as the classic bedside cue.
B: Correct. Merck identifies Chvostek and Trousseau signs for latent tetany of hypocalcemia; OpenStax lists positive Chvostek’s and Trousseau’s signs among hypocalcemia manifestations, including paresthesia around the lips.
C: Incorrect. Hypermagnesemia is not the classic association for Chvostek sign in these sources.
D: Incorrect. Chloride imbalance is not linked to Chvostek sign in the cited sources.
topic: Hypocalcemia — Chvostek/Trousseau and perioral paresthesia
units_note: Merck uses mg/dL and mmol/L for calcium; reference intervals vary by laboratory.

stem: A client taking a loop diuretic reports new muscle weakness and polyuria. Serum potassium is 2.8 mmol/L. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options:
A) Findings are consistent with hypokalemia, which can cause muscle weakness and cardiac effects.
B) Hypokalemia never affects skeletal muscle or the heart.
C) A potassium of 2.8 mmol/L is above the usual reference interval and indicates hyperkalemia.
D) Polyuria rules out any potassium imbalance.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck lists muscle weakness and polyuria among hypokalemia features and notes cardiac hyperexcitability with severe hypokalemia; OpenStax lists muscle weakness/cramps and ECG changes among hypokalemia manifestations, with serum potassium <3.5 mEq/L.
B: Incorrect. Both sources describe neuromuscular and cardiac effects of hypokalemia.
C: Incorrect. 2.8 mmol/L is below the usual ~3.5 mmol/L threshold cited for hypokalemia.
D: Incorrect. Merck includes polyuria among hypokalemia clinical features.
topic: Hypokalemia — muscle weakness and cardiac risk
units_note: Potassium mmol/L = mEq/L. Reference interval varies by laboratory.

stem: A nurse receives a written medication order that is missing the dose. According to College of Nurses of Ontario medication accountabilities and standard medication-order practice, what should the nurse do next?
options:
A) Administer a commonly used dose of the medication for this indication and document the estimate.
B) Do not administer the medication; follow up with the prescriber in a timely manner to clarify and correct the incomplete order.
C) Ask another nurse on the unit what dose is usually given and proceed with that dose.
D) Omit the dose for this shift and wait to see whether the client asks for the medication.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Guessing a dose from habit does not meet the requirement for a clear, complete, appropriate order.
B: Correct. CNO requires nurses to accept only clear, complete, and appropriate medication orders and, when an order is unclear, incomplete, or inappropriate, to not perform the medication practice and to follow up with a prescriber promptly; OpenStax likewise directs the nurse to contact the prescribing provider when any order component is missing.
C: Incorrect. Relying on a colleague’s usual dose does not clarify the incomplete order with the authorized prescriber.
D: Incorrect. Delaying without clarifying leaves the incomplete order unresolved and does not meet timely follow-up expectations.
topic: Medication orders — clarify incomplete; do not administer until complete
jurisdiction_note: CNO Medication practice standard sets Ontario accountabilities for accepting medication orders; OpenStax supports clarifying missing order components as general nursing practice.
source_1_section: Authority — accept orders that are clear, complete, appropriate; follow up when unclear/incomplete/inappropriate
source_1_source_date: Updated July 2025 (version transition noted toward Mar 1, 2027)

stem: A nurse is giving a structured handoff report about a client whose condition is deteriorating. Using the SBAR communication framework, which information belongs in the Situation step?
options:
A) A concise statement of what is currently happening, including who is calling and a brief description of the current problem.
B) A full chronological review of the client’s entire medical history since childhood.
C) Only the nurse’s preferred discharge destination for the client.
D) A list of every medication the client has ever taken, without stating the current concern.
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ describes Situation as stating what is currently happening, typically beginning with the communicator’s identity, patient identifiers, and a brief statement of the current problem; OpenStax presents SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) as an evidence-based handoff method for safe transfers.
B: Incorrect. Exhaustive lifelong history belongs in Background only as relevant context, not as the Situation step.
C: Incorrect. Discharge preference is not the Situation step’s focus during an acute deterioration handoff.
D: Incorrect. An unstructured medication list without the current problem does not frame the Situation.
topic: Handoff communication — SBAR Situation step
source_1_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)

stem: A nurse overhears a colleague make a discriminatory remark about a client’s cultural background during care planning. According to the College of Nurses of Ontario Code of Conduct and culturally safe practice principles, which action is required?
options:
A) Ignore the remark to avoid conflict, because cultural differences should not affect nursing care.
B) Take proper action to address the discrimination and advocate for equitable, culturally safe care free from discrimination.
C) Tell the client to adapt to the unit’s usual cultural practices so care can proceed smoothly.
D) Document that all cultural groups experience health care the same way, so no follow-up is needed.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. CNO expects nurses to take proper action when they observe or identify discrimination; ignoring it does not uphold culturally safe care.
B: Correct. CNO Principle 2 requires nurses to advocate for equitable and culturally safe care free from discrimination and to take proper action when they observe or identify discrimination; OpenStax identifies cultural imposition (forcing one’s own values onto another) as contrary to cultural humility.
C: Incorrect. Imposing unit cultural practices on the client is cultural imposition, which OpenStax states runs counter to cultural humility.
D: Incorrect. Assuming all cultural groups share identical experiences is cultural blindness and does not address discrimination.
topic: Culturally safe care — act on observed discrimination
jurisdiction_note: CNO Code of Conduct Principle 2 sets Ontario expectations for inclusive, culturally safe care; OpenStax supports cultural humility versus cultural imposition as concordant general practice.
source_1_section: Principle 2 — inclusive and culturally safe care; take action on discrimination

stem: A client with limited English proficiency needs to discuss a new diagnosis and consent for a procedure. Which nursing action best supports accurate, culturally safe communication?
options:
A) Ask the client’s adolescent child who speaks English to interpret the entire discussion.
B) Obtain a trained medical interpreter and speak directly to the client.
C) Proceed in English only, speaking loudly and slowly without interpretation support.
D) Skip the discussion and have the client sign the consent form later without explanation.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. OpenStax advises against using family members as interpreters because clients may withhold sensitive information and family may edit content or lack medical terminology.
B: Correct. OpenStax directs use of a trained medical interpreter and addressing the client directly; CNO expects inclusive, culturally safe care and clear communication of proposed care details.
C: Incorrect. Loud English without interpretation does not provide linguistically appropriate communication.
D: Incorrect. Consent and care explanations require clear communication; skipping explanation violates informed, respectful care expectations.
topic: Language access — trained medical interpreter, not family
jurisdiction_note: OpenStax linguistic competence guidance is general; CNO Code supports culturally safe, clear client communication in Ontario without prescribing US Joint Commission rules.
source_2_section: Principle 2 culturally safe care; Principle 1 clear timely communication of proposed care

stem: An interprofessional team is revising a client’s plan of care after a change in condition. Which nursing action best reflects College of Nurses of Ontario expectations for working with the health care team and collaborative practice?
options:
A) Collaborate and communicate with the health care team in a clear, effective way, contributing information needed for shared decisions about the plan of care.
B) Make all plan changes independently without informing other team members to save time.
C) Refuse to share assessment findings because documentation belongs only to nursing.
D) Address team members dismissively if their recommendations differ from the nurse’s preference.
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO Code Principle 4 requires nurses to collaborate and communicate with the health care team clearly and effectively; OpenStax collaborative practice emphasizes clear roles, shared decision-making, and personal accountability within the team.
B: Incorrect. Unilateral changes without team communication undermine collaborative practice and continuity.
C: Incorrect. Withholding relevant assessment findings from the team blocks effective collaboration.
D: Incorrect. CNO requires treating health care team members with respect; dismissive behaviour conflicts with Principle 4.
topic: Interprofessional collaboration — clear team communication
jurisdiction_note: CNO Code Principle 4 sets Ontario team-conduct expectations; OpenStax collaborative-practice competencies are a concordant second source.
source_1_section: Principle 4 — work respectfully with the health care team (4.5–4.6)
source_2_section: Clear Roles and Responsibilities; Using Shared Decision-Making and Collaboration

stem: A client is admitted with suspected meningococcal meningitis. Which infection-prevention action is indicated while awaiting response to antimicrobial therapy?
options:
A) Place the client on Droplet Precautions (with Standard Precautions), including wearing a mask on room entry, until 24 hours after initiation of effective therapy.
B) Use only Standard Precautions because bacterial meningitis never requires transmission-based precautions.
C) Place the client on Airborne Precautions in a negative-pressure room for the entire hospitalization regardless of treatment.
D) Wear only gloves at the doorway and leave the door open to promote ventilation.
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC Isolation Precautions Appendix A lists meningococcal disease (including meningococcal meningitis) as Droplet + Standard until 24 hours after initiation of effective therapy; OpenStax states Droplet Precautions include donning a mask upon entering the room.
B: Incorrect. CDC specifies Droplet Precautions for meningococcal meningitis, not Standard alone.
C: Incorrect. Meningococcal disease is managed with Droplet Precautions per CDC, not indefinite Airborne Precautions.
D: Incorrect. Droplet Precautions require a mask on entry; gloves alone at the doorway are insufficient.
topic: Meningococcal disease — Droplet Precautions until 24 hours of effective therapy
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_1_title: Appendix A: Type and Duration of Precautions Recommended for Selected Infections and Conditions
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A parent asks what to expect after a toddler’s routine immunizations. Which teaching statement is accurate based on Canadian immunization guidance and concordant vaccine safety information?
options:
A) Mild fever, fussiness, or injection-site soreness can occur and usually resolve within hours to a few days; acetaminophen or ibuprofen may be used afterward for fever or discomfort if needed, but giving oral analgesics before or at the time of injection to prevent pain is not recommended.
B) Any fever after vaccination means the vaccine failed and the doses must be repeated immediately.
C) Parents should always give acetaminophen immediately before every vaccine dose to prevent all reactions.
D) Mild fever after vaccination never occurs and should always be treated as a vaccine allergy.
rationales:
A: Correct. Canada.ca states mild fever and related symptoms are normal and usually resolve within hours to a few days, and medication may be given for fever or pain if needed; the Canadian Immunization Guide states oral analgesics are not recommended before or at the time of injection to reduce pain, but acetaminophen or ibuprofen can be used afterward for fever or injection-site discomfort; CDC MMR VIS also lists fever as a possible reaction after MMR.
B: Incorrect. Mild fever reflects an immune response, not automatic vaccine failure requiring immediate repeat dosing.
C: Incorrect. CIG specifically does not recommend oral analgesics prior to or at the time of vaccine injection for pain prevention.
D: Incorrect. Mild fever can occur after vaccination and is not by itself a severe allergic reaction.
topic: Childhood immunization — expected mild fever; analgesics after, not prophylactically before
jurisdiction_note: Canadian Immunization Guide and Canada.ca childhood vaccination pages are Canadian authorities; CDC VIS supports fever as a known post-MMR reaction as a concordant second-publisher safety fact.
source_1_publisher: Public Health Agency of Canada / Canada.ca
source_2_title: Vaccine administration practices: Canadian Immunization Guide
source_2_publisher: Public Health Agency of Canada / Canada.ca
source_2_section: Oral analgesics; Post-vaccination counselling and observation

source_3_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: One hour after a vaginal birth, the nurse finds the uterine fundus soft and boggy with increased vaginal bleeding. Which action should the nurse take first?
options:
A) Perform fundal massage to stimulate uterine contraction until the fundus becomes firm.
B) Encourage the client to ambulate in the hallway before reassessing the fundus.
C) Apply an ice pack to the perineum and delay fundal assessment until the next shift.
D) Discontinue all monitoring because early postpartum bleeding is always normal.
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax identifies fundal massage as almost always the first intervention for postpartum bleeding from a soft fundus, massaging until the uterus becomes firm; Merck lists uterine massage among primary treatments for postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony.
B: Incorrect. Ambulation delays immediate management of a boggy, bleeding uterus.
C: Incorrect. Delaying fundal assessment and massage allows ongoing atony-related bleeding.
D: Incorrect. A soft boggy fundus with increased bleeding requires prompt intervention, not discontinuation of monitoring.
topic: Postpartum hemorrhage — fundal massage for boggy uterus

stem: An older adult client is on bed rest and is at high risk for pressure injury. Which nursing intervention best reflects evidence-based pressure-injury prevention?
options:
A) Reposition the client at least every 2 hours and offload pressure from bony prominences.
B) Keep the client in one position for the entire shift to promote rest.
C) Massage reddened bony prominences vigorously every hour.
D) Raise the head of the bed as high as possible at all times to reduce shear.
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax describes turning and repositioning about every two hours (with individualized frequency) and off-loading pressure areas; Merck states bed-confined patients should be turned a minimum of every 2 hours as the most important pressure-reduction factor.
B: Incorrect. Prolonged immobility without repositioning increases pressure-injury risk.
C: Incorrect. Vigorous massage of reddened areas is not the prevention strategy supported by these sources; pressure relief is.
D: Incorrect. Merck advises keeping head-of-bed elevation minimal during repositioning considerations to limit shearing forces—not maximizing elevation at all times.
topic: Pressure injury prevention — reposition at least every 2 hours

stem: During a home visit, a nurse finds an older adult client without adequate food, soiled clothing, and no access to prescribed medications, while the caregiver controls the client’s finances. Which interpretation and action are most appropriate?
options:
A) Recognize possible elder abuse including neglect and financial exploitation, and follow agency policy to report and seek protective services.
B) Assume the situation is a normal part of aging and take no action.
C) Advise the caregiver that withholding food is acceptable if the client is difficult to care for.
D) Document only that the client prefers an untidy environment and discontinue follow-up.
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC defines neglect as failure to meet basic needs (including food, clothing, hygiene, and essential medical care) and financial abuse as improper use of an older adult’s resources, and advises learning to recognize and report abuse; OpenStax likewise describes elder abuse forms including neglect and financial abuse and notes caregiver mistreatment risk.
B: Incorrect. Failure to meet basic needs is not normal aging and warrants action.
C: Incorrect. Withholding food is neglect and is not acceptable caregiving.
D: Incorrect. Signs of unmet basic needs and financial control require reporting pathways, not dismissal.
topic: Elder abuse — recognize neglect and report
jurisdiction_note: CDC and OpenStax define abuse/neglect concordantly; local Canadian reporting pathways follow provincial legislation and employer policy (not tested as a specific statute here).
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_1_section: What is older person abuse?; Prevention

stem: An RN is organizing care with an unregulated care provider (UCP/assistive personnel). Which assignment decision is most appropriate?
options:
A) Assign routine assistance with activities of daily living for a stable client, while the RN retains overall accountability and performs assessments requiring nursing judgment.
B) Assign the UCP to complete the initial admission assessment and interpret abnormal laboratory results for an unstable client.
C) Ask the UCP to decide which controlled-act medication injections the client should receive today.
D) Transfer full legal accountability for all nursing outcomes to the UCP for the shift.
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Right Circumstance requires that delegated work involve patients in stable condition with expected responses; CNO describes assigning as allocating responsibility for particular aspects of care by nurses with necessary knowledge and judgment, while nurses remain accountable for decisions about UCP activities.
B: Incorrect. Initial assessment and interpreting labs for an unstable client require nursing judgment and are not appropriate UCP assignment.
C: Incorrect. Deciding medication injections is not an appropriate UCP assignment of nursing authority.
D: Incorrect. Nurses retain professional accountability and cannot transfer full legal accountability for nursing outcomes to a UCP.
topic: Assignment to UCP — stable ADLs; RN keeps nursing judgment tasks
jurisdiction_note: CNO Working With Unregulated Care Providers guides Ontario assignment/delegation language; OpenStax Five Rights of Delegation (Right Circumstance) is a concordant general framework.

stem: A nurse is teaching parents after a child’s immunizations. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Mild fever, fussiness, or redness at the injection site can occur and usually improve within hours to a few days.
B) The child should be observed for at least 15 minutes after immunization for possible acute reactions.
C) Acetaminophen or ibuprofen may be used after vaccination if needed for fever or injection-site discomfort.
D) Any mild fever means the child is having anaphylaxis and epinephrine is always required at home.
E) Oral analgesics should routinely be given before every vaccine dose because they are proven to prevent all vaccine reactions.
rationales:
A: Correct. Canada.ca lists mild fever, fussiness, and injection-site reactions as common and usually short-lived; CDC VIS also notes fever can follow MMR.
B: Correct. The Canadian Immunization Guide recommends observation for at least 15 minutes after immunization (30 minutes preferred when there is specific concern).
C: Correct. CIG states oral analgesics/antipyretics such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen can be used after vaccination for fever or injection-site discomfort.
D: Incorrect. Mild fever alone is a common expected reaction, not a definition of anaphylaxis requiring home epinephrine for every fever.
E: Incorrect. CIG does not recommend oral analgesics before or at the time of injection to reduce pain, noting lack of benefit for that purpose.
topic: Post-immunization teaching SATA — expected reactions, observation, aftercare analgesics
jurisdiction_note: Canadian Immunization Guide and Canada.ca are Canadian authorities; CDC VIS provides independent-publisher support that fever can occur after MMR.
source_1_publisher: Public Health Agency of Canada / Canada.ca
source_2_title: Vaccine administration practices: Canadian Immunization Guide
source_2_publisher: Public Health Agency of Canada / Canada.ca
source_2_section: Oral analgesics; Post-vaccination counselling and observation
source_2_source_date: Last complete chapter revision: November 2017 (page accessed 2026-11-25)
