stem: A postpartum client receiving a continuous intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion for preeclampsia with severe features develops loss of deep tendon reflexes and respiratory depression. According to maternity nursing practice standards for magnesium toxicity, what should the nurse do first?
options:
A) Continue the infusion at the same rate and reassess reflexes in 1 hour.
B) Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion immediately and notify the health-care provider.
C) Increase the infusion rate to deepen the anticonvulsant effect.
D) Administer an additional 4 g magnesium sulfate bolus now.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Continuing the infusion when toxicity signs (absent reflexes, respiratory depression) are present allows magnesium levels to rise further.
B: Correct. OpenStax directs the nurse to stop the magnesium infusion immediately and notify the provider when toxicity signs appear (loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression); Merck likewise treats significant magnesium toxicity symptoms with calcium gluconate after recognizing toxic levels.
C: Incorrect. Increasing the rate would worsen magnesium toxicity.
D: Incorrect. An additional bolus is used for seizure prevention/treatment dosing, not when toxicity is already evident.
topic: Magnesium sulfate toxicity — stop infusion immediately
source_1_section: Safe Administration and Monitoring of Magnesium Sulfate during Pregnancy

stem: A labouring client with preeclampsia with severe features is receiving intravenous magnesium sulfate. The nurse notes absent deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate 10/min, and oxygen saturation 89% on room air. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated at this time.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion immediately."}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Notify the health-care provider of the toxicity findings."}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Ensure calcium gluconate is available and administer as ordered."}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Increase the magnesium sulfate infusion rate to deepen neuromuscular blockade."}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Draw a serum magnesium level as directed after stopping the infusion."}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. OpenStax lists stopping the infusion immediately as the first response to magnesium toxicity signs such as decreased deep tendon reflexes and respiratory depression.
R2: Indicated. The provider must be notified promptly when toxicity signs appear so antidote therapy and further orders can be given.
R3: Indicated. OpenStax identifies calcium gluconate as the antidote that should be accessible (usually at the bedside) and administered as ordered; Merck supports calcium gluconate IV for significant magnesium toxicity symptoms.
R4: Not indicated. Increasing the infusion would worsen toxicity and is opposite to the required action.
R5: Indicated. OpenStax directs the nurse to draw a magnesium level immediately after stopping the infusion as part of the toxicity response.
topic: NGN matrix — magnesium toxicity indicated nursing actions
source_1_section: Safe Administration and Monitoring of Magnesium Sulfate during Pregnancy

stem: A client at 34 weeks’ gestation with known preeclampsia reports a new severe headache and blurred vision. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options:
A) Reassure the client that headache is common in late pregnancy and document the report.
B) Encourage ambulation in the hallway to relieve tension headache.
C) Notify the health-care provider promptly of possible worsening preeclampsia with severe features.
D) Delay assessment until the next scheduled prenatal visit in 1 week.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. New severe headache with visual change is a warning sign of severe-feature preeclampsia, not a benign late-pregnancy complaint to only document.
B: Incorrect. Ambulation does not address evolving neurologic end-organ involvement and may delay needed evaluation.
C: Correct. OpenStax and Merck identify severe headache and visual disturbances as features of preeclampsia with severe features that require prompt recognition and reporting so seizure prevention and delivery decisions can be made.
D: Incorrect. Waiting a week risks progression to eclampsia or other organ injury.
topic: Preeclampsia severe features — headache and visual changes require prompt reporting
source_2_section: Symptoms and Signs of Preeclampsia and Eclampsia

stem: A breastfeeding client at 3 weeks postpartum has unilateral breast erythema, warmth, and tenderness with fever. The provider diagnoses mastitis and starts oral antistaphylococcal antibiotics. Which teaching is most appropriate?
options:
A) Stop breastfeeding immediately and wean permanently to prevent spreading infection to the infant.
B) Continue breastfeeding and/or pumping to empty the affected breast during treatment.
C) Apply ice packs only and avoid emptying the breast until the fever resolves.
D) Bind both breasts tightly and withhold feeds for 48 hours.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Merck states breastfeeding and/or pumping should continue during treatment because emptying the affected breast is part of therapy.
B: Correct. Merck and WHO identify effective emptying of the affected breast—continuing breastfeeding and/or expressing/pumping—as essential treatment; stopping breastfeeding is not required for therapy.
C: Incorrect. Avoiding emptying promotes engorgement and works against recommended therapy.
D: Incorrect. Binding and withholding feeds are not recommended management for mastitis.
topic: Mastitis — continue breastfeeding/pumping to empty the affected breast
source_2_section: 9.2 Mastitis — Effective milk removal / Supportive counselling
source_2_source_date: WHO/FCH/CAH/00.13 (document date not restated on extracted text; revised ed. 1997 noted in related WHO materials)

stem: Parents of a 6-week-old infant ask how their child should ride in the family vehicle. Which instruction is most appropriate?
options:
A) Place the infant in a forward-facing seat with a lap belt only in the front passenger seat.
B) Use a rear-facing car seat installed in the back seat according to the manufacturer’s limits.
C) Hold the infant securely on an adult’s lap if the trip is shorter than 30 minutes.
D) Use an adult seat belt alone because infants under 3 months do not need a car seat.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Infants must ride rear-facing; the front seat is not the safest location for young children.
B: Correct. Canadian Paediatric Society Caring for Kids and NHTSA both state infants should use a rear-facing car seat and remain rear-facing as long as they fit the manufacturer’s height and weight limits; the back seat is safest.
C: Incorrect. Holding an infant on a lap does not provide crash protection.
D: Incorrect. All infants require an appropriate child restraint; adult belts alone are unsafe.
topic: Infant car seat — rear-facing in the back seat
jurisdiction_note: CPS Caring for Kids (Canada) and NHTSA (US) concord on rear-facing for infants and maximizing rear-facing duration within manufacturer limits.
source_1_publisher: Canadian Paediatric Society — Caring for Kids
source_1_section: What type of car seat should I use? — Rear-facing car seat
source_2_publisher: U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA)
source_2_section: Rear-Facing Car Seat — Birth–12 Months / 1–3 Years

stem: An alert 18-month-old with gastroenteritis has mild to moderate dehydration, is able to drink, and has no signs of shock. Which fluid plan is most appropriate initially?
options:
A) Immediate intravenous isotonic fluid boluses as first-line therapy for all mild dehydration.
B) Oral rehydration solution in frequent small amounts, reserving IV fluids for severe dehydration or inability to take oral fluids.
C) Undiluted fruit juice ad libitum as the preferred rehydration fluid.
D) Nothing by mouth for 12 hours to rest the bowel before any fluids.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Merck and CDC recommend oral rehydration for mild to moderate dehydration; IV is for severe dehydration or when oral intake is not possible.
B: Correct. AAP/WHO/Merck and CDC guidance support oral rehydration therapy for mild to moderate dehydration when the child can take fluids orally; severe dehydration with circulatory compromise needs IV fluids.
C: Incorrect. Commercial ORS with appropriate glucose–sodium composition is preferred over high-sugar juices that can worsen diarrhea.
D: Incorrect. Gut rest with prolonged NPO is not recommended; rehydration and early feeding are preferred.
topic: Pediatric mild–moderate dehydration — oral rehydration first
source_2_title: Managing Acute Gastroenteritis Among Children: Oral Rehydration, Maintenance, and Nutritional Therapy
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_2_section: Acute Gastroenteritis Therapy Based on Degree of Dehydration

stem: An otherwise healthy 8-month-old is diagnosed with typical viral bronchiolitis. Which statement best reflects evidence-based management?
options:
A) Routine nebulized salbutamol should be given to every wheezing infant with bronchiolitis.
B) Management is primarily supportive (hydration, gentle nasal suctioning, oxygen if needed); routine salbutamol is not recommended when the diagnosis is clear.
C) Systemic corticosteroids are first-line therapy to shorten every hospital stay.
D) Chest physiotherapy with percussion is required for all admitted infants.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. CPS states that when bronchiolitis diagnosis is clear, a trial of salbutamol is not recommended; Merck notes bronchodilators are not uniformly effective.
B: Correct. CPS and Merck describe supportive care as the mainstay (hydration, oxygen as needed, comfort measures); CPS explicitly does not recommend routine salbutamol for clear bronchiolitis.
C: Incorrect. CPS states corticosteroids are not recommended for routine use in bronchiolitis.
D: Incorrect. CPS states chest physiotherapy is not recommended for bronchiolitis treatment.
topic: Bronchiolitis — supportive care; no routine salbutamol
jurisdiction_note: CPS (Canada) and Merck (general) concord that care is primarily supportive and bronchodilators are not routinely effective/recommended in typical bronchiolitis.
source_1_title: Bronchiolitis: Recommendations for diagnosis, monitoring and management of children one to 24 months

stem: A client on a mental health unit becomes increasingly agitated but is not yet physically assaultive. Which nursing approach best reflects the right to least restrictive treatment?
options:
A) Apply four-point restraints immediately to prevent any future escalation.
B) Place the client in locked seclusion as the first intervention.
C) Attempt de-escalation first (calm communication, reduce stimuli, offer time-out or PRN medication as appropriate) before seclusion or restraint.
D) Ignore the agitation until violence occurs, then call security only.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Restraint is among the most restrictive measures and is reserved for last resort after less restrictive options fail.
B: Incorrect. Seclusion is a highly restrictive intervention used when less restrictive measures have not been effective.
C: Correct. OpenStax requires least restrictive measures first (de-escalation, reduce stimuli, time-out, PRN medication). Merck likewise states seclusion or restraint is a last resort after lesser restrictive interventions have been attempted.
D: Incorrect. Early intervention with least restrictive strategies is required; waiting for violence is unsafe and not therapeutic.
topic: Aggression — least restrictive alternatives before seclusion/restraint
jurisdiction_note: Least-restrictive principles are general; Ontario also has Patient Restraints Minimization Act for hospital restraints (tested separately).
source_1_section: Least Restrictive Alternatives to Managing Aggression / The Use of Seclusion
source_2_section: Seclusion or Physical Restraints / Potentially violent patients

stem: A young adult starts a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) for major depressive disorder and asks when to expect full benefit. Which teaching is most accurate?
options:
A) Full therapeutic effects are usually immediate within the first dose.
B) Effects may begin in about 2 weeks, with full therapeutic effects often by 4 to 6 weeks; report worsening depression or suicidal thoughts promptly.
C) If mood is not fully improved by day 3, stop the medication without contacting the provider.
D) SSRIs never require monitoring for mood changes after starting therapy.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. OpenStax and Merck indicate antidepressant benefit is delayed, not immediate after one dose.
B: Correct. OpenStax nursing implications state effects may start in about 2 weeks with full effects in 4–6 weeks, and clients must report increased depression or suicidal ideation; Merck notes improvement may not be apparent until after 1 to 4 weeks.
C: Incorrect. Stopping abruptly without guidance is unsafe; delayed onset is expected and the provider should be contacted for concerns.
D: Incorrect. Antidepressants require monitoring for worsening mood and suicidality, especially in younger clients.
topic: SSRI/antidepressant — delayed onset; monitor for worsening mood/suicidality

stem: A hospitalized client with major depression discloses a specific plan to die by suicide using available bed linens and refuses to leave the room. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Arrange for the client to be placed under observation.
B) Communicate therapeutically and provide emotional support.
C) Leave the client alone in the room with the door closed for privacy.
D) Work to limit access to lethal means as part of the safety plan.
E) Validate the client’s experiences and feelings.
F) Withhold all prescribed medications permanently without an order.
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax case guidance includes arranging observation for a client with an active inpatient suicide plan.
B: Correct. Therapeutic communication and emotional support are core nursing actions for a suicidal client.
C: Incorrect. Leaving a high-risk client alone reduces observation and safety.
D: Correct. Limiting access to lethal means is a crucial part of a safety plan.
E: Correct. Validating experiences and feelings supports engagement and assessment.
F: Incorrect. Withholding medications without an order is not an appropriate suicide-prevention action and may worsen depression.
topic: Suicide safety SATA — observation, means restriction, therapeutic support
source_1_section: Depression: Part 3 / Methods Used in Suicide

stem: A community health nurse teaches a caregiver about preventing childhood lead exposure in an older home. Which statement indicates correct understanding of primary prevention?
options:
A) Primary prevention means waiting until a blood lead level is high before any environmental action.
B) The most effective approach is to prevent exposure by controlling or removing lead hazards in the environment before a child is exposed.
C) Lead in household dust is harmless to toddlers because they do not ingest dust.
D) Sanding old lead paint without dust control is the preferred way to renovate a child’s bedroom.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. That describes delayed secondary action; CDC defines primary prevention as removing hazards before exposure.
B: Correct. CDC states primary prevention—removing lead hazards before a child is exposed—is the most effective approach; Health Canada likewise emphasizes reducing environmental lead exposure and safely managing lead paint/dust risks for children.
C: Incorrect. Health Canada notes babies and small children can ingest household dust through mouthing behaviours.
D: Incorrect. Health Canada warns mechanical removal/sanding can release hazardous lead dust and should be avoided.
topic: Childhood lead — primary prevention by removing environmental hazards
jurisdiction_note: CDC primary-prevention framing and Health Canada lead exposure reduction/safe paint management are concordant on preventing childhood exposure.
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_2_title: Lead information package — some commonly asked questions about lead and human health
source_2_section: Household dust / What should I do about lead-based paint in my home?

stem: A nurse is teaching a client on day 1 after a vaginal birth about reducing uterine afterpains and keeping the fundus firm. Which instruction is most appropriate?
options:
A) Limit fluid intake so the bladder stays full to cushion the uterus.
B) Empty the bladder often because a full bladder can displace the uterus and increase cramping.
C) Avoid breastfeeding for 48 hours to prevent oxytocin release.
D) Remain on complete bed rest without ambulating to the bathroom.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. A full bladder displaces the uterus and worsens afterpains; fluids should not be limited for that purpose.
B: Correct. OpenStax teaches that a full bladder displaces the uterus, requiring stronger contractions to stay firm and increasing pain; frequent emptying is encouraged. Merck notes early postpartum uterine afterpains during involution.
C: Incorrect. Breastfeeding-related oxytocin supports involution; avoiding feeding is not appropriate teaching for afterpain control.
D: Incorrect. Clients need to void; preventing bathroom access promotes bladder distention.
topic: Postpartum — empty bladder often to prevent uterine displacement and afterpains
source_1_title: 20.3 Nursing Care During the Postpartum Period

stem: An 82-year-old client with several chronic conditions is starting a new oral medication. According to safe prescribing principles for older adults, which nursing action best reduces medication-related risk?
options:
A) Encourage starting at the highest labelled adult dose to achieve a rapid effect.
B) Advocate for starting at the lowest effective dose and using the fewest medications necessary.
C) Advise crushing all extended-release tablets to improve absorption.
D) Recommend adding two over-the-counter supplements without reviewing the current regimen.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Older adults are more susceptible to adverse effects; starting at the highest adult dose increases toxicity risk.
B: Correct. Merck advises starting medications at the lowest effective dose and using the fewest medications necessary; OpenStax urges the least complicated regimen and review for drugs that can be discontinued.
C: Incorrect. OpenStax notes some capsules and extended-release pills should remain intact.
D: Incorrect. Adding supplements without reconciliation increases polypharmacy and interaction risk.
topic: Older adults — start lowest effective dose; fewest medications
source_1_section: Prevention — Before starting a new medication

stem: An ambulatory older adult who has fallen twice in the past year takes several medications, including an opioid analgesic. Which intervention should the nurse prioritize to reduce future fall risk related to medications?
options:
A) Advise that fall-risk medications cannot be changed once prescribed.
B) Collaborate for a medication review to stop or minimize fall-risk drugs when possible and use the lowest effective dose.
C) Increase the opioid dose at bedtime so the client sleeps through the night and avoids toileting.
D) Discourage medication review because falls are inevitable with aging.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Merck states medications that increase fall risk should be stopped when possible or adjusted to the lowest effective dose.
B: Correct. Merck recommends reviewing medications for fall-risk impact and stopping or dose-adjusting when possible; OpenStax notes narcotics increase fall risk in older adults and require caution and teaching.
C: Incorrect. Increasing an opioid can worsen sedation and fall risk.
D: Incorrect. Fall risk can be reduced with multifactorial interventions including medication review.
topic: Falls — medication review to reduce fall-risk drugs
source_1_section: Prevention of Falls and Injury Mitigation — Medical management
source_2_section: Narcotic Use and Risk of Falls in Older Adults

stem: The nurse is teaching a family how to communicate with an older adult who has age-related hearing loss (presbycusis). Which actions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Face the client so the speaker’s mouth is visible.
B) Reduce competing background noise when possible.
C) Encourage use of prescribed hearing aids or assistive listening devices.
D) Speak only from another room so the client practices listening.
E) Shout directly into one ear from behind the client.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck notes lip-/speech-reading helps discrimination and that professionals should position so the listener can see the speaker’s mouth.
B: Correct. OpenStax identifies noise as a physical communication barrier and advises reducing extraneous noise; Merck describes modifying noisy listening environments.
C: Correct. OpenStax recommends hearing aids or assistive listening devices for age-related hearing loss.
D: Incorrect. Speaking from another room removes visual speech cues and worsens understanding.
E: Incorrect. Shouting from behind prevents lip-reading and can distort speech.
topic: Hearing impairment — face client, reduce noise, use assistive devices
source_2_section: Alterations in Senses with Aging — Hearing

stem: An older adult living alone reports nearly falling at home after tripping on a throw rug in a dim hallway. For each nursing recommendation, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated to reduce environmental fall risk.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Clear walkways of clutter and secure or remove loose throw rugs."}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Improve lighting in hallways and pathways used at night."}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Encourage rushing to the bathroom in the dark to minimize time out of bed."}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Keep frequently used paths free of furniture that blocks movement."}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Add more loose scatter rugs for softer flooring in every room."}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. OpenStax advises clearing pathways and notes rugs increase fall risk; Merck identifies environmental hazards as extrinsic fall factors.
R2: Indicated. Inadequate lighting, especially at night, is a situational/environmental fall risk addressed by improving lighting.
R3: Not indicated. Merck lists rushing to the bathroom at night with inadequate lighting as a situational fall risk.
R4: Indicated. Clearing furniture that obstructs pathways reduces environmental hazards.
R5: Not indicated. Additional loose rugs increase trip hazards rather than reduce them.
topic: NGN matrix — home environmental fall-hazard interventions
source_1_section: Etiology of Falls — Extrinsic and situational factors

stem: An Ontario RN is deciding whether aspects of care may be performed by an unregulated care provider (UCP). Which client situation best supports assigning or having a UCP perform the activity?
options:
A) The client’s condition is unstable and expected to change unpredictably over the shift.
B) The client has established, well-defined care needs, a well-controlled condition not expected to change, and the UCP’s competence for the activity has been verified.
C) The RN has never verified the UCP’s competence but the procedure looks straightforward.
D) The activity requires nursing evaluation of an evolving response to a new medication titration.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. CNO’s decision tree asks whether the client’s condition is well controlled/managed and not expected to change; OpenStax likewise requires stable condition with expected outcomes before delegating.
B: Correct. CNO lists established well-defined needs and a well-controlled condition not expected to change among client factors, and requires knowing the UCP is competent for the client in the given circumstances; OpenStax right circumstance requires stability with expected outcomes.
C: Incorrect. CNO states a nurse cannot assume UCP competence regardless of how straightforward a procedure appears.
D: Incorrect. Evaluating response to treatment requires nursing judgment and is not appropriate UCP work in this context.
topic: Ontario UCP assignment — stable, well-defined needs and verified competence
jurisdiction_note: CNO Working With Unregulated Care Providers practice guideline is the Ontario authority for RN–UCP assignment decisions; OpenStax ANA-NCSBN five rights provide concordant stability guidance.
source_1_section: Appendix A: Decision Tree — The Client Assessment; Expectations for nurses who work with UCPs

stem: While preparing an intravenous antibiotic, a nurse notices the wrong vial was nearly selected and stops before administration. What is the most appropriate next action in a culture of safety?
options:
A) Discard the near miss quietly without reporting because no harm occurred.
B) Report the near miss through the organization’s safety reporting process so system improvements can be made.
C) Administer a double dose of the correct antibiotic to compensate for the almost-error.
D) Blame a coworker publicly at the nursing station without documenting the event.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Near misses are learning opportunities; failing to report prevents system improvement.
B: Correct. OpenStax describes reporting near-miss incidents so practice and policy can improve; AHRQ defines a culture of safety as including a blame-free environment where individuals can report errors or near misses without fear of reprimand.
C: Incorrect. Administering an unauthorized double dose is unsafe and unrelated to near-miss learning.
D: Incorrect. A just/safety culture emphasizes nonpunitive reporting and system learning, not public blaming.
topic: Near miss — report to support culture of safety
source_1_section: Near Events or Misses; Near Miss with Medication
source_2_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) — PSNet

stem: A public health nurse helps organize a community program that offers fecal immunochemical testing (FIT) to asymptomatic adults to detect colorectal cancer early. Which level of prevention does this activity represent?
options:
A) Primary prevention
B) Secondary prevention
C) Tertiary prevention
D) Quaternary prevention
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Primary prevention aims to prevent disease occurrence (for example, immunization campaigns), not detect existing subclinical disease.
B: Correct. OpenStax defines secondary prevention as early disease detection in healthy-appearing individuals with subclinical disease; CDC explains colorectal screening finds polyps/cancer early when treatment works best.
C: Incorrect. Tertiary prevention targets clinical disease to reduce severity and sequelae after diagnosis.
D: Incorrect. Quaternary prevention is not the OpenStax framework level described for population screening programs in this context.
topic: Secondary prevention — asymptomatic colorectal screening
jurisdiction_note: Item tests secondary-prevention concept (early detection), not a specific start-age recommendation that differs across jurisdictions.
source_1_title: 15.2 Health Promotion and Disease Prevention Interventions
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A community health nurse teaches a household preparedness class. Which teaching point best reflects recommended personal disaster preparedness?
options:
A) Wait until a disaster is announced before gathering any water or food supplies.
B) Assemble a household emergency kit in advance with multi-day water and non-perishable food, and know where the kit is kept.
C) Rely solely on neighbours to provide all medications after an emergency begins.
D) Store the only household kit in a locked attic that no family member can access quickly.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Preparedness includes accumulating supplies before a disaster occurs.
B: Correct. OpenStax states preparedness plans include accumulating disaster supplies; Ready.gov recommends a multi-day water/food kit kept in a designated, ready-to-grab location.
C: Incorrect. Ready.gov advises organizing prescription medications as part of the kit because pharmacies may be inaccessible.
D: Incorrect. The kit should be ready and known to household members for quick use or evacuation.
topic: Disaster preparedness — household emergency supply kit
source_2_publisher: U.S. Department of Homeland Security — Ready.gov
source_2_section: Basic Disaster Supplies Kit; Kit Storage Locations

stem: A parent asks what fever medicine is safe for a 7-year-old with influenza-like illness. Which teaching is correct?
options:
A) Give aspirin (ASA) because it is the preferred antipyretic for influenza.
B) Avoid aspirin (ASA); use acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed because aspirin increases Reye syndrome risk with certain viral illnesses.
C) Any salicylate-containing product is required to prevent Reye syndrome.
D) Aspirin is safer than acetaminophen for chickenpox and influenza in school-age children.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Merck and CPS advise avoiding aspirin in children because of Reye syndrome risk with illnesses such as influenza and varicella.
B: Correct. Merck states aspirin should be avoided in children because it increases Reye syndrome risk with influenza and varicella; CPS Caring for Kids likewise warns not to use ASA for fever when chickenpox, influenza, or certain other viral infections are present.
C: Incorrect. Salicylates increase, rather than prevent, Reye syndrome risk in this setting.
D: Incorrect. Aspirin is specifically discouraged for chickenpox and influenza in children.
topic: Pediatric fever — avoid aspirin due to Reye syndrome risk
source_1_section: Treatment of Fever in Infants and Children
source_2_publisher: Canadian Paediatric Society — Caring for Kids

stem: A toddler presents to the emergency department with a barky cough and mild croup without stridor at rest. Which pharmacologic intervention is most consistent with evidence-based croup management?
options:
A) Withhold all corticosteroids because mild croup never benefits from steroids.
B) Administer a single dose of dexamethasone as directed, which is recommended across mild to severe croup presentations.
C) Start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics as first-line therapy for typical viral croup.
D) Give repeated high-dose aspirin for airway inflammation.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. CPS recommends considering corticosteroids for all children presenting with croup from mild to severe; Merck also uses a long-acting glucocorticoid such as dexamethasone for mild disease.
B: Correct. CPS states dexamethasone (commonly 0.6 mg/kg orally once) is highly efficacious and steroids are the cornerstone across severity; Merck lists a single dose of long-acting glucocorticoid (e.g., dexamethasone) for mild croup.
C: Incorrect. Typical croup is viral; antibiotics are not first-line for uncomplicated viral croup.
D: Incorrect. Aspirin is not croup therapy and is unsafe in children with viral illness because of Reye syndrome risk.
topic: Croup — single-dose dexamethasone across severities
source_1_title: Acute management of croup in the emergency department

stem: A school-age client with cystic fibrosis and pancreatic insufficiency is preparing to eat lunch. Which medication teaching is correct?
options:
A) Skip pancreatic enzyme capsules on days when stools look normal.
B) Take pancreatic enzyme replacement with meals and snacks as prescribed.
C) Take pancreatic enzymes only at bedtime, never with food.
D) Stop enzymes permanently once antibiotic therapy for a pulmonary exacerbation begins.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Enzyme replacement is ongoing therapy for pancreatic insufficiency, not based on a single stool observation.
B: Correct. Merck states pancreatic enzyme replacement should be given with all meals and snacks in pancreatic insufficiency; OpenStax identifies administering pancreatic enzymes as a key gastrointestinal nursing intervention for CF.
C: Incorrect. Enzymes are timed with food to aid digestion/absorption, not reserved for bedtime only.
D: Incorrect. Antibiotics treat infection; they do not replace the need for enzyme therapy for pancreatic insufficiency.
topic: Cystic fibrosis — pancreatic enzymes with meals and snacks
source_2_title: 11.9 Disorders of the Lower Respiratory System: Cystic Fibrosis
source_2_section: Prioritizing Hypotheses, Generating Solutions, and Taking Action

stem: An older adult is admitted after a fall with a suspected lower-extremity fracture. Which assessment finding set should the nurse prioritize when monitoring the injured limb?
options:
A) Only wound drainage colour, ignoring pulses and sensation.
B) Neurovascular checks including pain, pulse, pallor, paresthesia, and paralysis (the 5 Ps).
C) Skin turgor on the contralateral arm as the sole priority assessment.
D) Capillary blood glucose every hour instead of limb perfusion checks.
rationales:
A: Incorrect. Fracture nursing care requires neurovascular monitoring for perfusion and nerve function, not drainage colour alone.
B: Correct. OpenStax directs frequent neurovascular examinations using the 5 Ps; Merck likewise emphasizes assessing for neurovascular injury and compartment syndrome signs (pain, pallor, paresthesias, coolness, pulselessness).
C: Incorrect. Contralateral skin turgor does not assess distal perfusion of the injured extremity.
D: Incorrect. Glucose monitoring does not replace neurovascular assessment of a fractured limb.
topic: Fracture care — neurovascular 5 Ps assessment
source_1_section: Nursing Care of the Patient with Bone Fractures

stem: An 79-year-old hospitalized client develops acute fluctuating confusion consistent with delirium. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated as supportive care while the underlying cause is treated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Keep the room quiet and well lit, with a clock and calendar visible."}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Encourage use of the client's eyeglasses and hearing aids if needed."}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Apply physical restraints routinely at the first sign of restlessness."}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Invite familiar family members to spend time at the bedside when appropriate."}, {"key": "R5", "text": "Move the client frequently between unfamiliar rooms to provide stimulation."}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. Merck advises a stable, quiet, well-lit environment with visual cues such as clocks and calendars; OpenStax lists a quiet well-lit room and clocks/calendars within view.
R2: Indicated. Merck and OpenStax both support minimizing sensory deficits by ensuring eyeglasses and hearing aids are used.
R3: Not indicated. OpenStax advises avoiding restraints; Merck states physical restraints should be minimized because they can worsen agitation and injury risk.
R4: Indicated. Both sources support involving family for reorientation, familiarity, and safety.
R5: Not indicated. Frequent unfamiliar room changes increase environmental stress; Merck emphasizes a stable environment and frequent reorientation in a consistent setting.
topic: NGN matrix — delirium supportive nursing interventions

stem: An older adult is admitted with new fluctuating confusion. Which factors should the nurse recognize as common precipitants or contributors to delirium? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Urinary tract infection or other acute infection
B) Dehydration
C) Recently started anticholinergic or opioid medications
D) A lifelong gradual decline in memory over several years without acute change
E) Sleep deprivation during hospitalization
F) Stable, well-controlled hypothyroidism treated for decades with no recent change
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck and OpenStax identify infection (including UTI) as a common precipitant of delirium in older adults.
B: Correct. Dehydration is listed by both Merck and OpenStax among common causes/precipitants.
C: Correct. Medications—especially anticholinergics and opioids—are leading causes of delirium in both sources.
D: Incorrect. Lifelong gradual memory decline describes dementia's slower course, not an acute delirium precipitant; delirium has sudden onset.
E: Correct. Sleep deprivation is a precipitating factor in Merck and a listed cause in OpenStax.
F: Incorrect. Long-stable treated hypothyroidism without change is not identified as an acute precipitant; acute metabolic/endocrine crises can be, but this option describes a non-acute stable state.
topic: Delirium — common precipitating factors in older adults

stem: An older adult reports light-headedness and near-falls when standing up from bed. Orthostatic hypotension is suspected. Which teaching best reduces orthostatic symptom risk?
options:
A) Rise slowly from a lying or sitting position and pause before walking.
B) Stand up as quickly as possible to shorten the dizzy period.
C) Limit daytime fluid intake to keep blood pressure from rising.
D) Remain on strict bed rest for several days to rest the cardiovascular system.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck nonpharmacologic care advises patients to rise slowly from a recumbent or sitting position; OpenStax supports progressive mobilization such as dangling at the bedside before standing.
B: Incorrect. Rapid standing worsens orthostatic drops; Merck links sudden upright posture to symptoms.
C: Incorrect. Merck advises adequate fluids; fluid restriction can worsen orthostasis.
D: Incorrect. Prolonged bed rest contributes to orthostatic intolerance; Merck encourages sitting up daily and activity when feasible.
topic: Orthostatic hypotension — rise slowly; progressive mobilization

stem: A toddler arrives with sudden high fever, drooling, and inspiratory stridor and is suspected to have epiglottitis. Which nursing action is the priority until a secure airway is available?
options:
A) Avoid upsetting interventions such as forcing an oral exam, and keep the child as calm as possible while preparing for urgent airway management.
B) Immediately use a tongue blade to visualize the pharynx at the bedside.
C) Force the child flat supine for a full physical examination before calling for help.
D) Send the child alone to radiology for a neck film without airway-capable staff present.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck states airway assessment/management takes priority and that in children with stridor, upsetting interventions that could trigger obstruction should be avoided until an airway is established; visualization is not done until full respiratory support is available.
B: Incorrect. Direct visualization is deferred until full respiratory support is available because agitation can precipitate obstruction.
C: Incorrect. Children often maintain a forward sniffing/tripod posture; forcing supine and unnecessary stimulation can worsen airway compromise.
D: Incorrect. Suspected epiglottitis requires hospitalization and airway-capable management; unattended transport for imaging is unsafe.
topic: Epiglottitis — prioritize airway; avoid upsetting exam until support available
source_2_title: Acute management of croup in the emergency department

stem: Which presentation should lead the nurse to suspect epiglottitis rather than typical viral croup?
options:
A) Sudden high fever, drooling, toxic appearance, and sitting forward without a barky cough
B) Gradual onset of a barky cough with mild fever after a few days of upper respiratory symptoms
C) Isolated nasal congestion without fever or respiratory distress
D) Chronic night-time cough for several weeks without acute distress
rationales:
A: Correct. CPS and Merck describe epiglottitis with sudden high fever, drooling, toxic/anxious appearance, forward sniffing posture, and absence of barky cough.
B: Incorrect. That pattern fits typical croup (more gradual; barky cough characteristic).
C: Incorrect. Lacks red-flag airway findings of epiglottitis.
D: Incorrect. Chronic cough without acute toxicity is not the fulminant epiglottitis pattern.
topic: Epiglottitis recognition — drooling, toxic, sniffing; no barky cough
source_1_title: Acute management of croup in the emergency department
source_2_section: Symptoms and Signs; Differentiating Epiglottitis From Croup

stem: A charge nurse on an Ontario medical unit is assigning care that involves an unregulated care provider (UCP). Which action best reflects safe assignment based on competence?
options:
A) Confirm the UCP is competent to perform the specific activity safely for this client in these circumstances before assigning it.
B) Assume any UCP can perform every procedure because the tasks look simple.
C) Assign complex unstable assessments to the UCP so the RN can finish charting.
D) Avoid verifying competence once the UCP has completed a general orientation week.
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO requires nurses who assign to UCPs to know the UCP is competent for the particular procedure/activity for the client in the given circumstances; OpenStax Right Person requires verified education/competencies before delegation.
B: Incorrect. CNO states a nurse cannot assume a UCP is competent regardless of how straightforward a procedure appears.
C: Incorrect. OpenStax Right Circumstance requires stable clients with expected outcomes for assistive personnel; nursing assessment/judgment stays with the RN.
D: Incorrect. Competence must be known for the particular activity and circumstances, not assumed from generic orientation alone.
topic: Ontario UCP assignment — verify competence for specific activity and circumstances
jurisdiction_note: CNO Working with Unregulated Care Providers sets Ontario expectations for verifying UCP competence; OpenStax/NCSBN five rights provide concordant Right Person principle.
source_1_section: Expectations for nurses who work with UCPs

stem: Which client situation is most appropriate for an RN to assign basic assistive care to unregulated care provider (UCP/assistive personnel) under the Right Circumstance principle?
options:
A) A stable client with expected outcomes who needs assistance with routine hygiene
B) A newly admitted client with unstable vital signs requiring continuous reassessment
C) A client with sudden respiratory distress needing immediate clinical judgment
D) A client whose condition just changed and has not yet been reassessed by the RN
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax states patients must be stable with expected outcomes before care responsibilities are delegated to assistive personnel; CNO likewise ties UCP assignment to appropriate client circumstances and competence.
B: Incorrect. Unstable clients needing continuous RN reassessment are not appropriate for AP/UCP-led care without direct RN management.
C: Incorrect. Acute distress requires RN clinical judgment and Take Action, not assistive-only assignment.
D: Incorrect. OpenStax requires the RN to reassess after condition changes before deciding whether delegation remains appropriate.
topic: Delegation — Right Circumstance requires stable client with expected outcomes
jurisdiction_note: OpenStax/NCSBN Right Circumstance is general; CNO reinforces appropriateness of UCP assignment to client circumstances in Ontario practice.
source_2_section: Expectations for nurses who work with UCPs

stem: Which community nursing intervention is the best example of tertiary prevention?
options:
A) Referring a stroke survivor to physical, occupational, and speech rehabilitation to reduce disability
B) Administering routine childhood immunizations to prevent vaccine-preventable disease
C) Organizing asymptomatic breast-cancer screening for early detection
D) Teaching a healthy community how to begin exercise before any disease risk factors appear
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax defines tertiary prevention as lessening impact and preventing complications through therapies and rehabilitation; CDC describes post-stroke rehabilitation with PT/OT/speech to treat stroke effects and support recovery.
B: Incorrect. Immunization is primary prevention (prevent disease before it occurs).
C: Incorrect. Screening asymptomatic people is secondary prevention (early detection).
D: Incorrect. Primordial/primary risk-factor prevention precedes disease; it is not tertiary care of established illness.
topic: Tertiary prevention — rehabilitation after stroke to reduce disability
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A nurse is teaching aspiration-prevention strategies for an older adult with dysphagia. Which actions should be included? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Maintain an upright position (at least 30 degrees) during and after meals
B) Encourage a slow pace while eating and drinking
C) Support oral hygiene and dental care to reduce harmful oral bacteria
D) Collaborate with a speech-language pathologist for safe-swallowing strategies
E) Have the client eat while fully flat in bed to conserve energy
F) Rush meal trays so feeding finishes in under five minutes
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax advises upright positioning at least 30 degrees during/after eating; Merck likewise elevates the head of bed >30° for aspiration-risk clients with decreased LOC.
B: Correct. OpenStax notes many patients benefit from a slow eating/drinking pace.
C: Correct. Both OpenStax and Merck support optimized oral hygiene to reduce pneumonia risk related to aspirated oral organisms.
D: Correct. OpenStax recommends SLP collaboration; Merck notes speech pathologist training in strategies such as chin tuck.
E: Incorrect. Flat positioning increases aspiration risk; upright positioning is indicated.
F: Incorrect. Rushing contradicts slow-pace guidance and increases aspiration risk.
topic: Aspiration precautions — upright meals, slow pace, oral hygiene, SLP
source_1_title: 11.7 Disorders of the Lower Respiratory System: Pneumonia and Aspiration
source_1_section: Evidence-Based Practice: Strategies to Prevent Aspiration Pneumonia
source_2_section: Prevention of Chemical Pneumonitis and Aspiration Pneumonia

stem: A nurse is donning full isolation PPE (gown, mask, eye protection, and gloves) before entering a client's room. Place the actions in the recommended order from first to last.
options:
A) Don gloves, extending cuffs over the gown wrists
B) Don the isolation gown and fasten neck and waist ties
C) Don goggles or a face shield and adjust to fit
D) Don the mask or respirator and secure it snugly
rationales:
B: Correct (1st). CDC and OpenStax place gown first: cover torso and fasten neck/waist.
D: Correct (2nd). Mask or respirator is donned after the gown.
C: Correct (3rd). Goggles/face shield are applied after the mask.
A: Correct (4th). Gloves are last so cuffs cover the gown wrists.
topic: PPE donning sequence — gown, mask, eye protection, gloves
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_1_title: Sequence for Putting On Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_1_section: Sequence for putting on PPE — steps 1–4
source_2_section: QSEN Competency: Donning Personal Protective Equipment

stem: A float nurse arrives to help on a telemetry unit. Which charge-nurse action best applies determination of clinical ability when making assignments?
options:
A) Match assignment complexity to the float nurse's demonstrated proficiency with similar tasks and current competencies
B) Give the float nurse the most unstable clients without reviewing competencies because all RNs have the same license
C) Assign tasks outside the float nurse's role description without training because the unit is short-staffed
D) Ignore the float nurse's current workload when adding multiple complex admissions
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax leadership guidance requires assessing skills/competencies and matching care complexity to demonstrated proficiency with similar tasks; CNO likewise requires knowing competence for the activity and circumstances.
B: Incorrect. Shared RN licensure does not replace unit-specific competency assessment for complex unstable assignments.
C: Incorrect. OpenStax Right Task requires activities within job description/policies and training for skilled competencies.
D: Incorrect. OpenStax requires considering current workload and impact on safe care when determining clinical ability.
topic: Assignment — match complexity to demonstrated clinical ability/competency
source_1_title: 18.3 Implementing Leadership and Management into Nursing Practice
source_2_section: Expectations for nurses who work with UCPs

stem: An 84-year-old client becomes newly confused after several psychoactive medications are started in hospital. Which nursing action best addresses a common medication-related contributor to delirium?
options:
A) Collaborate to review and minimize newly added anticholinergic or opioid medications when clinically appropriate
B) Add another sedative at bedtime to ensure the client sleeps through the night without reassessment
C) Encourage the family to bring all home anticholinergic OTC products for unrestricted use
D) Ignore medication review because delirium is never related to drugs in older adults
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck identifies medications—particularly anticholinergics and opioids—as leading causes of delirium and advises reducing number/doses when possible; OpenStax lists sedatives, opioids, anticholinergics among common causes and supports discontinuing contributing medications.
B: Incorrect. Adding sedatives can worsen delirium; OpenStax notes sedation can worsen symptoms.
C: Incorrect. Unreviewed anticholinergic OTCs increase delirium risk.
D: Incorrect. Both sources identify drug exposure as a major delirium etiology.
topic: Delirium — minimize anticholinergic/opioid contributors in older adults
source_2_section: Incidence and Causes; Nursing Treatment of Delirium

stem: A nurse in a school immunization clinic is teaching parents about human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination for a healthy child with no prior HPV doses. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
options:
A) Routine HPV vaccination is recommended at ages 11 or 12 years and may be started as early as age 9.
B) HPV vaccination should be deferred until the child is sexually active so immunity matches exposure timing.
C) HPV vaccine treats existing HPV infections and genital warts, so it is reserved for adolescents with known infection.
D) HPV vaccination is recommended only for girls; boys do not benefit from immunization.
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC recommends routine HPV vaccination at 11 or 12 years (can start at 9); Merck similarly states routine recommendation at ages 11 or 12 (can start at 9).
B: Incorrect. Both sources emphasize vaccination before HPV exposure; waiting until sexual activity reduces the preventive benefit.
C: Incorrect. CDC states HPV vaccination prevents new infections but does not treat existing HPV infection or disease.
D: Incorrect. CDC catch-up guidance applies to everyone through age 26 if not adequately vaccinated earlier; Merck discusses vaccine protection against HPV types causing warts and cancer without restricting to girls only for the routine age statement.
topic: HPV vaccination — routine ages 11–12 (start at 9)
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A community health nurse is teaching hikers how to reduce Lyme disease risk in an endemic area. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Apply an EPA-registered insect repellent containing an ingredient such as DEET when outdoors.
B) Check the body, clothing, and gear for ticks during and after outdoor activity.
C) Remove an attached tick promptly using fine-tipped tweezers close to the skin, pulling upward with steady pressure.
D) Wait several days after noticing an attached tick before removal so the tick detaches on its own.
E) Consider clothing treated with permethrin as an additional protective measure.
F) Assume backyard lawns are always risk-free, so prevention steps are needed only in remote forests.
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC lists EPA-registered repellents including DEET; Merck advises DEET-containing repellents on skin in endemic areas.
B: Correct. CDC advises checking body, clothing, gear, and pets; Merck stresses frequent searches for ticks.
C: Correct. Both CDC and Merck emphasize prompt removal; Merck details fine-tipped tweezers close to the skin with steady upward pull.
D: Incorrect. CDC warns delaying removal increases disease risk; Merck instructs removal when a tick is found attached.
E: Correct. CDC recommends permethrin-treated clothing/gear; Merck notes permethrin on clothing effectively kills ticks.
F: Incorrect. CDC notes many exposures occur in yards/neighborhoods, not only remote wooded areas.
topic: Lyme disease — primary prevention of tick bites
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A public health nurse is planning harm-reduction teaching for clients and families at elevated risk of opioid overdose. Which recommendation is most appropriate?
options:
A) Carry naloxone and ensure others know where it is, because bystanders can reverse an opioid overdose while awaiting emergency help.
B) Avoid keeping naloxone at home because using it without a prescription is illegal in all jurisdictions.
C) Give naloxone only after waiting 30 minutes to confirm the overdose is opioid-related.
D) Leave the person alone after the first naloxone dose so they can recover privately.
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC advises that people at increased overdose risk carry naloxone and that bystanders can give it; OpenStax describes community naloxone distribution and instructs administering naloxone for suspected overdose while calling emergency services.
B: Incorrect. CDC states naloxone is available over the counter and through community programs; OpenStax supports community distribution as harm reduction.
C: Incorrect. CDC and OpenStax urge prompt action for suspected overdose; CDC notes naloxone will not harm someone overdosing on non-opioids, so it is best to use it if overdose is suspected.
D: Incorrect. Both CDC and OpenStax instruct staying with the person until emergency help arrives.
topic: Community naloxone — carry and bystander use for opioid overdose
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_1_section: Who should carry naloxone? / How does naloxone work
source_2_title: 31.3 The Opioid Epidemic and Substance Use Disorders
source_2_section: Community Efforts / What to Do for a Suspected Overdose

stem: A parent calls after a previously well toddler had a brief generalized seizure during a fever. The seizure has stopped, and the child is breathing. Which instruction should the nurse give first for immediate safety during any future febrile seizure?
options:
A) Place the child on their side on a flat surface, do not put anything in the mouth, and call emergency services if the seizure lasts longer than a few minutes or the infant is younger than 6 months.
B) Hold the child firmly upright and insert a spoon between the teeth to protect the tongue.
C) Give an oral antipyretic during the seizure to stop the convulsions immediately.
D) Start continuous antiseizure medication at home after a single simple febrile seizure without clinician evaluation.
rationales:
A: Correct. CPS Caring for Kids advises side-lying on a flat surface, nothing between the teeth, and calling 911 if the seizure lasts longer than 3 minutes or the baby is younger than 6 months; Merck supports supportive management for brief seizures and urgent medication/support for prolonged seizures.
B: Incorrect. CPS explicitly says do not put anything between the teeth and do not hold the child down.
C: Incorrect. During an active seizure, oral medication is unsafe; Merck notes antipyretics may help symptoms but routine use may not prevent recurrence, and management during a brief seizure is supportive.
D: Incorrect. Merck states EEG/routine antiseizure prophylaxis is not indicated after a typical simple febrile seizure with normal exam; CPS advises medical evaluation after any seizure.
topic: Febrile seizure — immediate first-aid teaching
source_1_publisher: Canadian Paediatric Society — Caring for Kids
