stem: A client stabilized on lithium asks which new medications require extra caution because they may raise lithium levels. Select all that apply.
options:
A) Thiazide diuretics
B) Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) other than aspirin
C) Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors
D) Topical sunscreen used only on intact skin
E) Ordinary oral rehydration with consistent salt intake as previously taught
F) Acetaminophen used occasionally for mild headache if otherwise appropriate
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: thiazide diuretics can contribute to elevated lithium levels.
B: Correct. Merck: NSAIDs other than aspirin may contribute to hyperlithemia; OpenStax lists NSAIDs as interacting.
C: Correct. Both sources list ACE inhibitors among drugs that can raise lithium levels.
D: Incorrect. Topical sunscreen on intact skin is not identified as a lithium-elevating interaction in these sources.
E: Incorrect. Consistent hydration/salt as taught supports stability; this is not a hyperlithemia-causing drug.
F: Incorrect. Acetaminophen is not listed like NSAIDs as a classic lithium-elevating interaction in these citations.
topic: Lithium — drugs that raise levels (thiazides, NSAIDs, ACEI)
source_1_title: Medications for Treatment of Bipolar Disorders

stem: A client at 34 weeks’ gestation is hospitalized with preeclampsia with severe features. Which medication purpose should the nurse emphasize when intravenous magnesium sulfate is ordered?
options:
A) To prevent eclamptic seizures while plans for monitoring and timed delivery proceed.
B) To permanently dissolve all placental tissue so pregnancy continues indefinitely without delivery.
C) To replace the need for blood pressure assessment forever.
D) To treat iron-deficiency anemia as the sole indication.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: in preeclampsia with severe features, magnesium sulfate is given to prevent seizures. OpenStax: magnesium sulfate is started to prevent progression to seizures.
B: Incorrect. Delivery remains definitive treatment; magnesium does not dissolve the placenta or eliminate need for delivery decisions.
C: Incorrect. BP monitoring remains essential.
D: Incorrect. Magnesium sulfate is not treatment for iron-deficiency anemia.
topic: Magnesium sulfate — prevent seizures in severe preeclampsia

stem: Which teaching point best reflects why community-dwelling older adults need proactive protection from cold indoor environments?
options:
A) Older adults are at higher risk for hypothermia because of diminished temperature sensation, impaired mobility/communication, and less subcutaneous fat — even in cool indoor rooms — so keep living spaces adequately warm and address mobility limits.
B) Older adults never develop hypothermia indoors under any circumstances.
C) Only infants can lose heat; adults are immune to cold injury.
D) Hypothermia occurs only after immersion in tropical swimming pools above 30°C.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: older adults are at high risk due to diminished temperature sensation, impaired mobility/communication, and diminished subcutaneous fat; hypothermia can occur indoors in cool rooms. OpenStax links impaired thermoregulation to hypothermia risk and notes older-adult environmental vulnerabilities.
B: Incorrect. Merck explicitly notes indoor hypothermia risk for older adults.
C: Incorrect. Both age extremes are at risk (Merck).
D: Incorrect. Cool environments and impaired heat conservation drive hypothermia; tropical warm water is not the defining scenario.
topic: Older adults — indoor hypothermia risk and prevention
source_2_section: Risk for Impaired Thermoregulation; Older Adults

stem: A client at 28 weeks gestation arrives with sudden bright red vaginal bleeding and a soft, nontender uterus. Placenta previa has not yet been excluded. Which action is correct?
options:
A) Defer digital cervical examination until ultrasonography rules out placenta previa, because digital exam may provoke massive bleeding.
B) Perform a vigorous digital cervical exam immediately to estimate dilatation before any imaging.
C) Discharge home without assessment because third-trimester bleeding is always normal.
D) Encourage unsupervised intercourse to promote placental migration.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: if bleeding occurs after 20 weeks, pelvic examination by digital cervical examination is contraindicated until previa is first ruled out by ultrasonography. OpenStax: vaginal exams should be avoided with known previa or vaginal bleeding to prevent additional injury.
B: Incorrect. Merck warns digital exam may cause sudden massive bleeding when previa is present.
C: Incorrect. Third-trimester bleeding requires urgent evaluation for previa versus abruption.
D: Incorrect. Sexual activity is restricted with previa; it does not safely 'migrate' the placenta.
topic: Placenta previa — defer digital exam until ultrasound excludes previa

stem: A client of reproductive age with a positive pregnancy test develops sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding, syncope, tachycardia, and hypotension. Ultrasound shows no intrauterine pregnancy. Complete the bowtie: priority condition, two actions, and two parameters to monitor.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Mild cerumen impaction"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Stable, asymptomatic early intrauterine pregnancy without bleeding"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Establish large-bore IV access and begin ordered volume resuscitation while preparing for emergent surgical management"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Notify the provider/surgical team immediately for unstable ruptured ectopic pregnancy"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Discharge home with only oral antacids and no follow-up"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Encourage unsupervised heavy exercise before evaluation"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Give intramuscular methotrexate as first-line therapy while the client remains hemodynamically unstable"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Blood pressure, heart rate, and signs of ongoing hypovolemia/shock"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Abdominal/pelvic pain trend, bleeding, and neurologic status (alertness/syncope)"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Preferred cafeteria dessert flavours"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Favourite television channel"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Shoe colour preference"}]}
rationales:
K1: Correct. Merck: ectopic pregnancy can rupture with hemorrhagic shock. OpenStax: bleeding, pelvic pain, syncope, or shock may signal rupture.
K2: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not explain shock with positive pregnancy test.
K3: Incorrect. Cerumen impaction is unrelated.
K4: Incorrect. Findings indicate extrauterine pregnancy with instability, not a stable IUP.
A1: Correct. OpenStax hypovolemic shock care emphasizes volume resuscitation; Merck/OpenStax: unstable ectopic requires surgical management.
A2: Correct. OpenStax: unstable clients require emergent surgical intervention for rupture risk.
A3: Incorrect. Discharge without care is unsafe in suspected ruptured ectopic.
A4: Incorrect. Exercise delays emergency care.
A5: Incorrect. OpenStax: methotrexate is for selected hemodynamically stable clients, not unstable rupture.
P1: Correct. Vital signs track hypovolemic shock response (OpenStax hypovolemic shock; Merck rupture hemorrhage).
P2: Correct. Pain, bleeding, and neurologic status reflect ongoing hemorrhage (both sources).
P3: Incorrect. Unrelated parameter.
P4: Incorrect. Unrelated parameter.
P5: Incorrect. Unrelated parameter.
topic: NGN bowtie — ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hypovolemic shock
source_3_section: Volume Resuscitation for the Patient with Hypovolemic Shock

stem: A term newborn of a mother with insulin-treated diabetes is otherwise well. Which nursing action best helps prevent symptomatic neonatal hypoglycemia in the early hours after birth?
options:
A) Support early, frequent enteral feedings (e.g., breast-feeding initiation soon after birth) and follow facility glucose-monitoring policy for at-risk newborns.
B) Withhold all feedings for 12 hours to 'rest' the pancreas.
C) Give only free water bottles and delay any calorie source.
D) Encourage prolonged cold exposure to increase metabolic demand.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: well at-risk neonates should receive early, frequent feedings; infants of diabetic mothers may develop transient hypoglycemia and are given oral or IV glucose. OpenStax: IDM are at risk; encourage early breast-feeding and timely feeding/glucose.
B: Incorrect. Delayed feeding increases hypoglycemia risk (Merck: delayed feeding is a common cause).
C: Incorrect. Free water without calories does not prevent hypoglycemia.
D: Incorrect. OpenStax links cold stress to depleted glucose stores; warmth and early feeding are preferred.
topic: Neonatal hypoglycemia prevention — early frequent feeding for IDM
source_2_title: 24.2 Care of Common Problems in the Newborn
source_2_section: Hypoglycemia; Care of the Newborn with Hypoglycemia

stem: Complete the teaching for a client starting a nonselective MAOI antidepressant.
options: {"template": "Clients taking nonselective MAOIs must avoid foods high in {B1} because concurrent intake can trigger a {B2}. A classic high-risk example is {B3}.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "tyramine"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "vitamin C"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "insoluble fibre only"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "fluoride"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "hypertensive crisis (the 'cheese reaction')"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "harmless temporary freckling"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "improved wound tensile strength"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "exclusive night blindness"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "aged/mature cheese (and other aged or overripe tyramine-rich foods)"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "fresh cucumber water only"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "plain ice cubes"}, {"key": "B3d", "text": "sterile normal saline irrigant"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: tyramine-containing foods interact with MAOIs.
B1b: Incorrect. Vitamin C is not the MAOI dietary restriction focus.
B1c: Incorrect. Fibre is not the hypertensive interaction.
B1d: Incorrect. Fluoride is unrelated.
B2a: Correct. Merck: hypertensive crises with tyramine foods are called the cheese reaction; OpenStax lists hypertensive crisis as a key adverse effect.
B2b: Incorrect. Not a benign cosmetic effect.
B2c: Incorrect. Unrelated to MAOI–tyramine interaction.
B2d: Incorrect. Unrelated.
B3a: Correct. Merck cites mature cheese high tyramine content and lists aged/overripe foods to avoid; OpenStax lists aged cheeses among high-tyramine foods.
B3b: Incorrect. Not a classic high-tyramine example.
B3c: Incorrect. Unrelated.
B3d: Incorrect. Unrelated.
topic: NGN cloze — MAOI tyramine restriction and hypertensive crisis

stem: A nurse believes a planned action threatens client safety and needs a clear, assertive way to speak up on the team. Which TeamSTEPPS mutual-support script best fits this situation?
options:
A) Use CUS language: state 'I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue,' and escalate if the concern is not resolved.
B) Remain silent to avoid 'bothering' the team, even when safety is at risk.
C) Falsify the record so the unsafe plan appears completed.
D) Leave the unit without notifying anyone about the concern.
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ PSNet TeamSTEPPS mutual support includes CUS — 'I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue,' with escalation if unresolved. OpenStax frames advocacy as speaking up for safe, ethical care.
B: Incorrect. Silence allows preventable harm.
C: Incorrect. Falsification is unethical and unsafe.
D: Incorrect. Abandonment without communication worsens risk.
topic: TeamSTEPPS CUS — assertive speak-up for safety

source_2_section: Role of Nurses as Advocates; Advocacy for Patients

stem: An older adult reports infrequent, hard stools related to low activity and low fibre intake. Which teaching priority is most appropriate initially (assuming no red-flag surgical abdomen)?
options:
A) Increase dietary fibre with adequate fluids and encourage regular physical activity as tolerated.
B) Stop all oral fluids to 'dry out' the bowel.
C) Eliminate all fruits and vegetables permanently.
D) Remain on strict bed rest and avoid any fibre.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck Diet and behavior: enough fibre increases stool bulk and components absorb fluid to soften stool. OpenStax nursing management emphasizes fibre-rich diets, adequate hydration, and regular activity.
B: Incorrect. Dehydration worsens hard stool (OpenStax lists dehydration as a cause).
C: Incorrect. Fruits and vegetables are recommended fibre sources (both sources).
D: Incorrect. Decreased activity contributes to constipation.
topic: Constipation — fibre, fluids, and activity teaching

stem: A client is starting clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Which teaching and monitoring points are correct? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Absolute neutrophil count (ANC) monitoring is required because clozapine can cause severe neutropenia.
B) Severe neutropenia increases the risk of serious infection.
C) Report fever or other signs of infection promptly to the provider.
D) Laboratory blood monitoring can be skipped indefinitely after the first dose.
E) Doubling the dose whenever a fever starts is the preferred self-management plan.
F) Clozapine has no hematologic risks, so infection precautions are unnecessary.
rationales:
A: Correct. DailyMed boxed warning requires baseline ANC; OpenStax notes REMS monitoring of WBC/ANC for clozapine.
B: Correct. DailyMed: severe neutropenia is associated with increased risk of serious and fatal infections; OpenStax lists agranulocytosis/neutropenia among hematologic effects.
C: Correct. Infection risk with neutropenia requires prompt reporting of fever/infection signs (supports DailyMed infection risk + OpenStax hematologic monitoring).
D: Incorrect. Ongoing ANC monitoring is required; it is not a one-time check.
E: Incorrect. Dose escalation for fever is unsafe and not indicated.
F: Incorrect. Hematologic toxicity is a major boxed warning.
topic: Clozapine — ANC monitoring and infection risk teaching
source_1_publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed

stem: A client with known Graves disease develops high fever, marked tachycardia, severe agitation/confusion, vomiting, and diarrhea after an acute infection. Which interpretation and priority nursing action are best?
options:
A) Suspect thyroid storm — a life-threatening emergency — initiate cardiac/airway monitoring and support, and prepare for ordered antithyroid therapy plus supportive measures (e.g., cooling, fluids) while treating the precipitant.
B) Reassure that these findings are expected mild seasonal allergies requiring only outdoor jogging.
C) Stop all monitoring and discharge immediately without evaluation.
D) Apply only topical antifungal cream as definitive endocrine therapy.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: thyroid storm is a life-threatening emergency with fever, marked restlessness/confusion, GI symptoms, and tachycardia; treatment includes PTU, beta-blockade, cooling, fluids, and treating the cause. OpenStax: thyroid storm is a medical emergency managed with antithyroid medications and supportive care.
B: Incorrect. This presentation is not mild allergy.
C: Incorrect. Delaying care risks fatal arrhythmias/organ failure (OpenStax).
D: Incorrect. Antifungals do not treat thyrotoxic crisis.
topic: Thyroid storm — recognize emergency and support ordered therapy
source_1_section: Thyroid storm; Treatment of thyroid storm

stem: A community health nurse explains levels of prevention. Which activity is the best example of secondary prevention?
options:
A) Cervical cancer screening tests to detect disease early in asymptomatic clients.
B) Administering HPV vaccine before any exposure as the only secondary strategy.
C) Long-term rehabilitation after completed cancer treatment as secondary prevention.
D) Building playgrounds solely to change social determinants decades before disease risk as secondary prevention.
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: secondary prevention focuses on early detection; screening is the primary activity (cervical cancer screening listed as secondary). WHO: screening aims to identify asymptomatic abnormalities suggestive of cancer/pre-cancer for prompt diagnosis and treatment.
B: Incorrect. OpenStax table lists HPV vaccine as primary prevention.
C: Incorrect. Rehabilitation after disease is tertiary prevention (OpenStax).
D: Incorrect. Primordial/upstream structural actions are not secondary screening.
topic: Secondary prevention — screening for early detection

stem: For preventing wrong-patient or wrong-site invasive procedures, indicate whether each action is indicated or not indicated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Perform a planned pre-procedure time-out confirming client identity, procedure, and site."}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Ensure all team members participate without distraction and can speak up about safety concerns."}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Skip the time-out when the schedule is busy because checklists waste time."}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Start the incision before confirming the marked site if the surgeon is in a hurry."}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. AHRQ: time-outs before invasive procedures confirm patient identification, procedure, site, and key details.
R2: Indicated. AHRQ: all team members must participate without distraction and are empowered to speak up; OpenStax emphasizes speaking up to prevent never events.
R3: Not indicated. Skipping safety checklists increases wrong-site/wrong-patient risk (AHRQ).
R4: Not indicated. Starting before confirmation violates time-out purpose.
topic: NGN matrix — surgical time-out and speak-up to prevent never events
