stem: A client taking clozapine develops a new fever and sore throat. Which nursing action is the priority?
options:
A) Hold further clozapine pending provider guidance, notify the provider promptly, and facilitate urgent evaluation including ANC because fever may signal infection related to severe neutropenia.
B) Double the next clozapine dose to overcome the fever.
C) Advise the client that fever on clozapine is always harmless and needs no follow-up.
D) Stop all infection precautions permanently and discharge without labs.
rationales:
A: Correct. DailyMed warns severe neutropenia raises risk of serious/fatal infections and requires ANC monitoring. OpenStax links clozapine to agranulocytosis/neutropenia with REMS lab monitoring. Fever with pharyngitis warrants urgent evaluation.
B: Incorrect. Increasing the dose during possible infection/neutropenia is dangerous.
C: Incorrect. Fever is a warning sign, not a benign expectation.
D: Incorrect. Labs and provider notification are required.
topic: Clozapine — fever and infection signs require urgent ANC evaluation
source_1_publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed

stem: A 12-hour-old at-risk neonate has a confirmed low serum glucose and is becoming lethargic with poor feeding. Which intervention is the priority?
options:
A) Begin prompt enteral feeding if the infant can feed safely, or administer ordered IV dextrose, and continue glucose monitoring.
B) Withhold all glucose sources for 8 hours to stimulate gluconeogenesis alone.
C) Offer only ice chips without calories.
D) Delay treatment until the next routine well-baby visit in 2 weeks.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: treatment is enteral feeding or IV dextrose; prompt feeding/IV glucose when levels fall below treatment thresholds. OpenStax: timely feeding or intravenous glucose in severe cases.
B: Incorrect. Withholding glucose worsens hypoglycemia.
C: Incorrect. Ice chips provide no effective glucose replacement.
D: Incorrect. Symptomatic hypoglycemia requires immediate treatment.
topic: Neonatal hypoglycemia — prompt enteral feeding or IV dextrose
source_2_title: 24.2 Care of Common Problems in the Newborn

stem: A client who delivered the placenta 20 minutes ago has sudden heavy vaginal bleeding, a soft boggy fundus, tachycardia, and light-headedness. Complete the bowtie: priority condition, two actions, and two parameters to monitor.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Primary postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Mild cerumen impaction"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Stable, well-contracted fundus with scant lochia only"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Perform firm fundal massage and assist bladder emptying while notifying the obstetric provider"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Administer ordered uterotonic therapy (e.g., oxytocin) and support ordered volume resuscitation"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Discharge home immediately without assessment because early bleeding is always normal"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Encourage unsupervised heavy exercise before evaluation"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Withhold all assessment of the fundus and avoid notifying anyone"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Fundal tone/height, lochia amount, and blood pressure/heart rate"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Signs of hypovolemia (dizziness, pallor, ongoing bleeding) and response to massage/uterotonics"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Preferred cafeteria dessert flavours"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Favourite television channel"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Shoe colour preference"}]}
rationales:
K1: Correct. Merck: uterine atony is the most common cause of PPH and is managed with fundal massage and uterotonics. OpenStax: early PPH is most often from atony with a soft boggy fundus.
K2: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not explain heavy postpartum bleeding and shock signs.
K3: Incorrect. Cerumen impaction is unrelated.
K4: Incorrect. Findings show boggy fundus with heavy bleeding, not a well-contracted uterus.
A1: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: fundal massage stimulates contraction; a full bladder can impede tone.
A2: Correct. Merck lists uterotonics (e.g., oxytocin) and fluid resuscitation; OpenStax: oxytocin and fundal massage are first-line for atony.
A3: Incorrect. Heavy bleeding with hypovolemia is an emergency.
A4: Incorrect. Exercise delays emergency care.
A5: Incorrect. Fundal assessment and rapid notification are required.
P1: Correct. Fundal tone and vital signs track ongoing hemorrhage (both sources).
P2: Correct. OpenStax lists hypovolemia signs; both sources emphasize response to massage/uterotonics.
P3: Incorrect. Unrelated parameter.
P4: Incorrect. Unrelated parameter.
P5: Incorrect. Unrelated parameter.
topic: NGN bowtie — primary PPH from uterine atony
source_2_section: Tone; Fundal Massage; Oxytocin; Signs and Symptoms of Hypovolemia

stem: A nurse teaches caregivers of a 2-month-old about reducing sleep-related infant death risk. For each action, select Indicated or Not indicated.
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Place the infant supine (on the back) for every sleep, including naps"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Use a firm, flat, noninclined crib mattress with a fitted sheet only"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Add pillows, loose blankets, and soft toys in the sleep area for comfort"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Have the infant share an adult bed (bed-sharing) as the preferred sleep surface"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. Merck: back to sleep for every sleep; OpenStax: place infant on their back for all sleep.
R2: Indicated. Merck: firm, flat, noninclined sleep surface; OpenStax: firm, flat mattress with fitted sheet.
R3: Not indicated. Both sources: keep soft objects/loose bedding out of the sleep area.
R4: Not indicated. Merck: bed sharing is not recommended; OpenStax: crib/bassinet in parents' room, not adult bed-sharing as the sleep surface.
topic: NGN matrix — safe sleep actions to reduce SUID/SIDS risk
source_1_title: Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS)

stem: An older adult who cannot reposition independently is at high risk for pressure injury. Which nursing action best reduces sustained pressure over bony prominences?
options:
A) Reposition the client at least every 2 hours (or more often if needed) using a written turning schedule and pressure-redistributing supports.
B) Leave the client in one position for an entire 12-hour shift to 'rest the skin'.
C) Drag the client across the sheets without lifting devices when moving.
D) Keep the head of the bed maximally elevated at all times without pressure reduction.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: patients confined to bed should be turned a minimum of every 2 hours; frequent repositioning is the most important pressure-reduction factor. OpenStax: repositioning about every two hours is the usual prevention rule for at-risk clients.
B: Incorrect. Pressure must not continue over bony surfaces for prolonged periods (Merck).
C: Incorrect. Merck warns against dragging because friction increases injury risk.
D: Incorrect. Merck: minimize head-of-bed elevation to reduce shear; pressure reduction still required.
topic: Pressure injury prevention — frequent repositioning at least every 2 hours
source_1_section: Pressure reduction; Prevention of Pressure Injuries

stem: Complete the teaching for urgent nursing priorities in clinically significant hyperkalemia (ordered therapies).
options: {"template": "Intravenous {B1} promotes cellular uptake of potassium. Oral or rectal {B2} promotes potassium excretion in the stool. Nurses also prioritize {B3} because hyperkalemia can cause lethal dysrhythmias.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "insulin (given with glucose as ordered)"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "high-dose oral potassium chloride"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "unlimited banana milkshakes"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "topical sunscreen only"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) or another potassium-binding resin as ordered"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "extra dietary potassium tablets"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "iron supplements only"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "fluoride mouthwash"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "continuous cardiac (telemetry) monitoring and ECG surveillance"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "ignoring heart rhythm entirely"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "encouraging unsupervised heavy lifting only"}, {"key": "B3d", "text": "stopping all vital-sign checks"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. Merck: IV insulin with glucose lowers serum potassium by shifting it into cells. OpenStax: IV insulin promotes cellular uptake of potassium.
B1b: Incorrect. Adding potassium worsens hyperkalemia.
B1c: Incorrect. High-potassium foods are restricted (OpenStax).
B1d: Incorrect. Unrelated.
B2a: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) removes potassium via the GI tract/stool.
B2b: Incorrect. Extra potassium is contraindicated.
B2c: Incorrect. Unrelated to acute potassium removal.
B2d: Incorrect. Unrelated.
B3a: Correct. OpenStax: continuous telemetry to detect lethal dysrhythmias; Merck emphasizes ECG changes guiding urgency.
B3b: Incorrect. Rhythm surveillance is essential.
B3c: Incorrect. Unrelated and unsafe.
B3d: Incorrect. Monitoring must continue.
topic: NGN cloze — hyperkalemia insulin shift, binder excretion, cardiac monitoring
source_1_section: Mild hyperkalemia; Moderate to severe hyperkalemia
source_2_section: Nursing Care of Patients with Hyperkalemia; Table 10.7

stem: A toddler with acute gastroenteritis has mild-to-moderate dehydration, is alert, and can take fluids by mouth. Which initial rehydration approach is most appropriate?
options:
A) Begin oral rehydration therapy with an oral rehydration salts (ORS) solution as recommended for mild-to-moderate dehydration.
B) Withhold all fluids for 24 hours to 'rest the gut'.
C) Give only undiluted fruit juice ad lib without an ORS plan.
D) Skip assessment and immediately start only intravenous fluids for every mild case.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: AAP and WHO recommend oral rehydration for mild and moderate dehydration. WHO: key treatment is rehydration with ORS.
B: Incorrect. Withholding fluids worsens dehydration.
C: Incorrect. WHO specifies ORS (clean water, salt, sugar mixture), not unrestricted juice as the rehydration standard.
D: Incorrect. Merck notes most children succeed with oral rehydration; WHO reserves IV fluids for severe dehydration or shock.
topic: Pediatric dehydration — oral rehydration (ORS) for mild-to-moderate cases

stem: A nurse is transferring a postoperative client from the PACU to an inpatient unit and needs a structured handoff. Which communication framework best fits this purpose?
options:
A) Use a structured SBAR/ISBAR handoff (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation/Request, with Introduction as used locally) so key information is exchanged consistently.
B) Omit all clinical details to 'save time'.
C) Leave a sticky note with only the client's favourite colour.
D) Transfer without speaking to the receiving nurse.
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS presents SBAR as a tool for thorough team communication. OpenStax: ISBAR is used for formal handoff when moving a patient between units.
B: Incorrect. Incomplete handoffs threaten safety (communication failures).
C: Incorrect. Nonclinical trivia is not a handoff.
D: Incorrect. OpenStax requires structured communication with the receiving nurse.
topic: SBAR/ISBAR structured handoff communication
source_1_title: A Double “Never Event”: Wrong Patient and Wrong Side.
source_1_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) — PSNet

stem: A hospitalized adult meets sepsis criteria with hypotension concerning for septic shock. Which nursing/collaborative actions are indicated immediately? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Establish/confirm large-bore IV access and begin ordered rapid crystalloid fluid resuscitation to restore perfusion.
B) Obtain blood cultures (and other ordered cultures) promptly, then give ordered broad-spectrum antibiotics without delay.
C) Monitor lactate/perfusion response and escalate for vasopressors if hypotension persists after fluids per protocol.
D) Delay all antibiotics for 24 hours to 'await a full week of culture results' before any therapy.
E) Discharge home without treatment because fever always resolves alone.
F) Ignore hypotension and withhold fluids intentionally.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: IV crystalloids are first-line to restore perfusion; OpenStax: fluid replacement is essential in septic shock.
B: Correct. Merck: collect cultures then give prompt empiric antibiotics; OpenStax: cultures before antibiotics and timely first dose are critical.
C: Correct. Merck monitors lactate and may need vasopressors; OpenStax Surviving Sepsis bundle includes lactate, cultures, antibiotics, volume, possible vasopressors.
D: Incorrect. Delaying antibiotics increases mortality (both sources emphasize prompt therapy).
E: Incorrect. Septic shock requires urgent treatment.
F: Incorrect. Fluids are first-line perfusion support.
topic: Septic shock — early fluids, cultures, and antibiotics
source_2_section: Taking Action; Medical Therapies and Related Care

stem: A client with known primary adrenal insufficiency arrives with vomiting, severe weakness, hypotension, and confusion suggestive of adrenal crisis. Which action is the priority after activating emergency support?
options:
A) Administer ordered IV hydrocortisone promptly and begin ordered IV fluid resuscitation (e.g., dextrose in saline) without delaying steroid therapy.
B) Withhold all glucocorticoids until a multi-day outpatient endocrine workup is completed next month.
C) Encourage only oral water without notifying the provider.
D) Discharge home for 'watchful waiting' despite shock signs.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: institute glucocorticoid therapy immediately; hydrocortisone IV and saline/dextrose volume expansion. OpenStax: adrenal crisis is treated with IV fluids, dextrose, and hydrocortisone.
B: Incorrect. Merck warns delay in glucocorticoid therapy may be fatal.
C: Incorrect. Crisis requires IV steroids and volume support.
D: Incorrect. Shock requires emergency treatment.
topic: Adrenal crisis — immediate IV hydrocortisone and fluid resuscitation

stem: A trauma client develops sudden severe dyspnea, unilateral absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and progressive hypotension. Tension pneumothorax is suspected. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate immediately?
options:
A) Prepare for immediate needle decompression (needle thoracostomy) of the affected pleural space while supporting airway/oxygenation.
B) Encourage deep coughing only and postpone any pleural decompression.
C) Apply bilateral tourniquets to the thighs as first-line therapy.
D) Discharge home without assessment because chest pain after trauma is always benign.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: immediate needle decompression for tension pneumothorax. OpenStax: tension pneumothorax is treated with immediate needle decompression.
B: Incorrect. Delayed decompression risks arrest (Merck).
C: Incorrect. Unrelated and harmful distraction from airway/chest emergency.
D: Incorrect. This is a life-threatening emergency.
topic: Tension pneumothorax — anticipate immediate needle decompression
source_2_title: 11.6 Disorders of the Lower Respiratory System: Pneumothorax
source_2_section: Taking Action; Medical Therapies and Related Care

stem: An adolescent with anorexia nervosa has severe malnutrition and will begin nutritional rehabilitation. Which nursing priority is most accurate?
options:
A) Support slow, supervised refeeding with close monitoring for refeeding syndrome and cardiac complications; escalate for hospital-level care when medically unstable.
B) Encourage unsupervised binge eating of unlimited high-sugar foods in one sitting without monitoring.
C) Ignore vital signs and electrolytes during refeeding.
D) Advise complete permanent refusal of all nutrition.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: severe weight loss may require hospitalization and supervised nutritional supplementation. OpenStax: refeeding uses slow, measured intake with monitoring because refeeding syndrome can cause arrhythmias and death.
B: Incorrect. Rapid uncontrolled intake increases refeeding risk (OpenStax).
C: Incorrect. Electrolyte/cardiac monitoring is required (both sources).
D: Incorrect. Nutritional restoration is essential treatment (Merck).
topic: Anorexia nervosa — supervised refeeding and refeeding-syndrome monitoring

stem: A nurse teaches a new parent about mood changes after birth. Which statement correctly distinguishes postpartum blues from postpartum depression?
options:
A) Baby blues are relatively mild and usually resolve within about 2 weeks; postpartum depression lasts longer than 2 weeks and is disabling enough to interfere with daily functioning and infant care—seek prompt evaluation.
B) Any tearfulness on day 1 of life always equals lifelong psychosis with no treatment options.
C) Postpartum depression always ends in 24 hours without support.
D) Mood symptoms after birth should never be discussed with a clinician.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: blues last 2–3 days (up to 2 weeks) and are relatively mild; PPD lasts >2 weeks and is disabling. OpenStax: blues are short-term and should be over by 2 weeks; persistent symptoms indicate PPD needing care.
B: Incorrect. Overstates and mislabels transient blues.
C: Incorrect. PPD persists and needs treatment (both sources).
D: Incorrect. Both sources emphasize recognition and help-seeking.
topic: Postpartum blues versus postpartum depression — duration and severity teaching
source_1_section: Symptoms and Signs; introductory contrast with baby blues
source_2_title: 21.5 Postpartum Mood Disorders and Psychiatric Disorders
source_2_section: Baby Blues versus Depression; Nursing Plan and Implementation

stem: After giving complex discharge instructions, which technique best verifies that the client understood the teaching?
options:
A) Use a closed-loop check-back/teach-back: ask the client to repeat the key instructions in their own words and clarify any gaps.
B) Assume understanding if the client nods silently once, with no confirmation.
C) Speak only in unexplained jargon and leave immediately.
D) Refuse to answer any clarifying questions.
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ: check-back (repeat-back) is closed-loop communication to verify information was received; patients can use it for care instructions. OpenStax: teach-back has the patient restate the message in their own words to judge understanding.
B: Incorrect. Nodding alone does not confirm accurate understanding.
C: Incorrect. Barriers and unclear messages undermine teaching.
D: Incorrect. Clarification is part of effective communication (both sources).
topic: Check-back/teach-back to verify client understanding
source_1_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
source_2_section: Compare Response to Desired Communication Goals; Teach-Back Method

stem: A public health nurse teaches a community group about tuberculosis. For each statement, select Accurate or Not accurate.
options: {"columns": ["Accurate", "Not accurate"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Latent TB infection (LTBI) means the person has M. tuberculosis but is not ill and cannot transmit TB to others"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Active pulmonary TB disease can be contagious and is spread by airborne droplet nuclei from cough or similar respiratory force"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Everyone with a positive TB skin or blood test is highly contagious and must be placed in airborne isolation indefinitely without further evaluation"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Active TB disease may cause cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and other symptoms and requires treatment"}]}
rationales:
R1: Accurate. Merck: LTBI is asymptomatic and not infectious. OpenStax: LTBI — no symptoms; cannot transmit the bacteria.
R2: Accurate. Merck: TB is transmitted almost exclusively by inhalation of airborne particles (droplet nuclei) from people with active pulmonary TB. OpenStax: active TB is highly contagious via airborne transmission.
R3: Not accurate. A positive test indicates infection but further evaluation distinguishes LTBI from active disease; LTBI is not contagious (Merck; OpenStax).
R4: Accurate. Merck and OpenStax list cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss among active TB symptoms; active disease requires treatment.
topic: NGN matrix — latent TB not infectious vs active TB contagious teaching
source_1_section: Pathophysiology — Latent TB infection; Etiology — transmission
source_2_section: Tuberculosis — Table 13.3 LTBI vs TB disease

stem: An older adult arrives with unexplained bruises in several stages of healing and appears fearful when the caregiver answers for them. Which nursing action is the priority first step when elder abuse is suspected?
options:
A) Interview the older adult alone (at least for part of the encounter) using private, direct questions about safety and possible mistreatment, and follow mandatory reporting pathways (e.g., adult protective services) when abuse is suspected or identified.
B) Allow only the caregiver to provide the entire history and never speak with the older adult privately.
C) Ignore bruising because all older adults bruise easily and never document findings.
D) Confront the caregiver angrily in front of the client and refuse any further assessment.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: if elder abuse is suspected, interview the patient alone at least part of the time and ask direct questions; referral to Adult Protective Services is required in most jurisdictions when abuse is identified or suspected. OpenStax: report suspected elder abuse to adult protective services (or equivalent) and listen to older adults.
B: Incorrect. Merck warns caregiver reluctance to leave the older adult alone with a clinician is concerning; private interview is essential.
C: Incorrect. Unexplained injuries and inconsistent histories are red flags requiring assessment and documentation (Merck).
D: Incorrect. Merck advises avoiding confrontation that escalates risk; structured private assessment and reporting are required.
topic: Elder abuse — private interview and mandatory protective-services reporting
source_2_section: Elder abuse — mechanisms nurses can use to prevent

stem: A client at 30 weeks gestation is in preterm labour. Complete the teaching/plan: Antenatal {B1} are given primarily to promote {B2}, and short-term tocolysis may be used mainly to {B3}.
options: {"template": "A client at 30 weeks gestation is in preterm labour. Complete the teaching/plan: Antenatal {B1} are given primarily to promote {B2}, and short-term tocolysis may be used mainly to {B3}.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "corticosteroids (e.g., betamethasone or dexamethasone)"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "high-dose vitamin C only"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "routine antitussives"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "topical antifungal cream only"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "fetal lung maturity / reduce neonatal respiratory distress risk"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "maternal hair growth"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "elective induction at 28 weeks without indication"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "immediate permanent sterilization"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "gain time (often ~48 hours) for corticosteroids to take effect before birth"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "replace the need for any neonatal resuscitation planning"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "guarantee delivery will never occur preterm"}, {"key": "B3d", "text": "stop all fetal monitoring permanently"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: antenatal corticosteroids are standard when preterm birth is anticipated in the eligible gestational window.
B1b: Incorrect. Vitamin C is not the antenatal therapy that accelerates fetal lung maturity in preterm labour.
B1c: Incorrect. Antitussives are unrelated to fetal lung maturation.
B1d: Incorrect. Topical antifungals do not promote fetal surfactant/lung maturity.
B2a: Correct. OpenStax: corticosteroids promote fetal lung maturity/surfactant and reduce RDS risk; Merck: corticosteroids given in the preterm window for fetal benefit.
B2b: Incorrect. Not a fetal lung indication.
B2c: Incorrect. Goal is fetal maturation, not elective early induction.
B2d: Incorrect. Unrelated to antenatal corticosteroid purpose.
B3a: Correct. Merck: tocolytics can usually delay labour for at least 48 hours so corticosteroids can be given.
B3b: Incorrect. Tocolysis does not eliminate need for neonatal preparedness.
B3c: Incorrect. Tocolysis does not permanently prevent preterm birth.
B3d: Incorrect. Monitoring continues; tocolysis is time-limited bridge therapy.
topic: NGN cloze — preterm labour antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity

stem: A client on postpartum day 2 after cesarean birth has fever, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Notify the provider and anticipate ordered broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
B) Monitor vital signs and assess for worsening infection or early sepsis cues
C) Document uterine tenderness, lochia characteristics, and fever trend
D) Reassure that fever and foul lochia after cesarean never require evaluation
E) Withhold all assessment of the fundus and discharge home without follow-up teaching
F) Teach the client to report increasing pain, rising fever, or worsening foul discharge
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: treatment is broad-spectrum antibiotics; OpenStax: nurse administers ordered antibiotics for endometritis.
B: Correct. OpenStax: monitor for worsening infection/sepsis; Merck notes potential progression to severe infection.
C: Correct. Both sources describe fever, uterine tenderness, and abnormal/foul discharge as key findings to track.
D: Incorrect. These findings indicate postpartum endometritis needing prompt evaluation/treatment (Merck; OpenStax).
E: Incorrect. Assessment and teaching are required; endometritis can progress (OpenStax).
F: Correct. OpenStax discharge teaching includes contacting the provider for worsening infection signs.
topic: Postpartum endometritis — antibiotics, monitoring, and warning-sign teaching
source_2_section: Care of the Postpartum Person with Endometritis

stem: A young adult with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, Kussmaul respirations, glucose markedly elevated, and anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Complete the bowtie: priority condition, two actions, and two parameters to monitor.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) with hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Isolated cerumen impaction"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Stable euglycemia without acid-base disturbance"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Initiate ordered IV fluid volume resuscitation and continuous IV insulin per protocol"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Monitor and replace potassium as ordered while insulin/fluids are given"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Withhold all fluids and insulin because hyperglycemia is always self-limited"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Discharge home immediately without laboratory follow-up"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Encourage unsupervised intense exercise before treatment"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Blood glucose trend and resolution of acidosis/ketosis"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Serum potassium and cardiac/neurologic status during insulin and fluid therapy"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Only hair colour changes"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Only shoe size"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Only preferred music genre"}]}
rationales:
K1: Correct. Merck/OpenStax: DKA features hyperglycemia with ketonemia/acidosis; clinical picture matches.
K2: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not explain ketoacidosis.
K3: Incorrect. Unrelated to metabolic emergency.
K4: Incorrect. Client has marked hyperglycemia and acidosis.
A1: Correct. Merck: volume expansion and insulin replacement; OpenStax: aggressive IV fluids and IV insulin.
A2: Correct. Merck: prevent hypokalemia; OpenStax: monitor/correct potassium especially during treatment.
A3: Incorrect. DKA requires prompt fluids and insulin (both sources).
A4: Incorrect. DKA is an ICU/emergency condition needing monitored therapy.
A5: Incorrect. Exercise is not initial DKA management.
P1: Correct. Therapy is titrated to glucose and clearing of ketoacidosis (both sources).
P2: Correct. Potassium shifts with insulin; both sources emphasize potassium monitoring.
P3: Incorrect. Not a DKA monitoring parameter.
P4: Incorrect. Not clinically relevant here.
P5: Incorrect. Not clinically relevant here.
topic: NGN bowtie — DKA fluids, IV insulin, and potassium monitoring
source_1_title: Acute Complications of Diabetes Mellitus — Diabetic Ketoacidosis

stem: A client with bulimia nervosa who induces vomiting after binge episodes reports palpitations. Which nursing priority is most appropriate?
options:
A) Obtain ordered electrolyte laboratory studies (especially potassium), monitor cardiac status, and support supervised nutrition/anti-purging interventions while notifying the provider of concerning findings.
B) Encourage unsupervised intense laxative use after every meal.
C) Ignore palpitations because electrolyte imbalance never occurs in bulimia.
D) Withhold all vital signs and laboratory monitoring permanently.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: serious electrolyte disturbances, especially hypokalemia, can occur; measure electrolytes. OpenStax: hypokalemia and arrhythmia risk; interventions include labs, electrolyte replacement, and interrupting purging.
B: Incorrect. Laxative misuse worsens fluid/electrolyte imbalance (both sources describe purging harms).
C: Incorrect. Hypokalemia is a recognized complication (Merck; OpenStax).
D: Incorrect. Monitoring labs and cardiac status is essential (OpenStax care plan).
topic: Bulimia nervosa — electrolyte (hypokalemia) and cardiac monitoring priority
source_2_section: Nursing Care Planning; Life-Threatening Complications; Interventions

stem: A client suddenly develops intense fear with palpitations, shortness of breath, and a sense of doom. Immediate ECG and medical evaluation have ruled out acute coronary syndrome and other life-threatening medical causes. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate during the panic attack?
options:
A) Remain calm, move the client to a quieter less stimulating environment if possible, coach slow deep breathing, and offer brief reassurance that the attack will pass while continuing to monitor.
B) Crowd the client with loud multiple conversations and argue that the fear is imaginary.
C) Leave the client completely alone without observation in an unsafe isolated area.
D) Force the client to sprint immediately to 'burn off' the attack without assessment.
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: nurse remains calm, encourages slow deep breathing, offers reassurance, and uses a quiet calm environment. Merck: after medical causes are considered/excluded, panic attacks themselves are not medically dangerous; supportive care and psychotherapy approaches are used.
B: Incorrect. OpenStax advises reducing stimuli and remaining calm, not escalating sensory load or arguing.
C: Incorrect. Supportive presence and monitoring are indicated during intense symptoms (OpenStax).
D: Incorrect. Intense exercise is not the immediate panic-attack nursing intervention described in the sources.
topic: Panic attack — calm environment, slow breathing, reassurance after medical rule-out
source_1_section: Panic Attack — Nursing Strategies and Interventions

stem: A nurse teaches caregivers of toddlers about household poisoning prevention. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Store medications, cleaning products, and other toxic substances in secure locations out of children's reach
B) Keep the local poison control centre number readily available and call for advice after a possible poisoning exposure
C) Leave laundry pods and concentrated cleaners on low open shelves where toddlers play
D) Assume unlabeled household chemicals are always safe for children to taste
E) Use clear labeling of medication containers and never transfer poisons into food/drink containers
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: keep poisons out of reach of children. OpenStax: store toxic products safely away from children and pets.
B: Correct. Merck: call local poison center for advice; OpenStax: keep poison control numbers nearby and know when to get help.
C: Incorrect. Opposite of safe storage guidance (both sources).
D: Incorrect. Education includes recognizing toxic household products (OpenStax).
E: Correct. Merck emphasizes clear medication labeling as prevention; safe storage/identification prevents accidental ingestion.
topic: Pediatric household poisoning prevention — secure storage and poison control contact

stem: An older adult found outdoors has a measured core temperature of 33.5°C, is shivering, and has intact circulation without cardiovascular instability. Which intervention best matches initial management of mild hypothermia?
options:
A) Begin passive rewarming: move to a warm environment, apply insulating/heated blankets, and provide warm oral fluids if the client can safely swallow, while monitoring core temperature and perfusion.
B) Leave wet cold clothing on and keep the client in a drafty unheated area.
C) Apply ice packs to the trunk to further lower core temperature.
D) Withhold all temperature monitoring because shivering always means normal temperature.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: mild hypothermia (about 32–35°C) with intact thermoregulation is treated with passive rewarming (warm environment, heated blankets, warm fluids). OpenStax Clinical Skills defines hypothermia as core temperature <35°C (95°F), matching this presentation.
B: Incorrect. Merck/OpenStax emphasize removing cold exposure and supporting rewarming, not continued heat loss.
C: Incorrect. Cooling worsens hypothermia.
D: Incorrect. Core temperature guides severity and treatment (Merck Key Points).
topic: Mild hypothermia — passive rewarming with warm environment and blankets
source_2_section: The Danger of Low Temperature — hypothermia definition

stem: A 3-year-old with nonsevere acute otitis media is mildly ill, afebrile to low-grade fever only, and has reliable caregiver follow-up. Which teaching point is most accurate?
options:
A) Provide appropriate analgesia (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed) for ear pain, and understand that selected nonsevere cases may be observed for about 24–48 hours with planned reassessment, starting antibiotics if symptoms worsen or fail to improve.
B) Never treat pain because analgesics are never used in ear infections.
C) Immediate IV vancomycin is required for every mild earache without examination.
D) Ignore fever ≥39°C with severe systemic illness because observation is always mandatory.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: analgesia for all children with AOM; observation is an option for selected nonsevere cases with follow-up. CPS Caring for Kids: acetaminophen/ibuprofen for pain; watchful waiting 24–48 hours when illness is not severe, with antibiotics if no improvement or worsening.
B: Incorrect. Both sources emphasize treating pain.
C: Incorrect. Not first-line for uncomplicated nonsevere AOM (Merck prefers oral amoxicillin when antibiotics are indicated).
D: Incorrect. High fever/severe illness warrants prompt antimicrobials (CPS; Merck).
topic: Acute otitis media — analgesia for all and selective 24–48h observation
jurisdiction_note: CPS and Merck both support analgesia for AOM and selective observation for nonsevere cases with reliable follow-up.
source_2_publisher: Canadian Paediatric Society — Caring for Kids
source_2_section: How is an ear infection treated?

stem: A charge nurse wants to improve shared understanding of goals and roles before a high-risk shift. Which TeamSTEPPS leadership strategy best fits this need?
options:
A) Conduct a brief (short team session) at the start to clarify membership/roles, patient status, the care plan/goals, and resource/workload issues so everyone understands the plan.
B) Avoid any pre-shift communication so team members discover the plan only after errors occur.
C) Assign roles silently without stating goals or contingency plans.
D) Delay all discussion of the care plan until after discharge paperwork is filed.
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ: briefs share the care plan, team roles, patient status, and operational issues; often at beginning of shift/case. OpenStax: TeamSTEPPS recommends a brief checklist at the beginning so all members understand the plan.
B: Incorrect. Briefs exist to establish shared mental model before work begins (AHRQ; OpenStax).
C: Incorrect. Role clarity and articulated goals are core brief content (AHRQ).
D: Incorrect. Planning communication occurs before/during care, not only after discharge.
topic: TeamSTEPPS brief — share plan, roles, and goals at start of shift/case
source_1_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)

stem: A term newborn develops visible jaundice at 18 hours of life. Which interpretation and action is most appropriate?
options:
A) Treat as potentially pathologic jaundice: notify the provider promptly, obtain ordered bilirubin evaluation, and prepare for indicated therapy (often phototherapy) based on level and risk.
B) Assume all jaundice before 24 hours is always harmless physiologic jaundice requiring no evaluation.
C) Discharge without assessment because early jaundice never needs follow-up.
D) Start adult chemotherapy protocols for jaundice.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: pathologic hyperbilirubinemia includes jaundice appearing in the first 24 hours. OpenStax: jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathologic/nonphysiologic and warrants earlier evaluation/treatment, often phototherapy.
B: Incorrect. Physiologic jaundice typically appears after the first 24 hours (OpenStax; Merck timing).
C: Incorrect. Early-onset jaundice requires prompt evaluation (both sources).
D: Incorrect. Not the treatment pathway for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.
topic: Neonatal jaundice in first 24 hours — pathologic, prompt bilirubin evaluation
source_2_title: 24.2 Care of Common Problems in the Newborn
source_2_section: Care of the Newborn with Hyperbilirubinemia

stem: A public health nurse teaches a household about classic scabies. For each statement, select Accurate or Not accurate.
options: {"columns": ["Accurate", "Not accurate"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Scabies is most commonly spread by direct, prolonged skin-to-skin contact with a person who has scabies"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "All household members and close contacts should be treated at the same time, even if they have no symptoms yet"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Clothing, towels, and bedding used next to the skin should be washed in hot water or otherwise decontaminated as directed"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Scabies mites live for months on furniture and clothing, so environmental cleaning is useless and only the index client needs treatment"}]}
rationales:
R1: Accurate. CDC: human scabies most commonly spreads by direct, prolonged skin-to-skin contact. Merck: transmission involves close contact.
R2: Accurate. CDC: treat all household members and close contacts at the same time. Merck: empiric treatment of close contacts even if asymptomatic.
R3: Accurate. CDC: wash clothing/towels/bedding in hot water or dry-clean/seal items. Merck: environmental decontamination is a prevention strategy.
R4: Not accurate. Mites generally do not survive more than 2–3 days away from human skin (CDC); contacts need concurrent treatment (CDC; Merck).
topic: NGN matrix — scabies transmission, concurrent contact treatment, laundry/decontamination
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_1_section: How it spreads; Prevention/Control; Treatment and recovery

stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has severe neutropenia. Which nursing actions support neutropenic (protective) precautions and infection risk reduction? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Perform meticulous hand hygiene and uphold aseptic technique before client contact
B) Avoid fresh flowers in the room because of infection risk (e.g., Aspergillus)
C) Teach avoidance of fresh fruit and uncooked meats that may carry foodborne contaminants
D) Room the client with another client who has active influenza to 'boost immunity'
E) Ignore new fever because localized infection signs are always obvious in neutropenia
F) Ensure visitors/staff follow masking and other protective measures as ordered to reduce opportunistic exposure
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: meticulous hand hygiene and aseptic technique reduce nosocomial infection in neutropenia.
B: Correct. OpenStax neutropenic precautions: avoid fresh flowers (Aspergillus/chemical exposure risk).
C: Correct. OpenStax: avoid fresh fruit and uncooked meats to reduce foodborne contaminants.
D: Incorrect. Protective precautions aim to reduce pathogen exposure; placing with influenza increases risk.
E: Incorrect. Merck: focal infection signs may be muted in neutropenia, but fever is present in most serious infections and warrants immediate empiric antibiotics.
F: Correct. OpenStax: providers, staff, and visitors wear masks to protect the patient from opportunistic infections.
topic: Neutropenic precautions — hand hygiene, avoid flowers/raw foods, mask visitors; fever not ignored
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

stem: After a critical resuscitation, the charge nurse wants a short TeamSTEPPS after-action review focused on learning. Which action best matches a debrief?
options:
A) Facilitate a brief end-of-event discussion (often initiated by the leader) that reviews what went well and what to improve, reinforces successful behaviours, and captures lessons for the next plan—without assigning individual blame.
B) Skip any review so the team never discusses performance.
C) Publicly shame one team member for any perceived mistake.
D) Wait until the next annual performance appraisal to discuss the event for the first time.
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ: debriefs recount/analyze events, discuss lessons, reinforce what went well, avoid blame; often short and leader-facilitated. OpenStax: TeamSTEPPS debrief checklist at the end for reflection and continuous improvement.
B: Incorrect. TeamSTEPPS advocates after-action debriefs after critical team events (AHRQ).
C: Incorrect. AHRQ: avoid assigning blame; focus on performance improvement and learning.
D: Incorrect. Debriefs are timely after events (AHRQ), not deferred to annual appraisal only.
topic: TeamSTEPPS debrief — after-action learning without blame
source_1_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)

stem: A pregnant client in the first trimester has persistent severe vomiting with signs of significant dehydration, ketosis, and weight loss. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options:
A) This presentation is consistent with hyperemesis gravidarum and may require hospitalization for fluid and electrolyte replacement and further management.
B) Severe vomiting with dehydration and weight loss in early pregnancy is always harmless 'morning sickness' that never needs evaluation.
C) All first-trimester nausea requires immediate chemotherapy.
D) Weight loss and ketosis prove the client should stop all prenatal care.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: hyperemesis gravidarum is persistent severe pregnancy-induced vomiting causing significant dehydration, often with electrolyte abnormalities, ketosis, and weight loss. OpenStax: severe nausea/vomiting with electrolyte imbalance, weight loss, malnutrition, and dehydration may require hospitalization for fluid/electrolyte replacement.
B: Incorrect. Ordinary nausea/vomiting of pregnancy is common; hyperemesis is the severe form needing evaluation/possible hospital care (Merck; OpenStax).
C: Incorrect. Not the treatment pathway described for hyperemesis in these sources.
D: Incorrect. Clients need supportive care and prenatal follow-up, not cessation of care.
topic: Hyperemesis gravidarum — severe vomiting with dehydration/ketosis/weight loss may need hospital fluids
source_1_title: Nausea and Vomiting During Early Pregnancy

stem: Complete the teaching for a pregnant client about HELLP syndrome associated with severe preeclampsia.
options: {"template": "HELLP stands for {B1}, elevated liver enzymes, and {B2}. It can develop in some clients with severe preeclampsia/eclampsia and requires {B3}.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "hemolysis"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "hypercalcemia"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "hyponatremia only"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "high hemoglobin concentration"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "low platelet count"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "elevated platelet count"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "low bilirubin only"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "increased clotting factor VII only"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "prompt evaluation and close monitoring because it can be life-threatening to the pregnant person and fetus"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "no follow-up because HELLP is always harmless"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "routine delayed outpatient labs in 6 months only"}, {"key": "B3d", "text": "immediate homeopathy without clinician involvement"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: H = hemolysis in HELLP.
B1b: Incorrect. Hypercalcemia is not the H in HELLP.
B1c: Incorrect. Hyponatremia is not the defining H component.
B1d: Incorrect. HELLP involves hemolysis, not high hemoglobin as the acronym letter.
B2a: Correct. Merck/OpenStax: LP = low platelets.
B2b: Incorrect. Platelets are low, not elevated.
B2c: Incorrect. Low bilirubin alone is not the LP component.
B2d: Incorrect. Not the LP meaning in HELLP.
B3a: Correct. OpenStax: HELLP can be life-threatening; close monitoring and prompt evaluation are necessary. Merck: HELLP develops in a subset with severe preeclampsia/eclampsia.
B3b: Incorrect. HELLP is a serious complication.
B3c: Incorrect. Prompt evaluation is required, not remote delayed labs only.
B3d: Incorrect. Not evidence-based management from cited sources.
topic: NGN cloze — HELLP = hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets; prompt monitoring

stem: A breastfeeding client on postpartum day 4 has firm, swollen, painful breasts with a flattened nipple that makes latch difficult. Which teaching is most appropriate?
options:
A) Use warm compress or a warm shower and hand-express a small amount of milk to soften the breast and help the nipple protrude for latch; continue frequent feeding; cool compresses between feedings may reduce inflammation.
B) Stop breastfeeding permanently at the first sign of engorgement.
C) Avoid any feeding or expression so milk pressure rises indefinitely.
D) Apply ice packs continuously for 24 hours without feeding the infant.
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: warm compress/shower and hand expression to soften for latch; cool compress between feedings. Merck: expressing milk (warm shower/pump) temporarily for pressure relief and breastfeeding on a regular schedule for those who will breastfeed.
B: Incorrect. Engorgement is managed while continuing lactation support for breastfeeding clients (both sources).
C: Incorrect. Regular feeding/appropriate expression relieves engorgement (Merck; OpenStax).
D: Incorrect. Continuous icing without feeding is not the cited breastfeeding engorgement plan; cool packs are adjunct between feeds (OpenStax).
topic: Breast engorgement — warm soften/hand express for latch, frequent feeding, cool between feeds

stem: A nurse teaches expected postpartum lochia changes. For each statement, select Accurate or Not accurate.
options: {"columns": ["Accurate", "Not accurate"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Lochia rubra is grossly bloody/red discharge expected in the first few postpartum days"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Lochia then typically becomes pale brown (serosa) and later yellowish white (alba)"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Saturating a peripad in less than 1 hour is considered excessive and needs prompt uterine assessment"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Foul-smelling discharge is expected normal lochia and never needs clinician contact"}]}
rationales:
R1: Accurate. Merck: lochia rubra grossly bloody for ~3–4 days. OpenStax: lochia rubra bright/dark red for about the first 1–4 days.
R2: Accurate. Merck: pale brown (serosa) then yellowish white (alba). OpenStax describes progression of lochia types with assessment teaching.
R3: Accurate. OpenStax: saturating a pad in <1 hour is excessive and requires immediate uterine assessment. Merck advises contacting clinician for concern about heavy bleeding.
R4: Not accurate. OpenStax: foul odor may signal uterine infection—contact the provider.
topic: NGN matrix — lochia rubra→serosa→alba; heavy pad soak and foul odor are red flags
source_2_title: 20.1 Physiologic Changes During the Postpartum Period

stem: Which nursing strategies help prevent or reduce hospital delirium risk in an older adult? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Maintain orientation with cues (e.g., date/time, staff names, visual reminders) and involve family for familiarity when appropriate
B) Promote sleep hygiene and protect rest when possible
C) Support mobility/assistance with movement and address pain, nutrition, and hydration
D) Add as many new psychoactive medications as possible without review
E) Keep the same caregivers as much as possible to reduce confusion
F) Leave sensory aids (glasses/hearing devices) unavailable all admission so the client 'adjusts'
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck prevention: maintain orientation; family can help. OpenStax: whiteboards/cues and family familiarity.
B: Correct. Merck: ensure sleep. OpenStax: promote sleep hygiene.
C: Correct. Merck: mobility, nutrition, hydration, pain relief. OpenStax: assist with movement; treat pain; proper nutrition.
D: Incorrect. Merck: reduce number/doses of medications if possible; new meds can precipitate delirium.
E: Correct. OpenStax: keep the same caregivers as much as possible.
F: Incorrect. Sensory impairment predisposes to delirium (Merck); aids should be available, not withheld.
topic: Delirium prevention — orientation, sleep, mobility, nutrition/hydration/pain, consistent caregivers

stem: A nurse educates a client with asthma and the caregiver about self-management. Which teaching point is most strongly supported?
options:
A) Provide a written asthma action plan describing day-to-day management and what to do for exacerbations (often guided by the client's best personal peak flow), plus inhaler/spacer technique and trigger awareness.
B) Tell the client never to have any written plan because asthma cannot be self-monitored.
C) Advise using peak-flow–based decisions only against a stranger's predicted normal value and never the client's personal best.
D) Recommend waiting until severe respiratory failure before any early glucocorticoid use discussed in an action plan.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: every patient should have a written action plan for daily and acute management based on best personal peak flow; education includes triggers and inhaler/spacer technique. OpenStax: implement an asthma action plan to monitor symptoms and adjust medications; written personalized plans help caregivers/patients stay safe.
B: Incorrect. Written action plans improve control/adherence (Merck; OpenStax).
C: Incorrect. Merck emphasizes the patient's best personal peak flow rather than predicted normal alone.
D: Incorrect. Merck notes importance of early glucocorticoid use in exacerbations as part of education.
topic: Asthma written action plan — personal best peak flow, inhaler/spacer, triggers
source_2_title: 11.4 Disorders of the Lower Respiratory System: Asthma

stem: A nurse cares for a large-for-gestational-age newborn of a mother with diabetes. Which priority approach is most appropriate regarding neonatal hypoglycemia risk?
options:
A) Follow facility protocol for glucose monitoring of at-risk newborns, support early feeding (often within the first hour), and treat confirmed hypoglycemia with enteral feeding or IV dextrose as ordered—do not wait for seizures before acting.
B) Never monitor glucose in infants of diabetic mothers because hypoglycemia never occurs in this group.
C) Withhold all feeds for 12 hours to 'test' hypoglycemia tolerance.
D) Treat only with adult oral hypoglycemic tablets crushed into formula.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: risk factors include maternal diabetes; treatment is enteral feeding or IV dextrose; signs can include seizures/apnea. OpenStax: IDM/LGA are at risk; monitor at-risk newborns per policy; encourage early breastfeeding; prevent cold stress; do not wait for all term newborns to become symptomatic before protocol monitoring.
B: Incorrect. Infants of diabetic mothers are a classic risk group (Merck; OpenStax).
C: Incorrect. Early feeding is preventive/supportive (OpenStax; Merck treatment includes feeding).
D: Incorrect. Not the neonatal pathway in cited sources (feeding/IV dextrose).
topic: Neonatal hypoglycemia risk (IDM/LGA) — protocol monitoring, early feeding, IV dextrose if needed
units_note: Glucose thresholds vary by source/protocol; item keys risk recognition and feeding/IV dextrose management, not a single cut-off number.
source_2_title: 24.2 Care of Common Problems in the Newborn
source_2_section: Care of the Newborn with Hypoglycemia

stem: A client with chemotherapy-related severe neutropenia develops a new fever. Complete the bowtie: identify the priority condition, two actions, and two parameters to monitor.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Febrile neutropenia / presumed serious infection due to severe neutropenia"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Uncomplicated seasonal allergies without infection risk"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Stable iron-deficiency anemia only"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Resolved otitis externa from childhood"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Notify the provider and initiate ordered empiric high-dose broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Delay all antibiotics for 48 hours to 'see if fever resolves alone'"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Obtain ordered cultures and implement protective/neutropenic precautions (hand hygiene, limit exposure)"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Send the client to a crowded public event without masking"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Stop temperature monitoring for the shift"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Temperature / fever trend"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Absolute neutrophil count and signs of clinical instability (e.g., hypotension)"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Favourite television channel only"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Shoe size"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Hair colour"}]}
rationales:
K1: Correct. Merck: with fever in neutropenia, infection is presumed and immediate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics are necessary.
K2: Incorrect. Not the acute life-threatening problem described.
K3: Incorrect. Does not explain febrile neutropenia urgency.
K4: Incorrect. Irrelevant childhood history.
A1: Correct. Merck: immediate empiric high-dose broad-spectrum IV antibiotics when fever/hypotension present.
A2: Incorrect. Delaying antibiotics is unsafe in febrile neutropenia (Merck).
A3: Correct. Cultures are part of infection evaluation; OpenStax emphasizes protective precautions and infection surveillance.
A4: Incorrect. Increases opportunistic exposure (OpenStax precautions).
A5: Incorrect. OpenStax: routine temperature surveillance is essential.
P1: Correct. Fever drives urgent treatment decisions (Merck); OpenStax monitors temperature.
P2: Correct. Neutrophil count severity and hypotension guide urgency (Merck); OpenStax monitors ANC and infection signs.
P3: Incorrect. Not a clinical parameter for this emergency.
P4: Incorrect. Not relevant.
P5: Incorrect. Not relevant.
topic: NGN bowtie — febrile neutropenia: empiric IV antibiotics, cultures/precautions, monitor fever/ANC
source_2_section: Nursing Care — neutropenic precautions and surveillance

stem: Which finding best aligns with the definition of preeclampsia used in standard clinical references?
options:
A) New-onset (or worsening) hypertension with proteinuria after 20 weeks' gestation (with evaluation for end-organ involvement as indicated)
B) Isolated mild headache at 8 weeks with normal blood pressure and no proteinuria
C) Chronic hypertension diagnosed years before pregnancy with no change after 20 weeks and no proteinuria
D) Postprandial fullness in the second trimester without hypertension
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: preeclampsia is new onset or worsening hypertension with proteinuria after 20 weeks, with evaluation for end-organ damage. OpenStax covers hypertensive disorders of pregnancy including preeclampsia after mid-pregnancy with monitoring/management implications.
B: Incorrect. Too early and lacks hypertension/proteinuria criteria (Merck: after 20 weeks).
C: Incorrect. Pre-existing chronic hypertension without new features is a different category (OpenStax/Merck distinguish hypertensive disorders).
D: Incorrect. Not diagnostic for preeclampsia.
topic: Preeclampsia definition — hypertension with proteinuria after 20 weeks

stem: A school nurse teaches caregivers after a child is diagnosed with pinworm (enterobiasis). Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Treat the infected child, household members, and caregivers with the same timed medication course as directed.
B) Wash hands with soap and warm water after toileting, after diaper changes, and before handling food.
C) Wash clothing, towels, and bedding used by the affected person in hot water and dry on high heat when possible.
D) Give only one lifetime dose of anthelmintic medication because eggs are also killed permanently by a single dose.
E) Ignore household contacts because pinworms never spread within families.
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: treat infected persons, caretakers, and household members at the same time (two-dose schedule). Merck: multiple household infestations are common; treatment of the entire family may be necessary.
B: Correct. CDC and Merck: handwashing with soap and warm water after toilet/diapers and before food is the key prevention step.
C: Correct. CDC: wash clothes/washcloths/towels/bedding in hot water and dry hot. Merck: frequently wash clothing, bedding, and toys.
D: Incorrect. CDC: two doses about two weeks apart because medication kills worms but not eggs. Merck: single dose repeated in 2 weeks.
E: Incorrect. CDC and Merck: household members and caregivers are at increased risk; concurrent treatment/prevention is needed.
topic: Pinworm — concurrent household treatment, handwashing, hot laundry; two-dose schedule
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A public health nurse teaches a family about head lice. For each statement, select Accurate or Not accurate.
options: {"columns": ["Accurate", "Not accurate"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Head lice spread mainly by direct head-to-head (hair-to-hair) contact"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Children diagnosed with head lice must be sent home from school immediately mid-day and kept out until every nit is removed"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Avoid sharing hats, combs, brushes, and towels; wash recently used linens and clothing in hot water when possible"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Fumigant sprays or fogs are required to disinfect the entire home after any lice case"}]}
rationales:
R1: Accurate. CDC: most common spread is head-to-head contact. Merck: easily transmitted by close contact in households/classrooms.
R2: Not accurate. CDC: children need not be sent home early; go home end of day, start treatment, return after treatment begun. Merck cites CDC school guidance.
R3: Accurate. CDC: do not share hats/combs/brushes/towels; hot-water laundry for recent items. Merck discusses washing/drying hot for personal items.
R4: Not accurate. CDC: do not use fumigant sprays/fogs — not necessary and can be toxic.
topic: NGN matrix — head lice head-to-head spread, school return after treatment started, laundry, no fumigants
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_1_section: How it spreads; Prevention; Reminder school guidance
source_2_section: Head lice — transmission and school guidance

stem: A toddler is referred after a caregiver notices a firm swelling in the abdomen. Imaging is consistent with Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma). Which finding is the most frequent presenting feature of Wilms tumor?
options:
A) A painless, palpable abdominal mass
B) Night sweats with migratory polyarthritis as the sole finding
C) Painless jaundice from birth without a mass
D) Isolated petechiae covering the trunk without organomegaly
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: the most frequent finding is a painless, palpable abdominal mass. OpenStax: Wilms tumor/nephroblastoma presents in childhood with kidney enlargement (and often hypertension).
B: Incorrect. Not the classic primary presentation of Wilms tumor (Merck lists mass as most frequent).
C: Incorrect. Jaundice is not the most frequent Wilms presentation (Merck).
D: Incorrect. Petechiae alone are not the characteristic Wilms presentation (Merck).
topic: Wilms tumor — painless palpable abdominal mass most frequent finding
source_1_section: Symptoms and Signs of Wilms Tumor

stem: A school-age client newly diagnosed with celiac disease is learning diet teaching. Complete the statements.
options: {"template": "Celiac disease is treated with a {B1} diet. The client must avoid gluten proteins found in {B2}.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "short-term low-fat only"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "lifelong strict gluten-free"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "high-purine unrestricted"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "clear-liquid forever"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "wheat, barley, and rye"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "only pure table salt"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "all fresh fruits forever"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "only purified water"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Incorrect. Treatment is lifelong gluten-free diet, not a short-term low-fat diet (OpenStax; Merck).
B1b: Correct. OpenStax: lifelong strict gluten-free diet. Merck: mucosal changes resolve with a strict gluten-free diet.
B1c: Incorrect. Not the celiac diet prescription (OpenStax; Merck).
B1d: Incorrect. Clear liquids are not lifelong celiac therapy (OpenStax; Merck).
B2a: Correct. Merck: gliadin fraction of gluten in wheat; similar proteins in rye and barley. OpenStax: gluten in wheat, barley, and rye.
B2b: Incorrect. Salt is not the gluten source to avoid (Merck; OpenStax).
B2c: Incorrect. Fresh fruit is not the gluten source requiring lifelong exclusion (Merck; OpenStax).
B2d: Incorrect. Water is not a gluten grain protein (Merck; OpenStax).
topic: NGN cloze — celiac lifelong gluten-free diet; avoid wheat/barley/rye
source_1_title: 19.5 Disorders of the Lower GI System

stem: An infant younger than 1 year has severe foreign-body airway obstruction (cannot cry effectively, weak cough, cyanosis). Which action is correct?
options:
A) Give repeated cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 chest thrusts until the object is expelled or the infant becomes unresponsive; do not use abdominal thrusts.
B) Perform only abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) as the sole first-line method for infants.
C) Do blind finger sweeps immediately to dig deeply in the mouth before any other action.
D) Offer the infant a large drink of water to wash the object into the stomach.
rationales:
A: Correct. AHA/AAP Pediatric BLS 2025: infants with severe FBAO — cycles of 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts not recommended. Merck: back blows followed by chest thrusts for severe infant choking.
B: Incorrect. Abdominal thrusts are not recommended in infants (AHA/AAP; Merck uses chest thrusts for infants).
C: Incorrect. AHA/AAP: blind finger sweeps should not be performed.
D: Incorrect. Giving fluids does not relieve severe FBAO and delays effective relief (AHA/AAP; Merck procedure).
topic: Infant severe FBAO — 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts; no abdominal thrusts
source_1_publisher: American Heart Association / American Academy of Pediatrics
source_2_title: How To Treat the Choking Conscious Infant

stem: An 8-month-old suddenly cannot cry, has a weak cough, and looks blue around the lips after playing with a small toy. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, 2 priority actions, and 2 parameters that support severe obstruction.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Mild foreign-body airway obstruction with effective cough"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Severe foreign-body airway obstruction in an infant"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Simple nasal congestion without airway compromise"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Resolved choking with no residual risk"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Activate emergency response and begin cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 chest thrusts"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Perform abdominal thrusts only as first-line infant relief"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Allow the infant to keep trying without intervention while severe signs persist"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "If the infant becomes unresponsive, start CPR beginning with compressions and remove a visible object when opening the airway"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Give a bottle of milk to push the object down"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Inability to cry or make much sound"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Strong, effective coughing with good air movement"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Cyanosis or color change with severe obstruction signs"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Quiet comfortable play with normal feeding"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Afebrile ear tugging without respiratory distress"}]}
rationales:
K1: Incorrect. Mild FBAO allows effective cough/sounds; this infant cannot cry effectively (AHA/AAP; Merck).
K2: Correct. Severe infant FBAO: cannot cry effectively, weak cough, cyanosis (AHA/AAP; Merck).
K3: Incorrect. Presentation matches severe FBAO, not simple congestion.
K4: Incorrect. Severe signs are present now.
A1: Correct. Activate EMS and cycles of 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts (AHA/AAP; Merck).
A2: Incorrect. Abdominal thrusts not recommended in infants (AHA/AAP).
A3: Incorrect. Severe FBAO requires immediate intervention (AHA/AAP; Merck).
A4: Correct. If unresponsive, start CPR with compressions; remove visible object when opening airway (AHA/AAP).
A5: Incorrect. Fluids do not relieve FBAO and delay care.
P1: Correct. Inability to cry/make sound indicates severe obstruction (AHA/AAP; Merck).
P2: Incorrect. Strong effective cough suggests mild FBAO — observe rather than force relief maneuvers (AHA/AAP; Merck).
P3: Correct. Cyanosis/color change is a severe obstruction sign (AHA/AAP; Merck).
P4: Incorrect. Not consistent with severe FBAO.
P5: Incorrect. Ear tugging without distress does not identify this airway emergency.
topic: NGN bowtie — infant severe FBAO recognition and back-blow/chest-thrust relief
source_1_publisher: American Heart Association / American Academy of Pediatrics
source_2_title: How To Treat the Choking Conscious Infant

stem: A client is hospitalized with invasive meningococcal disease. Which action best protects close contacts?
options:
A) Offer recommended antibiotic chemoprophylaxis to close contacts (for example household contacts and others with unprotected exposure to respiratory secretions) as directed by public health/clinician guidance.
B) Tell household contacts that antibiotics are never used after meningococcal exposure.
C) Advise casual hallway passersby with no close contact that they all require the same immediate chemoprophylaxis as household members.
D) Wait until the index client finishes a full month of therapy before considering any contact measures.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: close contacts should receive prophylactic antibiotics. CDC isolation appendix: postexposure chemoprophylaxis for household contacts and HCWs exposed to respiratory secretions.
B: Incorrect. Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for close contacts (Merck; CDC).
C: Incorrect. Prophylaxis targets close contacts/unprotected respiratory exposure, not all casual contacts (Merck; CDC).
D: Incorrect. Close-contact prophylaxis is timely after exposure; do not delay for a month (Merck; CDC).
topic: Meningococcal disease — antibiotic chemoprophylaxis for close contacts
client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
source_2_title: Appendix A: Type and Duration of Precautions
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: An older adult is being transferred from hospital to a skilled nursing facility. Which nursing action best reduces medication-related harm during the transition?
options:
A) Perform medication reconciliation — identify and communicate an accurate list of current medications (name, dose, frequency, route) and resolve discrepancies at the handoff.
B) Omit the medication list from the transfer so the receiving nurse can rediscover drugs by trial and error.
C) Stop all chronic medications without review because hospitalization always eliminates every prior indication.
D) Rely only on the client's memory for high-alert drug doses and skip verification with the record.
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: inadequate communication at care transitions is a major cause of adverse drug effects; medication reconciliation at admission/discharge/other transitions can prevent many problems. AHRQ MATCH toolkit: medication reconciliation at transitions and clinical handoffs.
B: Incorrect. Omitting the list increases transition errors (Merck; AHRQ).
C: Incorrect. Ongoing need should be reevaluated, not blindly stopped without reconciliation (Merck).
D: Incorrect. Reconciliation uses a verified current list, not memory alone (Merck; AHRQ).
topic: Medication reconciliation at care transitions to prevent adverse drug events
source_2_title: Medications at Transitions and Clinical Handoffs (MATCH) Toolkit
source_2_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)

stem: During a rapid response, the team lead needs to share critical information with everyone at once and assign a named person to act. Which TeamSTEPPS tool fits best?
options:
A) Call-out — communicate important or critical information to all team members simultaneously, help them anticipate next steps, and direct responsibility by name to the person accountable for the task.
B) Remain silent so no one hears vital changes until after the event.
C) Send only an unsigned sticky note without confirming who will act.
D) Whisper to one person while others continue unaware of the critical change.
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS: a call-out communicates important/critical information, informs all members simultaneously, helps anticipate next steps, and directs responsibility by name. Closed-loop communication uses call-outs (with check-backs/teach-back). OpenStax: TeamSTEPPS is an AHRQ teamwork/communication framework nurses use to enhance performance and safety.
B: Incorrect. TeamSTEPPS emphasizes timely critical communication (AHRQ).
C: Incorrect. Call-outs direct accountability to a named individual (AHRQ).
D: Incorrect. Call-outs inform the whole team simultaneously (AHRQ).
topic: TeamSTEPPS call-out — critical info to all; named accountability
source_1_title: Section 1: Overview of Key Concepts and Tools
source_1_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
source_2_title: 6.2 Effective Communication in the Nurse-Patient Relationship

stem: An adolescent reports abdominal pain that began near the umbilicus with anorexia and nausea and later settled in the right lower quadrant. Which condition does this classic pattern most strongly suggest?
options:
A) Acute appendicitis
B) Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis alone
C) Simple tension headache without abdominal findings
D) Stable healed fracture of a finger
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: classic acute appendicitis — epigastric/periumbilical pain followed by nausea/vomiting/anorexia, then pain shifts to the right lower quadrant. OpenStax: appendicitis presents with right lower quadrant or periumbilical pain; anorexia, nausea, vomiting.
B: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not explain this abdominal pain pattern.
C: Incorrect. Headache alone does not match the described abdominal progression.
D: Incorrect. Irrelevant musculoskeletal finding.
topic: Appendicitis — periumbilical pain shifting to right lower quadrant with anorexia/nausea

stem: A child is admitted with active head lice infestation requiring inpatient care. Which transmission-based precaution plan is appropriate?
options:
A) Contact Precautions plus Standard Precautions until 24 hours after initiation of effective therapy.
B) Airborne infection isolation with N95 for all staff indefinitely, regardless of treatment.
C) No precautions beyond open cohorting with immunocompromised roommates.
D) Droplet Precautions only, without considering contact measures for lice.
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC Appendix A: Pediculosis (lice) — Contact + Standard until 24 hours after initiation of effective therapy. Merck: head lice transmitted by close contact; treat with topical pediculicides.
B: Incorrect. Lice are not managed with indefinite airborne isolation (CDC lists Contact + Standard for pediculosis).
C: Incorrect. Contact Precautions are indicated until 24 hours after effective therapy begins (CDC).
D: Incorrect. CDC specifies Contact + Standard for pediculosis, not Droplet-only.
topic: Pediculosis — Contact Precautions until 24 hours after effective therapy

stem: A child is in the PACU after tonsillectomy. Which nursing actions help detect postoperative hemorrhage early? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Monitor vital signs and oxygen saturation for hypotension, tachycardia, or other instability.
B) Assess the surgical site and dressings/drainage for bleeding, including hidden pooling.
C) Notify the surgical team promptly if hemorrhage is suspected and prepare for ordered interventions.
D) Assume bright red continuous bleeding is expected and never reassess the wound.
E) Skip circulation checks because bleeding never occurs after tonsillectomy.
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: PACU nurse monitors for hypotension, shock, and hemorrhage using vital signs/oxygenation. Merck postop: monitor hemodynamic status.
B: Correct. OpenStax: frequent wound checks for drainage/pooling reveal bleeding. Merck: check wound for increasing drainage/infection signs.
C: Correct. OpenStax: if hemorrhaging, notify charge/surgeon/anesthesia and prepare fluids/blood products/possible return to OR.
D: Incorrect. Continuous bright bleeding requires reassessment and escalation (OpenStax hemorrhage intervention).
E: Incorrect. Hemorrhage is a key PACU risk to monitor after surgery, including tonsillectomy scenarios (OpenStax).
topic: Post-tonsillectomy PACU — monitor vitals/wound for hemorrhage and escalate

source_2_section: Fluids and hemodynamic status; Wound care

stem: A community nurse teaches a neighbourhood group how to reduce West Nile virus risk. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Use an Environmental Protection Agency–registered insect repellent when outdoors during mosquito season.
B) Wear long, loose-fitting shirts and pants to reduce skin exposure to mosquito bites.
C) Avoid outdoor exposure between dusk and dawn when West Nile–carrying mosquitoes are most active, when possible.
D) Rely on a licensed human West Nile vaccine as the primary prevention strategy for everyone.
E) Use window and door screens or air conditioning to keep mosquitoes outside the home.
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: use EPA-registered insect repellent. Merck: personal protective measures including DEET-type repellents.
B: Correct. CDC: wear long, loose-fitting shirts and pants. Merck: protective attire to decrease mosquito exposure.
C: Correct. CDC: avoid being outside between dusk and dawn when mosquitoes that spread West Nile are most active.
D: Incorrect. CDC and Merck: no licensed West Nile vaccines are available for use in humans.
E: Correct. CDC: use screens on windows and doors or air conditioning to keep mosquitoes outside.
topic: West Nile — mosquito bite prevention; no human vaccine
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_2_section: Prevention of West Nile Virus; Key Points

stem: A home-care nurse reviews hot-weather safety with an older adult who lives alone. For each teaching point, select Accurate or Not accurate.
options: {"columns": ["Accurate", "Not accurate"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Stay in air-conditioned spaces as much as possible; use cooling centres or other cool public places if home has no air conditioning"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Rely on a household fan alone as the main cooling method when outdoor temperatures are extremely high"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Drink more water than usual and do not wait until thirst appears (unless a clinician has limited fluids)"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Wear loose, lightweight, light-coloured clothing outdoors in the heat"}]}

R1: Accurate. CDC (older adults): stay in air-conditioned buildings; locate cooling shelters if needed. Merck: older adults should not remain in unventilated residences without air-conditioning in excessive heat.
R2: Not accurate. CDC: do not rely on a fan as the main cooling source when it is really hot. Merck emphasizes environmental modification and air-conditioning for older adults.
R3: Accurate. CDC: drink more water than usual and do not wait until thirsty; ask clinician if fluids are limited. Merck: maintain adequate hydration.
R4: Accurate. CDC: wear loose, lightweight, light-colored clothing. Merck: wear light, loose-fitting clothing.
