stem: An outdoor worker is brought to triage after collapsing on a hot day. Which finding cluster best supports heatstroke rather than heat exhaustion?
options:
A) Core temperature greater than 40 °C with altered mental status (confusion, delirium, or coma)
B) Mild fatigue with intact mental status and temperature clearly below 40 °C
C) Isolated muscle cramps after exercise with a normal neurologic examination
D) Afebrile seasonal rhinitis without heat exposure history
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: heatstroke is differentiated by CNS dysfunction and temperature > 40 °C; hallmark is CNS dysfunction with core temperature > 40 °C.
B: Incorrect. Merck: heat exhaustion lacks the heatstroke defining pair of CNS dysfunction with temperature > 40 °C (heat exhaustion has intact CNS and usually lower temperature).
C: Incorrect. Isolated cramps without CNS dysfunction/high core temperature are not heatstroke (Merck; CDC describes heat stroke as more severe progression).
D: Incorrect. No heat-illness picture (Merck).
topic: Heatstroke vs heat exhaustion — CNS dysfunction and core temperature > 40 °C
source_1_section: Symptoms and Signs; Diagnosis; Key Points
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A runner collapses after a long race on a humid day. Rectal temperature is 41.2 °C and the client is confused and combative. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, 2 priority actions, and 2 parameters that support heatstroke.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Heat exhaustion with intact mentation"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Heatstroke with hyperthermia and CNS dysfunction"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Isolated heat cramps without systemic illness"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Mild dehydration without heat illness"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Begin rapid aggressive cooling (cold-water immersion when available, or evaporative cooling) and arrange urgent transport/hospital care"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Delay cooling until laboratory confirmation of a rare pathogen"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Provide only oral fluids and observe outdoors in full sun without cooling"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Support airway/circulation as needed and give intravenous fluid/electrolyte replacement while cooling"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Apply heavy insulating blankets to raise core temperature further"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Core temperature greater than 40 °C"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Altered mental status (confusion or combativeness)"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Normal mentation with temperature clearly under 39 °C"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Isolated sneezing without heat exposure"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Comfortable rest in a cool room with no symptoms"}]}
rationales:
K1: Incorrect. Heat exhaustion has intact CNS and usually lower temperature (Merck).
K2: Correct. Heatstroke: hyperthermia with systemic inflammatory response and CNS dysfunction; temp >40 °C (Merck).
K3: Incorrect. Cramps alone are not heatstroke (Merck overview).
K4: Incorrect. Mild dehydration without CNS/temp criteria is not heatstroke.
A1: Correct. Merck: rapid aggressive cooling is essential; cold-water immersion preferred when available; evaporative cooling also effective; transport/hospital care.
A2: Incorrect. Cooling must not wait for unrelated lab pathogen workups (Merck emphasizes rapid cooling).
A3: Incorrect. Leaving the client in sun without cooling worsens heatstroke (Merck/CDC cool and hydrate principles).
A4: Correct. Merck treatment includes IV fluid/electrolyte replacement and supportive care with cooling.
A5: Incorrect. Goal is rapid cooling, not further heating (Merck).
P1: Correct. Defining feature includes temperature >40 °C (Merck).
P2: Correct. CNS dysfunction is the hallmark (Merck).
P3: Incorrect. Intact mentation and lower temp fit exhaustion, not stroke (Merck).
P4: Incorrect. Unrelated to heatstroke cues.
P5: Incorrect. Not a heatstroke parameter.
topic: NGN bowtie — heatstroke: rapid cooling + IV support; temp >40 °C and CNS change

stem: During a busy shift, a client's condition changes and the current care plan is no longer working. Which TeamSTEPPS leadership action best fits this moment?
options:
A) Convene a huddle to communicate adjustments to the plan, update situational awareness, and realign the team
B) Wait until the next scheduled annual performance appraisal to discuss the change
C) Avoid telling teammates so each person can invent a separate plan
D) Delete the prior brief from the record and never revisit goals
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS: a huddle monitors/modifies an existing plan when patient condition, team membership, or plan effectiveness changes; any team member can convene. PSNet: huddles share information and raise safety concerns.
B: Incorrect. Huddles are timely ad-hoc/shift tools, not annual appraisals (AHRQ).
C: Incorrect. TeamSTEPPS requires shared updated plans so the team knows the current care approach (AHRQ).
D: Incorrect. Briefs/huddles/debriefs support ongoing plan communication; deleting plans without team update is unsafe (AHRQ).
topic: TeamSTEPPS huddle — adjust plan and restore situational awareness when conditions change

stem: A client with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) reports intrusive memories and hypervigilance. Which nursing priority best aligns with evidence-based initial support?
options:
A) Help establish personal safety and a supportive environment, then facilitate access to trauma-focused psychotherapy and coordinated care
B) Argue that the traumatic event never happened until the client agrees
C) Encourage heavy daily alcohol use to suppress all memories
D) Isolate the client from all family and community contact permanently
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: treatment includes trauma-focused CBT; self-care begins with personal safety and healthy routines. OpenStax: nurses provide a safe supportive environment, education, self-care strategies, and referrals to psychotherapy/medication.
B: Incorrect. Do not invalidate trauma; OpenStax/Merck emphasize supportive processing and evidence-based therapy, not denial.
C: Incorrect. Merck: intoxicating substances such as alcohol should be used sparingly if at all after trauma.
D: Incorrect. Merck: maintain schedule and social engagement when possible; OpenStax supports coordinated supportive care, not permanent isolation.
topic: PTSD — safety/supportive environment and access to trauma-focused psychotherapy
source_2_section: Nursing Interventions for PTSD; Treatment of PTSD

stem: A high-risk older adult presents on day 1 of influenza-like illness. The provider plans antiviral therapy. Which teaching point is most accurate?
options:
A) Antivirals work best when started early—ideally within about 1 to 2 days after symptom onset
B) Antibiotics are first-line therapy for uncomplicated influenza virus infection
C) Antivirals only help if started after two full weeks of untreated fever
D) No influenza antiviral medicines exist for any patient group
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: antivirals work best when started early, ideally within two days of symptom onset. Merck: antivirals given within 1 to 2 days of onset decrease fever duration and severity.
B: Incorrect. CDC: antibiotics do not treat viruses such as influenza. Merck: antibiotics only for complicating bacterial infection.
C: Incorrect. Benefit is greatest with early start within 1–2 days (CDC; Merck).
D: Incorrect. Neuraminidase inhibitors and other antivirals are available (Merck; CDC).
topic: Influenza antivirals — start within 1–2 days of symptom onset
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A clinic nurse counsels an older adult about reducing risk of serious pneumococcal disease and community-acquired pneumonia. Which statement is most accurate?
options:
A) Pneumococcal vaccination helps protect against serious pneumococcal infection; influenza vaccination also helps prevent some pneumonias
B) No vaccines exist that reduce risk of any form of community-acquired pneumonia
C) Only infants ever benefit from pneumococcal vaccination; adults never do
D) Pneumococcal disease is never serious in older adults
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck CAP Prevention lists pneumococcal and influenza vaccines among vaccines that prevent some forms of CAP. CDC: pneumococcal vaccines protect against serious pneumococcal infections; older adults are at greatest risk of serious illness and death.
B: Incorrect. Merck lists several vaccines that prevent some forms of CAP.
C: Incorrect. CDC recommends pneumococcal vaccination for adults based on age/risk as well as children.
D: Incorrect. CDC: older adults are at greatest risk of serious illness and death from pneumococcal disease.
topic: Pneumococcal and influenza vaccines to reduce pneumonia/pneumococcal disease risk

stem: A client presents after a possible bat exposure with a small puncture wound. Which immediate actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water right away
B) Seek urgent public health/medical assessment for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (vaccine ± rabies immune globulin as indicated)
C) Ignore wildlife exposures because human rabies never requires prophylaxis
D) Report the animal type and circumstances to the healthcare/public health team assessing exposure risk
E) Delay all wound cleaning for several days to 'seal in' any virus
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: wash wounds immediately with soap and water (flush). Merck: cleanse immediately and thoroughly with soap and water.
B: Correct. CDC: PEP includes wound washing, rabies immune globulin, and vaccine as indicated; seek care urgently. Merck: prompt PEP almost always prevents human rabies; bat contact is an absolute indication for PEP.
C: Incorrect. CDC/Merck: exposures can require urgent PEP assessment; bat contact is high concern.
D: Correct. CDC: tell clinicians the animal type and abnormal behaviour; assessment depends on animal/circumstances (Merck table).
E: Incorrect. Immediate cleaning is required; delaying cleaning is opposite of CDC/Merck guidance.
topic: Rabies exposure — immediate soap-and-water wound wash and urgent PEP assessment

stem: An older adult with limited mobility asks how to stay safer during a heat wave at home. Which instruction is most appropriate?
options:
A) Use air conditioning or visit a cooling centre; avoid relying on a fan alone when it is extremely hot, and drink fluids as advised
B) Cook large meals with the oven all afternoon to 'dry out' the apartment air
C) Stop all prescribed medicines without contacting the clinician because heat always cancels prescriptions
D) Wear heavy dark layered clothing outdoors at midday to trap heat intentionally
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC older-adult guidance: prioritize air-conditioned spaces/cooling shelters; do not rely on a fan alone when really hot; drink more water unless clinician limits fluids. Merck: older adults should not remain without air-conditioning in excessive heat; maintain hydration.
B: Incorrect. CDC: avoid using the stove/oven because it heats the home.
C: Incorrect. CDC: do not stop or change medicines until talking with a clinician.
D: Incorrect. CDC/Merck: wear loose, lightweight, light-coloured clothing.
topic: Older adult heat wave — AC/cooling centre, not fan-alone, hydrate as advised
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A public health nurse prepares heat-wave messaging for the community. Which prevention messages are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Schedule outdoor activity for cooler parts of the day when possible and take shade breaks
B) Drink fluids regularly; limit excess alcohol and very sugary drinks during extreme heat
C) Check on older neighbours and people who live alone during heat waves
D) Leave infants and older adults in closed parked cars during midday heat to 'acclimatize'
E) Wear light, loose-fitting clothing outdoors in hot weather
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: do outdoor activities during coolest parts of day; stay in shade; take breaks. Merck: rest breaks in shade; modify environment.
B: Correct. CDC: stay hydrated; limit sugary, caffeinated, and alcoholic drinks. Merck: maintain adequate hydration.
C: Correct. CDC: check on family, friends, and neighbours, especially those who live alone or have chronic illness; older adults are high risk.
D: Incorrect. Merck: older adults and children must not be left in automobiles in the hot sun. CDC identifies infants and older adults as high risk.
E: Correct. CDC and Merck: wear light, loose-fitting clothing.
topic: Community heat-wave prevention — cool hours, hydrate, check-ins, loose clothing; never leave people in hot cars
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: During a busy shift, a nurse notices a colleague is overloaded with tasks while a stable client’s care is delayed. Using TeamSTEPPS mutual support (task assistance), which action best fits the model?
options:
A) Offer help in the context of patient safety (for example, “I have 10 minutes—how can I help?”) and assist as appropriate
B) Ignore the overload so the colleague ‘learns resilience’ without assistance
C) Publicly criticize the colleague for poor time management in front of the client
D) Leave the unit without notifying anyone so the colleague has fewer people to manage
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS mutual support (task assistance): foster a climate where assistance is sought and offered; place offers/requests in the context of patient safety; asking “I have 10 minutes. How can I help?” strengthens team resilience. OpenStax: mutual support means knowing team member needs and taking steps to meet them.
B: Incorrect. Mutual support expects assistance to be actively sought and offered to protect from work overload (AHRQ).
C: Incorrect. Formative/supportive teamwork focuses on behaviours and safety, not public personal criticism (AHRQ feedback principles).
D: Incorrect. Abandoning the unit worsens safety and is not mutual support.
topic: TeamSTEPPS mutual support — task assistance offered for patient safety

stem: A charge nurse reviews TeamSTEPPS with new staff. Complete the teaching statement.
options: {"template": "TeamSTEPPS core skills include team leadership, communication, {B1}, and {B2} (also called backup behaviour), which involves assisting teammates and advocating when safety is threatened.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "situation monitoring"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "punitive silence"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "unilateral decision-making without shared awareness"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "mutual support"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "ignoring workload imbalance"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "withholding safety concerns"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. OpenStax and AHRQ: situation monitoring is a TeamSTEPPS core competency/skill.
B1b: Incorrect. Punitive silence is not a TeamSTEPPS skill.
B1c: Incorrect. TeamSTEPPS emphasizes shared situation awareness, not unilateral unshared decisions.
B2a: Correct. AHRQ: mutual support (backup behaviour) includes assisting teammates and assertive advocacy for safety. OpenStax lists mutual support as a core competency.
B2b: Incorrect. Mutual support addresses workload and assistance rather than ignoring overload.
B2c: Incorrect. Advocacy/assertion is part of mutual support, not withholding concerns.
topic: NGN cloze — TeamSTEPPS situation monitoring and mutual support

stem: A community health nurse teaches adults how to prevent hepatitis A. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Hepatitis A vaccination is the best way to prevent infection
B) Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water after using the bathroom, after caring for someone who is ill, after changing diapers, and before preparing or eating food
C) Practise good personal hygiene and food/water safety to reduce fecal–oral transmission
D) Rely on isolation of infected persons as the primary community prevention strategy because hygiene and vaccine add little
E) International travelers and other higher-risk groups should discuss hepatitis A vaccination with a clinician
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: vaccination is the best way to prevent hepatitis A.
B: Correct. CDC: good hand hygiene with soap and water at key times helps prevent spread.
C: Correct. Merck: good personal hygiene and food/water safety help prevent fecal–oral transmission.
D: Incorrect. Merck: isolation does little to prevent HAV spread; hygiene/vaccine are the prevention focus.
E: Correct. CDC and Merck list international travelers and other higher-risk groups among those recommended for vaccination.
topic: Hepatitis A — vaccine best prevention plus hygiene and food/water safety
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: An 82-year-old client living in a retirement residence develops new confusion over 12 hours without reported dysuria. Which nursing interpretation is most accurate?
options:
A) Acute confusion in an older adult can be an atypical presentation of urinary tract infection and warrants prompt clinical evaluation (including urine testing as indicated)
B) New delirium in older adults is almost never related to infection, so infection workup can be deferred indefinitely
C) UTI in older adults always presents with classic dysuria and frequency, so absent dysuria rules out UTI
D) Confusion should be attributed only to dementia progression without assessing acute medical causes
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: older adults may present with sepsis and delirium without urinary-tract symptoms. OpenStax: older adults’ UTIs often present atypically with confusion/delirium; OpenStax delirium text notes UTI as a common cause and that older adults may lack pain.
B: Incorrect. Infection (including UTI) is a common precipitant of delirium (Merck Delirium etiology; OpenStax).
C: Incorrect. OpenStax and Merck emphasize atypical presentations without classic dysuria.
D: Incorrect. Acute confusion requires evaluation for reversible causes such as infection (OpenStax/Merck).
topic: Older adult UTI — atypical presentation with acute confusion/delirium
source_1_section: Symptoms and Signs of Bacterial UTIs

stem: A home-care nurse assesses an older adult with sudden personality change and new incontinence. For each statement, select Accurate or Not accurate.
options: {"columns": ["Accurate", "Not accurate"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "UTI in older adults may present with confusion or delirium rather than classic burning/frequency"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "New acute confusion in an older adult should prompt evaluation for infection such as UTI"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Absence of dysuria completely excludes UTI in older adults"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Delirium from a treatable infection can improve when the underlying infection is treated"}]}
rationales:
R1: Accurate. OpenStax: older-adult UTIs often present atypically with confusion/delirium. Merck: may lack urinary symptoms.
R2: Accurate. OpenStax delirium: obtain urine sample when acute confusion noted; UTI is a common cause in older adults.
R3: Not accurate. Merck/OpenStax: classic urinary symptoms may be absent.
R4: Accurate. OpenStax: delirium resolves with successful treatment of the underlying condition (e.g., antibiotics for UTI).
topic: NGN matrix — older adult UTI atypical cues and evaluation

stem: A client arrives after prolonged outdoor cold exposure with a numb, pale finger. Which initial rewarming approach is most appropriate if medical care is arranged and refreezing will not occur?
options:
A) Immerse the frostbitten area in warm (about 37–39 °C / warm-to-touch, not hot) water; do not rub or massage the area
B) Rub snow vigorously onto the finger to ‘restore circulation’
C) Place the numb finger directly on a stove burner or heating pad for rapid dry heat
D) Ignore the finding because numbness means tissue injury cannot occur
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: rewarm by immersion in 37–39 °C water; avoid rubbing. CDC: place frostbitten areas in warm-to-touch (not hot) water; do not rub/massage; avoid heating pads/stoves.
B: Incorrect. CDC/Merck: do not rub or massage frostbitten tissue (worsens injury).
C: Incorrect. CDC/Merck: avoid uncontrolled dry heat (stove, heating pad) because numbness risks burns.
D: Incorrect. Numbness is a classic frostbite finding and needs care (CDC/Merck).
topic: Frostbite — warm-water rewarming; do not rub or use dry heat
units_note: Temperature stated in °C with warm-to-touch guidance (CDC).
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A hiker has a cold, numb, white fingertip after hours in sub-freezing wind. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two monitoring parameters.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Frostbite of a distal extremity"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Heatstroke with core temperature > 40 °C"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Isolated anxiety attack without cold exposure"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Move to a warm shelter and arrange prompt medical evaluation"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Rewarm the affected part in warm (≈37–39 °C / warm-to-touch) water without rubbing"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Massage the area firmly with snow to restore colour"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Apply a heating pad directly to the numb skin for rapid dry heat"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Encourage prolonged walking on frostbitten feet to ‘work out’ stiffness"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Colour, sensation, and pain response of the rewarming digit"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Signs of concurrent hypothermia (confusion, shivering, drowsiness)"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Daily pollen count as the primary outcome"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Core temperature trending above 40 °C as the expected goal"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Ability to complete a marathon within 1 hour"}]}
rationales:
K1: Correct. Cold, numb, white distal tissue after freezing exposure fits frostbite (Merck/CDC).
K2: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not explain freezing tissue injury.
K3: Incorrect. Heatstroke is heat illness, not freezing injury.
K4: Incorrect. History is cold exposure with tissue findings.
A1: Correct. CDC: seek medical attention; get into a warm room/shelter.
A2: Correct. Merck/CDC: warm-water rewarming; do not rub.
A3: Incorrect. Do not rub/massage or use snow (CDC/Merck).
A4: Incorrect. Avoid heating pads/dry heat on numb tissue (CDC/Merck).
A5: Incorrect. CDC: avoid walking on frostbitten feet/toes unless necessary.
P1: Correct. Clinical course after rewarming includes colour/pain/edema changes (Merck).
P2: Correct. CDC: check for hypothermia, which is a more serious emergency.
P3: Incorrect. Irrelevant to frostbite.
P4: Incorrect. >40 °C is heatstroke territory, not frostbite goal.
P5: Incorrect. Not a frostbite monitoring parameter.
topic: NGN bowtie — frostbite recognition, warm-water rewarming, hypothermia check
units_note: Rewarming water ≈37–39 °C (Merck; CDC Yellow Book).
source_1_section: Symptoms and Signs; Treatment — Prehospital care
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A client with known primary adrenal insufficiency develops vomiting, abdominal pain, and hypotension after a gastrointestinal illness. Which action is the immediate priority?
options:
A) Recognize possible adrenal crisis and ensure emergency glucocorticoid therapy (e.g., IV hydrocortisone) with fluid resuscitation is instituted without delay
B) Withhold all steroids indefinitely because illness means hormones are unnecessary
C) Focus only on outpatient scheduling of elective imaging before any hormone replacement
D) Give a large dose of insulin as first-line therapy for adrenal crisis
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: institute therapy immediately on suspicion of adrenal crisis; delay in glucocorticoid therapy may be fatal; hydrocortisone IV and volume expansion. OpenStax: adrenal crisis treated with IV fluids, dextrose, and hydrocortisone; emergency—notify provider immediately.
B: Incorrect. Illness/stress increases glucocorticoid need; abrupt inadequate dosing precipitates crisis (OpenStax/Merck).
C: Incorrect. Emergency hormone/fluid therapy precedes elective diagnostics (Merck: do not delay treatment).
D: Incorrect. Insulin is not first-line adrenal crisis therapy; hydrocortisone and fluids are.
topic: Adrenal crisis — immediate IV hydrocortisone and fluid resuscitation

stem: A client with central diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency) has massive polyuria. Which medication teaching is most accurate?
options:
A) Desmopressin (a vasopressin analogue) is used to replace antidiuretic activity and reduce polyuria
B) Desmopressin is used primarily to raise blood glucose in diabetic ketoacidosis
C) No hormone replacement exists; only lifelong fluid restriction without medication is used for complete central DI
D) Desmopressin is an antibiotic taken to sterilize the urinary tract in DI
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: desmopressin is the synthetic vasopressin analogue used for hormonal treatment of arginine vasopressin deficiency. OpenStax: desmopressin replaces vasopressin and acts as an antidiuretic to treat polyuria.
B: Incorrect. Desmopressin is not a DKA glucose therapy.
C: Incorrect. Hormone replacement with desmopressin is standard (Merck/OpenStax).
D: Incorrect. Desmopressin is not an antibiotic.
topic: Central diabetes insipidus — desmopressin replaces antidiuretic hormone activity
source_2_section: Diabetes Insipidus — Medical Therapies and Related Care

stem: A clinic implements a trauma-informed approach. Which organizational priority best reflects a core trauma-informed principle?
options:
A) Ensure participants and staff feel physically and psychologically safe, and structure care to avoid re-traumatization
B) Maximize unpredictable loud announcements and crowded, poorly lit waiting areas to ‘desensitize’ clients
C) Ignore power dynamics and withhold collaboration because clients should not share decisions
D) Use seclusion as the first response to mild anxiety without attempting less restrictive supports
rationales:
A: Correct. SAMHSA: Safety—participants and staff feel physically and psychologically safe. OpenStax: creating a safe environment is a top priority; avoid re-traumatization.
B: Incorrect. OpenStax emphasizes good lighting, reduced noise/distractions, and welcoming environments for safety.
C: Incorrect. SAMHSA principles include collaboration/mutuality and empowerment, not withholding collaboration.
D: Incorrect. SAMHSA materials emphasize eliminating harmful seclusion/restraint practices; safety supports come first.
topic: Trauma-informed care — physical and psychological safety as a core principle
source_1_publisher: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA)

stem: A nurse teaches an older adult who walks outdoors in winter how to reduce frostbite risk. Which instruction is best?
options:
A) Cover commonly affected areas (nose, ears, cheeks, chin, fingers, toes) with warm, dry clothing such as a hat, scarf/mask, mittens, and layered loose clothing; limit prolonged outdoor exposure in extreme cold
B) Wear a single thin damp cotton layer and leave ears and fingers uncovered to ‘toughen’ the skin
C) Rub snow on exposed skin every few minutes as primary prevention
D) Stay outdoors longer when numb because numbness means protection is complete
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC winter guidance: cover nose/ears/toes/cheeks/chin/fingers; hat, mittens, layered loose clothing; limit extreme cold exposure. Merck: distal extremities and exposed skin are most often affected.
B: Incorrect. CDC emphasizes covering high-risk areas and proper layered dry clothing.
C: Incorrect. Rubbing snow is harmful for frostbite care and is not prevention (CDC).
D: Incorrect. Numbness is a frostbite warning sign, not reassurance (CDC/Merck).
topic: Frostbite prevention — cover ears/nose/fingers/toes; layered warm clothing
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A public health nurse prepares winter safety messaging. Which points are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) When possible, limit outdoor time during extreme cold and dress in several layers of loose-fitting clothing
B) Cover ears, nose, cheeks, chin, fingers, and toes with warm dry clothing
C) Check on older adults who may have inadequate heating, food, or clothing
D) Treat numbness of fingers after freezing exposure by vigorous massage with snow
E) Seek medical care for suspected frostbite and watch for hypothermia warning signs such as confusion or drowsiness
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: stay indoors if possible in extreme cold; wear several layers of loose-fitting clothing.
B: Correct. CDC: cover body parts most often affected by frostbite.
C: Correct. CDC: older adults with inadequate food, clothing, or heating are at higher hypothermia risk.
D: Incorrect. CDC: do not rub or massage frostbitten areas; do not use snow.
E: Correct. CDC: seek medical care for frostbite; hypothermia signs include confusion and drowsiness.
topic: Community winter safety — layered clothing, cover extremities, check older adults
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_2_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: An Ontario client in independent nursing practice asks to discontinue nursing services. According to CNO accountabilities, which action is required?
options:
A) Arrange timely alternative or replacement services, or give the client a reasonable opportunity to arrange alternative services
B) Stop all contact immediately without arranging or allowing time for alternative care
C) Refuse the client’s request and continue visits indefinitely regardless of the client’s wishes
D) Transfer the client’s health records to social media so the public can find another nurse
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO Code of Conduct 3.13 and the Discontinuing or Declining to Provide Care standard: when services are discontinued at the client’s request, nurses arrange timely alternative or replacement services or provide a reasonable opportunity to arrange alternatives. Professional misconduct rules likewise require alternatives or a reasonable opportunity unless the client requests discontinuation (which still requires ensuring ongoing access).
B: Incorrect. Abrupt cessation without arranging alternatives or a reasonable opportunity abandons needed care and conflicts with CNO continuity accountabilities.
C: Incorrect. Capable clients may request discontinuation; nurses must respect the request while ensuring ongoing access pathways (CNO).
D: Incorrect. Sharing PHI on social media violates privacy and is not an alternative-care arrangement.
topic: CNO discontinuing care — arrange alternative/replacement or reasonable opportunity
jurisdiction_note: CNO Discontinuing or Declining to Provide Care practice standard and Code of Conduct 3.13; Ontario professional misconduct regulation referenced in the standard.
source_1_title: Discontinuing or Declining to Provide Care
source_3_section: Ethical Principles in Nursing — Fidelity; Nonmaleficence

stem: A home-care client asks the nurse to borrow $50 until the next pension cheque. Which response best upholds professional boundaries?
options:
A) Decline financial transactions unrelated to care (do not lend or borrow money) and, if needed, refer the client to appropriate resources
B) Lend the money from personal funds because the amount is small and the client seems trustworthy
C) Ask the client to add the nurse as a joint bank-account holder to ‘help manage bills’
D) Accept a larger cash ‘gift’ from the client in exchange for the loan
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO Professional Boundaries: nurses must not engage in financial transactions unrelated to care with a client or family (e.g., borrowing money). OpenStax: social boundaries require avoiding nontherapeutic socialization/personal entanglement; keep the focus on the client’s care needs and refer appropriately.
B: Incorrect. Lending money is a prohibited financial transaction outside care (CNO).
C: Incorrect. Joint finances create a major boundary violation and conflict of interest (CNO).
D: Incorrect. Exchanging gifts/money for personal benefit blurs boundaries and risks misconduct (CNO).
topic: CNO professional boundaries — no borrowing/lending money with clients
jurisdiction_note: CNO Professional Boundaries and Nurse-Client Relationships practice standard (updated Dec 2025 / in effect Mar 1, 2026).
source_2_section: Social Boundaries; Treatment Issues and Obstacles

stem: A nurse slept only 3 hours before a busy shift and feels less sharp than usual. Using the TeamSTEPPS I’M SAFE checklist, which action best supports situation monitoring?
options:
A) Alert the team about fatigue (for example, ask colleagues to watch more closely today) so the team can support safe performance
B) Hide the fatigue and refuse any help so no one questions competence
C) Drink alcohol before the shift to ‘relax into the workload’
D) Skip handoffs entirely to conserve energy
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ I’M SAFE: Fatigue — team members should alert the team (e.g., “Watch me a little closer today. I only had 3 hours of sleep last night.”). Situation monitoring supports shared awareness so the team can compensate. OpenStax lists situation monitoring among TeamSTEPPS core competencies.
B: Incorrect. I’M SAFE expects honest awareness and disclosure of factors that impair safety, not concealment.
C: Incorrect. Alcohol/drugs is an I’M SAFE risk factor that impairs focus; using alcohol worsens safety.
D: Incorrect. Skipping handoffs removes critical communication and increases risk.
topic: TeamSTEPPS I’M SAFE — disclose fatigue so team can support safety
source_1_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
source_1_section: How To Effectively Use the I'M SAFE Checklist — Fatigue
source_2_title: 6.2 Effective Communication in the Nurse-Patient Relationship

stem: A charge nurse teaches situation monitoring using the TeamSTEPPS STEP tool. Complete the teaching statement.
options: {"template": "STEP prompts teams to monitor the {B1} (including vitals and care plan), the status of {B2} (including fatigue and workload), the {B3} (staffing, equipment, acuity), and {B4} toward established goals so the plan can be revised when needed.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "status of the patient"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "stock prices of vendors"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "personal social media metrics"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "team members"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "unrelated celebrities"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "only off-duty staff at home"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "environment"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "colour of the break-room walls only"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "parking fines of visitors"}], "B4": [{"key": "B4a", "text": "progress"}, {"key": "B4b", "text": "punitive silence"}, {"key": "B4c", "text": "withholding of safety concerns"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. AHRQ STEP monitors patient status (history, vitals, medications, exam, care plan, psychosocial factors).
B1b: Incorrect. Vendor stock prices are not a STEP patient-status element.
B1c: Incorrect. Social media metrics are unrelated to clinical situation monitoring.
B2a: Correct. AHRQ STEP includes awareness of team members (fatigue, workload, task performance, skill, stress).
B2b: Incorrect. Celebrity status is not a TeamSTEPPS team-member element.
B2c: Incorrect. STEP focuses on the working team’s current functioning, not only off-duty staff.
B3a: Correct. AHRQ STEP assesses environment (occupancy, staffing, triage acuity, outbreaks, equipment).
B3b: Incorrect. Decorative wall colour alone is not the environmental monitoring intent.
B3c: Incorrect. Parking fines are unrelated to care-environment monitoring.
B4a: Correct. AHRQ STEP monitors progress toward goals so the plan can be revised or resources added.
B4b: Incorrect. Punitive silence is not a STEP element.
B4c: Incorrect. Withholding concerns opposes TeamSTEPPS safety culture.
topic: NGN cloze — TeamSTEPPS STEP: patient, team, environment, progress
source_1_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
source_2_title: 6.2 Effective Communication in the Nurse-Patient Relationship

stem: A community health nurse teaches adults how to prevent hepatitis B virus infection. Which statement is the priority prevention teaching point?
options:
A) Getting vaccinated is the best way to prevent hepatitis B
B) Isolation of infected persons is the primary community prevention strategy because vaccine adds little
C) Hepatitis B is mainly spread by casual hugging and sharing utensils, so avoid all social contact
D) There is no vaccine; only herbal teas prevent infection
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC: the best way to prevent hepatitis B is vaccination. Merck: routine HepB vaccination is recommended to prevent infection; vaccination in endemic areas has dramatically reduced prevalence.
B: Incorrect. Merck notes isolation of patients is of no value for HBV prevention; vaccination and risk-behaviour counselling are the focus.
C: Incorrect. CDC: HBV is not spread by hugging, sneezing, coughing, or sharing utensils; it spreads via blood and certain body fluids.
D: Incorrect. Safe, effective HepB vaccines exist and are recommended (CDC/Merck).
topic: Hepatitis B — vaccination as best prevention
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_1_section: Key points; How it spreads; Prevention tips
source_2_section: Prevention of Acute Hepatitis B; Vaccination

stem: A pregnant client at 28 weeks’ gestation asks about whooping cough (pertussis) protection for the newborn. Which teaching is appropriate?
options:
A) Receive one Tdap dose during every pregnancy, preferably early in weeks 27 through 36
B) Skip Tdap in pregnancy if a dose was given 2 years ago for a tetanus booster
C) Tdap is never given in pregnancy; wait until the child is 5 years old
D) Only the newborn needs vaccination at birth for pertussis; maternal Tdap is unnecessary
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC and Merck: give a single Tdap during every pregnancy, preferably in the early part of gestational weeks 27–36, regardless of the interval since prior Tdap.
B: Incorrect. Additional Tdap is recommended each pregnancy regardless of interval since the previous dose (CDC/Merck).
C: Incorrect. Tdap in pregnancy is specifically recommended to protect infants (CDC/Merck).
D: Incorrect. Maternal vaccination in pregnancy is recommended to transfer antibodies; infants begin DTaP later in infancy, not a birth pertussis dose as the sole strategy.
topic: Tdap during every pregnancy at 27–36 weeks for infant pertussis protection
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A client begins to disclose a painful personal experience. The nurse feels uncomfortable and quickly asks about the weather instead. Which evaluation of this response is accurate?
options:
A) Changing the subject is a nontherapeutic barrier that can seem insensitive and shut down disclosure
B) Changing the subject is the preferred therapeutic technique for painful topics
C) Changing the subject always increases trust more than active listening
D) Nurses should change the subject whenever clients show emotion
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax PMH: changing the subject dismisses important disclosure and can seem uncaring; use active listening instead. OpenStax Fundamentals: changing the subject is listed among nontherapeutic techniques.
B: Incorrect. Changing the subject is classified as nontherapeutic, not preferred therapy.
C: Incorrect. Active listening supports trust; changing the subject undermines it.
D: Incorrect. Emotional disclosure is a cue to stay present therapeutically, not to divert.
topic: Therapeutic communication — changing the subject is nontherapeutic

stem: For each nursing response, indicate whether it is a barrier to therapeutic communication (Avoid) or a therapeutic approach (Use).
options: {"columns": ["Avoid (barrier)", "Use (therapeutic)"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Providing false reassurance that is not based on facts"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Changing the subject when the client discloses something painful"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Using active listening and clarifying questions to keep the message flowing"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Minimizing the client’s concern (for example, ‘it could be worse’)"}]}
rationales:
R1: Avoid (barrier). OpenStax lists providing false reassurances among barriers/nontherapeutic techniques.
R2: Avoid (barrier). Changing the subject is a listed barrier/nontherapeutic technique.
R3: Use (therapeutic). OpenStax: instead of changing the subject, use active listening and clarifying questions.
R4: Avoid (barrier). Minimizing remarks (e.g., ‘it could be worse’) are nontherapeutic barriers.
topic: NGN matrix — therapeutic communication barriers vs active listening
source_1_section: Barriers to Therapeutic Communication; Changing the Subject; Making Remarks That Are Minimizing; Providing False Reassurance

stem: A client with schizophrenia firmly believes hospital food is poisoned despite evidence to the contrary. After safety is assured, which nursing communication approach is most appropriate?
options:
A) Establish trust with therapeutic communication, then help the client focus on reality-based themes rather than arguing about the delusion
B) Agree that the food is poisoned to build rapport
C) Loudly argue until the client retracts the belief
D) Ignore the client and withhold all meals indefinitely
rationales:
A: Correct. OpenStax: for clients experiencing delusions, establish therapeutic communication and trust, then help focus on reality-based themes. Merck: delusions are erroneous beliefs maintained despite clear contradictory evidence — arguing facts alone rarely erases the belief; supportive, reality-oriented psychosocial care is part of treatment.
B: Incorrect. Reinforcing a delusion is not therapeutic and can worsen safety planning.
C: Incorrect. Confrontational arguing is nontherapeutic and may escalate distress.
D: Incorrect. Withholding meals is harmful and unrelated to therapeutic communication.
topic: Schizophrenia — focus on reality-based themes; do not argue the delusion
source_2_section: Symptom categories in schizophrenia — Delusions; Treatment

stem: A 5-week-old infant has forceful, nonbilious vomiting after feeds, still seems hungry, and has a firm olive-like mass in the right epigastrium. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
options:
A) Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
B) Uncomplicated physiologic gastroesophageal reflux with bilious emesis only
C) Typical viral gastroenteritis with predominantly watery diarrhea and no vomiting
D) Simple overfeeding without gastric outlet obstruction risk
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis typically presents at 3–6 weeks with forceful/projectile nonbilious emesis after eating; an olive-like pyloric mass may be palpable. NCBI StatPearls physiology text: IHPS presents with projectile nonbilious vomiting and a palpable olive; definitive treatment is pyloromyotomy after fluid/electrolyte correction.
B: Incorrect. Classic pyloric stenosis emesis is nonbilious; bilious vomiting suggests a different obstruction pattern.
C: Incorrect. The vignette centres on postprandial projectile vomiting and an olive mass, not diarrhea-predominant gastroenteritis.
D: Incorrect. Progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting with an olive mass indicates gastric outlet obstruction needing evaluation, not simple overfeeding.
topic: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis — projectile nonbilious vomiting and olive mass
source_1_section: Symptoms and Signs of Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis

stem: A public health nurse teaches daycare staff how to limit spread of hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Wash hands often with soap and water, especially after diaper changes and toileting
B) Clean and disinfect frequently touched surfaces and shared toys
C) Avoid close contact such as hugging or kissing persons who are infected
D) Rely on a routinely available HFMD vaccine in Canada/US as the primary prevention method
E) Avoid contact with open skin lesions and oral secretions (drool) when caring for ill children
rationales:
A: Correct. CDC and Merck emphasize meticulous hand hygiene, especially around diaper changes/stooling.
B: Correct. CDC: clean and disinfect frequently touched surfaces and shared items including toys.
C: Correct. CDC: avoid close contact with infected persons (hugging/kissing).
D: Incorrect. CDC: no HFMD vaccine in the United States; Merck: EV-A71 vaccines exist in China but none approved in the US.
E: Correct. Merck: avoid contact with open skin lesions and oral secretions to limit spread; CDC notes spread via blister fluid.
topic: HFMD prevention — hand hygiene, disinfection, avoid close contact/lesions; no US/Canada routine vaccine
source_1_title: About Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease
source_1_publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

stem: A 4-week-old has projectile nonbilious vomiting, remains eager to feed, and has a palpable olive-like epigastric mass. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Uncomplicated lactose intolerance without obstruction"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Acute appendicitis"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Simple overfeeding only"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Support airway/breathing as needed and keep NPO pending surgical evaluation"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Correct dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities with IV fluids as ordered before surgery"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Encourage unlimited formula immediately before emergent laparotomy without fluid resuscitation"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Prepare for pyloromyotomy after medical stabilization as ordered"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Discharge home without evaluation because vomiting is always normal at this age"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Hydration status and urine output"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Serum electrolytes (watch for hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis)"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Stock market indices"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Unrelated school grades of siblings"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Weight trend / ongoing vomiting frequency"}]}
rationales:
K1: Incorrect. Lactose intolerance does not produce an olive-like pyloric mass with classic projectile nonbilious pattern of IHPS.
K2: Correct. Merck/NCBI: IHPS — projectile nonbilious vomiting in early weeks with possible olive mass.
K3: Incorrect. Appendicitis is not the classic 3–6 week olive-mass presentation.
K4: Incorrect. Progressive projectile vomiting with olive mass is not simple overfeeding.
A1: Incorrect. While NPO pending evaluation may occur, the sourced priority actions are fluid/electrolyte correction and pyloromyotomy after stabilization.
A2: Correct. Merck: correct dehydration and electrolyte/acid-base abnormalities before pyloromyotomy.
A3: Incorrect. Feeding without correcting fluids/electrolytes and rushing without stabilization is unsafe.
A4: Correct. Definitive treatment is pyloromyotomy after medical stabilization (Merck/NCBI).
A5: Incorrect. This presentation requires prompt evaluation, not casual discharge.
P1: Correct. Dehydration risk is central; monitor hydration/urine output (Merck).
P2: Correct. Classic abnormality is hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (Merck/NCBI).
P3: Incorrect. Irrelevant parameter.
P4: Incorrect. Irrelevant parameter.
P5: Plausible monitoring but not selected as a keyed parameter for this item; electrolytes and hydration are the highest-yield sourced parameters.
topic: NGN bowtie — pyloric stenosis recognition; fluid/electrolyte correction; pyloromyotomy
source_1_section: Symptoms and Signs; Treatment of Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis

stem: A capable adult client asks an Ontario nurse for a romantic and sexual relationship while still receiving nursing care. Which response meets CNO accountabilities?
options:
A) Decline; any sexual relationship with a current client is sexual abuse and is never permissible
B) Accept if the client signs a consent form agreeing to the relationship
C) Accept after work hours because off-duty contact is not regulated
D) Accept if the nurse feels mutual attraction and documents it in the chart
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO: any sexual relationship with a patient is sexual abuse; there is no circumstance in which sexual interaction between a nurse and a patient is permissible. OpenStax: therapeutic relationships are never sexual.
B: Incorrect. Client agreement does not make a sexual relationship permissible under CNO/RHPA sexual-abuse rules.
C: Incorrect. Boundary and sexual-abuse accountabilities apply regardless of on- or off-duty timing while the therapeutic relationship exists (and for a defined period after).
D: Incorrect. Attraction or charting does not authorize a sexual or romantic relationship with a client.
topic: CNO — no sexual/romantic relationship with a current client (sexual abuse)
jurisdiction_note: CNO Professional Boundaries and Nurse-Client Relationships practice standard (in effect Mar 1, 2026) and RHPA Health Professions Procedural Code sexual abuse definition.

stem: A home-care client offers an Ontario nurse an expensive personal gift of jewellery. Which action best maintains professional boundaries?
options:
A) Decline the valuable personal gift; avoid gift exchange that blurs boundaries, and do not solicit gifts
B) Accept the jewellery if the client insists it is a thank-you
C) Accept the gift and give the client preferential visiting times in return
D) Ask the client’s family for a matching gift so the exchange feels fair
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO: nurses should avoid giving and accepting gifts that blur boundaries; gifts should never have more than token value and must not be solicited. OpenStax: therapeutic relationships are not social relationships in which personal exchanges meet the nurse’s needs.
B: Incorrect. Client insistence does not authorize accepting a valuable personal gift that risks conflict of interest and altered clinical judgment (CNO).
C: Incorrect. Preferential treatment in return for a gift is a boundary violation and conflict of interest.
D: Incorrect. Soliciting or expanding gift exchange worsens the boundary breach (CNO: do not solicit gifts).
topic: CNO boundaries — avoid non-token gifts; do not solicit gifts
jurisdiction_note: CNO Professional Boundaries and Nurse-Client Relationships — Gifts section.

stem: An Ontario nurse prepares a video visit that will discuss sensitive personal health information. Which action best protects privacy and security during virtual care?
options:
A) Use an encrypted clinical platform and ensure the interaction occurs in a private setting for nurse and client
B) Conduct the visit on speakerphone in a crowded staff lounge so colleagues can help
C) Use the nurse’s personal public social-media video chat without encryption safeguards
D) Record the entire visit to a public cloud folder shared with anyone who has the link
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO: ensure virtual interactions occur in a private setting and use technology encrypted to safeguard PHI. OpenStax: telemedicine requires secure/encrypted platforms and private settings.
B: Incorrect. A non-private environment risks unauthorized disclosure of PHI (CNO/OpenStax).
C: Incorrect. Personal public social-media tools do not meet clinical encryption/privacy expectations for PHI.
D: Incorrect. Publicly shared recordings violate confidentiality and security requirements.
topic: CNO virtual care — private setting and encrypted technology for PHI
jurisdiction_note: CNO Virtual Care practice guideline (updated November 2026) — privacy, confidentiality, and security; concordant with OpenStax telemedicine privacy guidance.

stem: Complete the cloze describing TeamSTEPPS check-back (closed-loop) communication for a verbal medication order.
options: {"template": "In TeamSTEPPS check-back, the {B1} initiates the message (for example, a verbal order). The {B2} accepts the message and provides feedback by repeating it. Then the original sender {B3} that the message was received as intended (for example, 'That's correct').", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "receiver only"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "sender"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "uninvolved bystander"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "medical records clerk with no role in the order"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "receiver"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "pharmacy robot without human verification"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "visitor in the hallway"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "social media commenter"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "ignores the read-back"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "double-checks / confirms"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "changes the dose silently without speaking"}, {"key": "B3d", "text": "leaves the unit immediately without verifying"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Incorrect. The sender initiates the message in check-back.
B1b: Correct. AHRQ/Pocket Guide: sender initiates the message.
B1c: Incorrect. An uninvolved bystander is not the sender.
B1d: Incorrect. The order sender (e.g., prescriber) initiates the clinical message.
B2a: Correct. Receiver accepts the message and provides feedback (repeat-back).
B2b: Incorrect. Check-back requires human closed-loop verification as described in TeamSTEPPS.
B2c: Incorrect. A hallway visitor is not the clinical message receiver.
B2d: Incorrect. Social media is not part of TeamSTEPPS check-back.
B3a: Incorrect. Closing the loop requires sender confirmation.
B3b: Correct. Sender double-checks to ensure the message was received as intended.
B3c: Incorrect. Silent dose changes without verification defeat closed-loop safety.
B3d: Incorrect. Leaving without verification fails closed-loop communication.

stem: A charge nurse must give formative feedback after a teammate omitted a safety check. Which approach best matches TeamSTEPPS mutual-support guidance?
options:
A) Give timely, respectful, behaviour-specific feedback directed toward improvement, preferably privately for negative feedback
B) Wait several weeks so emotions cool, then criticize the teammate’s personality in front of the whole unit
C) Assume the teammate is lazy and announce that judgment at the nursing station
D) Never give feedback unless you are the formal manager doing an annual evaluation
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS: formative feedback should be timely, respectful (behaviour not personality), specific, directed toward improvement, and considerate; negative feedback should not be given in front of other team members.
B: Incorrect. Delayed, personality-focused, public criticism violates timely/respectful/private guidance.
C: Incorrect. Attributing poor performance to internal traits (lazy) and public shaming undermine mutual support.
D: Incorrect. Any team member can give formative feedback; it is not limited to formal leaders or annual reviews.
topic: TeamSTEPPS formative feedback — timely, respectful, specific, private if negative
source_1_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
source_2_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)

stem: During a scheduled Ontario virtual visit, the nurse determines the client’s condition requires a hands-on physical assessment that cannot be completed virtually. Which action is most appropriate?
options:
A) Use professional judgment to arrange in-person care (or consult the team for other options) rather than continuing with an inadequate virtual assessment
B) Continue the video visit only and document that virtual care is always sufficient
C) End the call without arranging any alternative care pathway
D) Ask the client to self-diagnose using internet forums instead of clinical follow-up
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO: nurses exercise professional judgment to determine when the client’s condition warrants in-person care; if the nurse cannot provide in-person care, consult the team for other options. OpenStax: determine appropriateness of telemedicine visits and use secure, clinically appropriate approaches.
B: Incorrect. Virtual care is not always feasible or appropriate when in-person assessment is needed (CNO).
C: Incorrect. Ending contact without arranging alternatives abandons needed care.
D: Incorrect. Internet forums are not a substitute for clinical assessment and follow-up.
topic: CNO virtual care — escalate to in-person care when assessment requires it
jurisdiction_note: CNO Virtual Care practice guideline — nursing competence / when in-person care is warranted.
source_2_section: Take Action: Determining Appropriateness of Telemedicine Visits; Data Security and Privacy

stem: A community health nurse teaches a household about indoor radon and lung cancer risk. Which statement is most accurate?
options:
A) Testing the home is the only way to know the radon level; radon is linked to lung cancer risk
B) If you cannot smell radon, the level is always safe
C) Radon is visible as a coloured vapour, so visual inspection replaces testing
D) Only apartment buildings need testing; detached homes never have radon
rationales:
A: Correct. Health Canada and CDC: testing is the only way to know radon levels; radon exposure increases lung cancer risk (leading cause in non-smokers in Canada; major cause after smoking in US messaging).
B: Incorrect. Radon is odourless; smell cannot determine safety (Health Canada/CDC).
C: Incorrect. Radon is invisible; visual inspection cannot replace testing.
D: Incorrect. Guidance recommends testing homes/dwellings; radon can accumulate in many enclosed buildings.
topic: Radon — testing is the only way to know home levels; lung cancer risk
jurisdiction_note: Concordant teaching point with CDC/EPA: testing is the only way to know home radon levels. Canadian guideline threshold (200 Bq/m³) differs from US EPA action level (4 pCi/L); this item keys only the shared 'test to know' fact, not the numeric cut-off.
source_1_title: Radon: What you need to know (factsheet)

stem: Which community teaching points about radon exposure are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Test the home because testing is the only way to know the radon level
B) If levels are high, arrange professional radon reduction/mitigation
C) Smoking further increases lung cancer risk from radon exposure
D) Rely on household bleach scent to detect radon day to day
E) Assume a neighbour’s low result means your home is safe without testing
rationales:
A: Correct. Health Canada/CDC: testing is the only way to know levels.
B: Correct. Both advise mitigation/reduction systems when levels are high (thresholds differ by jurisdiction; action principle is shared).
C: Correct. Health Canada and CDC: smoking plus radon further elevates lung cancer risk.
D: Incorrect. Radon is odourless; scent of bleach does not detect radon.
E: Incorrect. Levels vary home to home; each dwelling needs its own test (Health Canada).
topic: Radon teaching SATA — test, mitigate if high, smoking increases risk
jurisdiction_note: Actions (test; mitigate if high; smoking increases risk) are concordant across Health Canada and CDC. Numeric action levels differ by country and are not keyed here.

stem: An 84-year-old develops new fluctuating confusion over 24 hours with marked inattention after a UTI. Which interpretation best distinguishes this presentation from typical dementia?
options:
A) Acute onset with fluctuating course and impaired attention suggests delirium and needs urgent evaluation of causes
B) Any confusion in older adults is dementia and never reversible
C) Sudden fluctuating confusion always means Alzheimer disease beginning overnight
D) Delirium never occurs in clients who also have dementia
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: delirium has sudden onset, fluctuating course, mainly impaired attention, often reversible when the cause is treated. OpenStax: delirium starts suddenly over hours to days and often comes and goes.
B: Incorrect. Mistaking delirium for dementia is a common error; delirium is often reversible (Merck).
C: Incorrect. Dementia/major NCD is typically gradual and progressive, not overnight (Merck/OpenStax).
D: Incorrect. Delirium commonly occurs superimposed on dementia (Merck).
topic: Delirium vs dementia — acute fluctuating onset with inattention
source_1_section: Overview of Delirium and Dementia — Differences Between Delirium and Dementia

stem: For each feature, select whether it is more characteristic of delirium or of typical dementia as described in authoritative comparisons.
options: {"columns": ["More characteristic of delirium", "More characteristic of dementia"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Sudden onset over hours to days with a relatively definite beginning"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Slow, gradual onset with an uncertain beginning point"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Attention and awareness prominently impaired early"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Primarily gradual memory/cognitive decline that is usually irreversible"}]}

R1: More characteristic of delirium. Merck/OpenStax: delirium begins suddenly over hours to days.
R2: More characteristic of dementia. Merck/OpenStax: dementia/major NCD has slow, gradual onset.
R3: More characteristic of delirium. Merck: delirium mainly affects attention and awareness.
R4: More characteristic of dementia. Merck/OpenStax: dementia is gradual, progressive, usually irreversible.

stem: An older adult with recurrent aspiration risk is receiving nursing care. Besides positioning and swallow strategies, which comfort/hygiene intervention helps reduce aspiration pneumonia risk?
options:
A) Optimize oral hygiene (for example, assisted toothbrushing/denture care) to reduce harmful oral bacteria
B) Stop all oral care because moisture always increases aspiration
C) Keep the mouth colonized intentionally to 'train' immunity
D) Replace oral care with routine application of petroleum products into the airway
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: optimizing oral hygiene may help prevent pneumonia/abscess in patients who repeatedly aspirate. OpenStax: improve oral hygiene and assist with toothbrushing/denture care to decrease harmful oral bacteria.
B: Incorrect. Oral care is a prevention strategy, not something to eliminate solely for aspiration risk.
C: Incorrect. Colonization with oral pathogens increases pneumonia risk after aspiration.
D: Incorrect. Putting petroleum products into the airway is unsafe and not an oral-hygiene strategy.
topic: Aspiration pneumonia prevention — oral hygiene / dental care
source_1_section: Prevention of Chemical Pneumonitis and Aspiration Pneumonia
source_2_title: 11.7 Disorders of the Lower Respiratory System: Pneumonia and Aspiration
source_2_section: Evidence-Based Practice: Strategies to Prevent Aspiration Pneumonia

stem: An older adult develops sudden fluctuating confusion and inattention over 18 hours during hospitalization for pneumonia. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Typical slow-onset Alzheimer dementia as the sole explanation"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Delirium (acute confusional state), often secondary to acute illness"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Uncomplicated loneliness without cognitive change"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Stable lifelong intellectual disability without acute change"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Urgently evaluate and treat reversible contributors (e.g., infection, medications, metabolic issues) while supporting safety"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Provide a calm supportive environment; avoid restraints when possible"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Assume the change is permanent dementia and cancel medical workup"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Discharge immediately without assessing causes of acute confusion"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Start high-dose recreational sedatives without clinical assessment"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Mental status / attention and fluctuation pattern"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Vital signs and clinical indicators of the precipitating illness"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Stock ticker symbols"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Unrelated celebrity news headlines"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Fashion trends on social media"}]}
rationales:
K1: Incorrect. Overnight fluctuating confusion is not explained solely as typical gradual Alzheimer dementia (Merck/OpenStax).
K2: Correct. Sudden fluctuating confusion with inattention is delirium, often from acute illness (Merck/OpenStax).
K3: Incorrect. Marked acute cognitive change is not uncomplicated loneliness.
K4: Incorrect. A new acute change is not a stable lifelong disability pattern.
A1: Correct. Delirium management centres on identifying/treating underlying causes; needs immediate attention (Merck/OpenStax).
A2: Correct. OpenStax: supportive environment; avoid restraints. Merck: treat underlying condition.
A3: Incorrect. Cancelling workup risks missing reversible causes.
A4: Incorrect. Acute delirium requires evaluation, not casual discharge.
A5: Incorrect. Unassessed sedatives can worsen delirium and are unsafe.
P1: Correct. Track mental status/attention and fluctuation (core delirium features).
P2: Correct. Monitor vitals/illness indicators tied to precipitants (e.g., infection).
P3: Incorrect. Irrelevant parameter.
P4: Incorrect. Irrelevant parameter.
P5: Incorrect. Irrelevant parameter.
topic: NGN bowtie — delirium recognition; treat causes; supportive care; monitor mentation/vitals
source_1_section: Overview; Differences Between Delirium and Dementia
source_2_section: Diagnosing Delirium; Nursing Treatment of Delirium

stem: A nurse must address a colleague’s hostile, publicly demeaning behaviour that is undermining teamwork and safety. Using TeamSTEPPS DESC guidance, which action is most appropriate?
options:
A) Hold a timely private discussion using “I” statements and aim for a constructive win-win resolution
B) Confront the colleague loudly in front of the client so others witness accountability
C) Ignore the behaviour because interpersonal conflict never affects patient safety
D) Post a detailed complaint on social media before speaking with the colleague
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS DESC: choose a private location (not in front of patient/team), use “I” statements, time the discussion, and work toward a win-win solution for interpersonal conflict.
B: Incorrect. DESC advises a private location so parties can focus on resolving conflict rather than saving face; public confrontation can escalate harm.
C: Incorrect. DESC is indicated when hostile/harassing behaviours put patients or staff at risk of harm.
D: Incorrect. Social-media airing is not a TeamSTEPPS conflict-resolution method and breaches professionalism.
topic: TeamSTEPPS DESC — private timely discussion with I-statements for interpersonal conflict
source_1_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
source_1_section: Tool: DESC — strategic use (location, I statements, win-win)

stem: A nurse prepares to use TeamSTEPPS DESC for interpersonal conflict. Which actions are indicated?
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Choose a private location away from the client and other team members"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Use “I” statements rather than blaming statements"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Aim for a win-win solution the parties can live with"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Publicly humiliate the colleague to force immediate compliance"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. AHRQ DESC: private location not in front of patient/team.
R2: Indicated. AHRQ: use I statements; OpenStax supports assertive professional communication.
R3: Indicated. AHRQ: work on win-win despite interpersonal conflict.
R4: Not indicated. Public humiliation contradicts private, constructive DESC guidance.

stem: During a sterile procedure, a nurse notices a colleague’s glove touch a nonsterile surface. Which TeamSTEPPS situation-monitoring action best describes speaking up to correct the break?
options:
A) Cross-monitoring — watching each other’s back as a team safety net to catch errors early
B) Spying — covertly gathering evidence to punish the colleague later
C) Ignoring the break to avoid hurting the colleague’s feelings
D) Waiting until after patient harm occurs before discussing sterility
rationales:
A: Correct. AHRQ: cross-monitoring means monitoring others’ actions, providing a safety net, and catching mistakes early (“watching each other’s back”); example includes calling out a break in sterile technique.
B: Incorrect. AHRQ explicitly states cross-monitoring is not spying.
C: Incorrect. Failing to interrupt an error misses the purpose of cross-monitoring as error prevention.
D: Incorrect. Cross-monitoring aims to correct issues before harm occurs.
topic: TeamSTEPPS cross-monitoring — safety net to catch errors early (not spying)
source_1_publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)

stem: An Ontario nurse realizes recent untreated health issues are impairing concentration and may endanger clients. Which response best meets CNO Code of Conduct accountabilities?
options:
A) Self-reflect, seek help, and do not practise while impaired by any substance or unsafe health state
B) Continue full independent practice while keeping the health issue secret from all supports
C) Use alcohol at work to steady nerves so clients are unaware
D) Ask a friend without nursing credentials to cover medication administration unsupervised
rationales:
A: Correct. CNO Code 6.7–6.8: nurses self-reflect on health and seek help if health affects safe practice, and do not practise when impaired by any substance. OpenStax: impaired practice endangers clients; nurses must address impairment appropriately.
B: Incorrect. Secrecy without seeking help conflicts with the duty to seek help when health affects safe practice.
C: Incorrect. Practising while substance-impaired is expressly prohibited (CNO 6.8).
D: Incorrect. Unregulated coverage of nursing medication administration does not meet safe, competent care or accountability requirements.
topic: CNO Code — seek help if health affects safe practice; do not practise impaired
jurisdiction_note: CNO Code of Conduct Principle 6 (updated March 2026) — fitness/self-health and impairment accountabilities.
source_2_section: Ethical Care and Safety — Table 5.2 impaired colleague

stem: A client with contamination obsessions and washing compulsions begins evidence-based psychotherapy. Which treatment element is essential?
options:
A) Gradual exposure to anxiety triggers while preventing the usual compulsive ritual (exposure and response prevention)
B) Encouraging longer and more frequent washing until anxiety disappears permanently
C) Arguing that the client’s obsessions are deliberately invented for attention
D) Withholding all explanation of treatment because insight never varies in OCD
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: CBT with exposure and response/ritual prevention gradually exposes the client to triggers while preventing rituals.
B: Incorrect. Increasing rituals reinforces the OCD cycle rather than preventing the compulsive response.
C: Incorrect. Obsessions are unwanted/intrusive; arguing or blaming is nontherapeutic.
D: Incorrect. Insight varies; education and collaborative ERP are standard.
topic: OCD — exposure and response (ritual) prevention as essential CBT element

stem: For a client with OCD starting exposure and response prevention, which nursing actions are indicated?
options: {"columns": ["Indicated", "Not indicated"], "rows": [{"key": "R1", "text": "Support gradual exposure to triggers while the client refrains from the usual compulsion"}, {"key": "R2", "text": "Teach relaxation techniques to help reduce anxiety"}, {"key": "R3", "text": "Mock the client’s obsessions as attention-seeking"}, {"key": "R4", "text": "Educate about prescribed SSRI therapy and monitor for side effects when ordered"}]}
rationales:
R1: Indicated. ERP requires exposure with response prevention (Merck/OpenStax).
R2: Indicated. OpenStax nursing interventions include teaching relaxation techniques.
R3: Not indicated. Obsessions are unwanted; mocking is nontherapeutic and harmful.
R4: Indicated. SSRIs are pharmacologic treatment; nurses monitor/educate (Merck/OpenStax).
topic: NGN matrix — OCD ERP support, relaxation, SSRI education; do not mock obsessions
source_2_section: Treatment of OCD; Nursing Interventions for OCD

stem: A client who abruptly stopped long-term opioid use has yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, and piloerection. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options:
A) Findings fit opioid withdrawal; assess with a validated scale (e.g., COWS) and manage symptoms
B) Findings fit opioid overdose; the priority is that pupils are always pinpoint
C) Opioid withdrawal is usually immediately life-threatening like status epilepticus and needs deep sedation first
D) These autonomic signs only occur with alcohol withdrawal, never opioid withdrawal
rationales:
A: Correct. Merck: mydriasis, piloerection, lacrimation/rhinorrhea, and yawning are specific opioid-withdrawal signs. OpenStax: use COWS/CINA and focus on symptom management in withdrawal.
B: Incorrect. Overdose triad includes pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression (OpenStax); mydriasis fits withdrawal more than typical overdose.
C: Incorrect. Merck: opioid withdrawal is distressingly symptomatic but not itself typically life-threatening.
D: Incorrect. These signs are described for opioid withdrawal (Merck).
topic: Opioid withdrawal — yawning, mydriasis, piloerection, lacrimation; COWS/symptom management
source_2_section: Opioid Intoxication; Planning Nursing Care for Opioid Withdrawal/Detoxification

stem: A client 24 hours after stopping heroin has anxiety, yawning, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, gooseflesh, and abdominal cramps. Complete the bowtie.
options: {"conditions": [{"key": "K1", "text": "Opioid overdose with respiratory depression"}, {"key": "K2", "text": "Opioid withdrawal"}, {"key": "K3", "text": "Serotonin syndrome"}, {"key": "K4", "text": "Hypoglycemia alone"}], "actions": [{"key": "A1", "text": "Assess withdrawal severity with a validated scale (e.g., COWS) and provide ordered symptom-focused care"}, {"key": "A2", "text": "Administer high-dose naloxone repeatedly as the only intervention for these findings"}, {"key": "A3", "text": "Supportive monitoring and anticipate agonist/partial-agonist therapy (e.g., methadone or buprenorphine) per protocol"}, {"key": "A4", "text": "Encourage immediate unsupervised return to street opioid use to “self-treat”"}, {"key": "A5", "text": "Ignore autonomic signs because withdrawal never needs nursing assessment"}], "parameters": [{"key": "P1", "text": "Vital signs and withdrawal symptom trend"}, {"key": "P2", "text": "Hydration and gastrointestinal symptom control"}, {"key": "P3", "text": "Pupil size only once at admission with no reassessment"}, {"key": "P4", "text": "Whether the client can leave without any safety or follow-up plan"}, {"key": "P5", "text": "Response to ordered medications for withdrawal symptoms"}]}
rationales:
K1: Incorrect. Overdose features respiratory depression/pinpoint pupils; this vignette matches withdrawal.
K2: Correct. Yawning, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, piloerection, cramps fit opioid withdrawal (Merck).
K3: Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome is a different toxidrome not supported by this cue set.
K4: Incorrect. Hypoglycemia alone does not explain this autonomic cluster.
A1: Correct. OpenStax: assess with COWS and manage symptoms.
A2: Incorrect. Naloxone is for overdose/respiratory depression, not first-line for this withdrawal picture.
A3: Correct. Merck: substitution with methadone or buprenorphine plus supportive care.
A4: Incorrect. Unsupervised return to use is unsafe and not treatment.
A5: Incorrect. Withdrawal requires assessment and supportive management.
P1: Correct. Trend vital signs and withdrawal symptoms to guide care.
P2: Incorrect. Although GI comfort matters, the keyed monitoring priorities here are vital/withdrawal trends and medication response.
P3: Incorrect. Single unchecked pupil assessment is inadequate monitoring.
P4: Incorrect. Discharge without plan is unsafe.
P5: Correct. Monitor response to ordered withdrawal medications.

stem: Which teaching point is most important for preventing diabetic foot complications?
options:
A) Examine the feet daily and wear properly fitting footwear; do not walk barefoot
B) Ignore small cuts because neuropathy means injuries cannot become infected
C) Soak feet in the hottest water tolerable without testing temperature first
D) Apply moisturizing lotion heavily between the toes every hour
rationales:
A: Correct. Diabetes Canada: examine feet daily and wear properly fitting footwear. Merck: inspect daily; avoid walking barefoot; well-fitting shoes.
B: Incorrect. Diabetes Canada: unnoticed injuries can become infected and lead to serious complications.
C: Incorrect. Diabetes Canada: test bath water with the hand first because neuropathy may blunt heat sensation.
D: Incorrect. Diabetes Canada: moisturize if dry but not between the toes (maceration/infection risk).
topic: Diabetic foot care — daily inspection, proper footwear, avoid barefoot

stem: Which actions belong in a safe daily diabetic foot-care routine? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Examine feet and legs daily for cuts, blisters, or colour changes
B) Wear properly fitting footwear
C) Test bath water with the hand before stepping in
D) Walk barefoot indoors to “toughen” the skin
E) Apply lotion between the toes to keep the web spaces wet
F) Seek care promptly for corns, calluses, or wounds that are not healing
rationales:
A: Correct. Diabetes Canada/Merck: daily foot examination.
B: Correct. Properly fitting footwear is recommended.
C: Correct. Test bath water with the hand first.
D: Incorrect. Merck: avoid walking barefoot.
E: Incorrect. Lotion not between the toes (Diabetes Canada).
F: Correct. Diabetes Canada advises professional care for corns/calluses/problems; Merck stresses early attention to ulcers/injury.

stem: A community nurse teaches home fire safety. Which instruction about smoke alarms is best?
options:
A) Test smoke alarms every month and replace units that are more than 10 years old
B) Testing once every 10 years is sufficient if the alarm looks clean
C) Smoke alarms are unnecessary if the home has a fire extinguisher
D) Never place alarms near bedrooms because nighttime waking is harmful
rationales:
A: Correct. Health Canada and NFPA: test monthly; replace alarms more than 10 years old.
B: Incorrect. Monthly testing is required; a 10-year interval is for replacement, not testing.
C: Incorrect. Smoke alarms provide early warning and are not replaced by extinguishers alone.
D: Incorrect. Install alarms in/near bedrooms and on every level, including basement.
topic: Smoke alarms — monthly testing; replace units older than 10 years

stem: Which home smoke-alarm actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options:
A) Install alarms in bedrooms, outside sleeping areas, and on every level including the basement
B) Test alarms monthly using the test button
C) Replace alarms that fail testing or are more than 10 years old
D) Disable alarms permanently after one nuisance alarm from cooking
E) Create and practise a home fire escape plan
rationales:
A: Correct. Health Canada/NFPA placement guidance for bedrooms, hallways/outside sleeping areas, every level including basement.
B: Correct. Monthly testing is required.
C: Correct. Replace failed or >10-year-old units.
D: Incorrect. Do not permanently disable alarms; investigate false alarms and keep working devices (Health Canada).
E: Correct. Both advise having/practising an escape plan alongside working alarms.
topic: Smoke-alarm SATA — placement, monthly test, replace old units, escape plan

stem: Complete the TeamSTEPPS DESC mnemonic used for conflict resolution.
options: {"template": "D = {B1}; E = {B2}; S = {B3}; C = {B4}.", "blanks": {"B1": [{"key": "B1a", "text": "Describe the specific situation"}, {"key": "B1b", "text": "Deny that conflict exists"}, {"key": "B1c", "text": "Delay all feedback forever"}, {"key": "B1d", "text": "Delegate blame to the client"}], "B2": [{"key": "B2a", "text": "Express concerns about the action"}, {"key": "B2b", "text": "Erase the medical record"}, {"key": "B2c", "text": "Encourage public shaming"}, {"key": "B2d", "text": "Exclude safety concerns"}], "B3": [{"key": "B3a", "text": "Suggest other alternatives"}, {"key": "B3b", "text": "Silence the colleague permanently"}, {"key": "B3c", "text": "Substitute insults for solutions"}, {"key": "B3d", "text": "Skip straight to punishment"}], "B4": [{"key": "B4a", "text": "State the consequences"}, {"key": "B4b", "text": "Conceal outcomes from everyone"}, {"key": "B4c", "text": "Celebrate personal victory"}, {"key": "B4d", "text": "Cancel the conversation mid-sentence without closure"}]}}
rationales:
B1a: Correct. D — Describe the specific situation.
B1b: Incorrect. Denial is not Describe.
B1c: Incorrect. DESC includes timely discussion, not endless delay.
B1d: Incorrect. Clients are not blamed as the Describe step.
B2a: Correct. E — Express concerns about the action.
B2b: Incorrect. Not Express.
B2c: Incorrect. Public shaming is contrary to DESC.
B2d: Incorrect. Safety concerns must be addressed.
B3a: Correct. S — Suggest other alternatives.
B3b: Incorrect. Not Suggest.
B3c: Incorrect. Insults are not alternatives.
B3d: Incorrect. Suggest alternatives before punitive framing.
B4a: Correct. C — Consequences should be stated.
B4b: Incorrect. Consequences are stated, not concealed.
B4c: Incorrect. Focus on what is right, not who wins.
B4d: Incorrect. DESC aims for constructive closure.
